## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## The Sixteen Great Chapters (Mahāvāra)
## Explanation of the Chapter on Enactment (Paññattivāra)

In the Dispensation of the Buddha, who is surrounded by pure Arahants and whose body is the Dhamma,
The Vinaya called Parivāra, which follows immediately after the Khandhakas (Mahāvagga and Cūḷavagga),
Was included in the Council. Setting aside the methods of decision previously mentioned in that Parivāra text,
I shall now compose an explanation of the terms with obscure meanings.

In that Parivāra text, the summary meaning of the question beginning with "What was enacted by that Blessed One..." is as follows: That Blessed One, requested by the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta—who, with a surge of reverence and great respect for the True Dhamma, placed his joined palms upon his head—enacted the Vinaya rules based on the ten reasons for the long-lasting of the Dispensation. That Blessed One, knowing the time of enactment for each training rule, seeing the ten reasons for the enactment of each training rule; furthermore, knowing through the knowledge of past lives and so forth, seeing with the divine eye, knowing through the three knowledges or the six supernormal powers, seeing with the "All-seeing Eye" (Samantacakkhu) which is unobstructed in all objects, knowing with the wisdom capable of knowing all things, seeing even those material forms beyond the range of the eyes of beings, such as those behind walls, with the extremely pure physical eye, knowing with the penetrative wisdom which has concentration as its proximate cause and which accomplishes one's own benefit, seeing with the teaching wisdom which has compassion as its proximate cause and which accomplishes the benefit of others; that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, asked: "Where was that first Pārājika enacted? Concerning whom was it enacted? On what matter was it enacted? Is there an enactment there... who brought it down in succession?"
138:
In the question and answer, the statement "That Blessed One, knowing, seeing, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, enacted the first Pārājika" is merely a restatement of the initial phrase found in the question. "Where was it enacted? It was enacted in Vesālī. Concerning whom? Concerning Sudinna, the son of Kalanda." In this manner, each term is questioned and answered again here.

"Should any bhikkhu engage in sexual intercourse, he is defeated and no longer in communion"—this is the single enactment (paññatti). "Even with a female animal" and "without renouncing the training"—these two, taught by way of the cases of the monkey and the Vajjiputtakas, are the additional enactments (anupaññatti). By this much, two parts of the question "Is there an enactment, an additional enactment, or an enactment before an offense in that Pārājika?" have been answered. To answer the third part, it is said: "There is no enactment before an offense (anuppannapaññatti) in that Pārājika." What is called an enactment before an offense is a rule enacted before a fault has occurred; that occurs only for the bhikkhunīs by way of the eight weighty rules (garudhamma), and not elsewhere. Therefore, it is said: "There is no enactment before an offense in that Pārājika."

It is called a universal enactment (sabbattha-paññatti) because it is enacted for all places, both in the Middle Country and in the border regions. For, these four training rules—ordination by a group of five including a Vinaya-expert, multi-layered sandals, frequent bathing, and skin rugs—are enacted only for the Middle Country. An offense is incurred through these only in the Middle Country, not in the border regions. All remaining training rules are called universal enactments.

It is called a common enactment (sādhāraṇa-paññatti) because it pertains to both bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs. A training rule enacted for bhikkhus alone or for bhikkhunīs alone is called a specific enactment (asādhāraṇa-paññatti). Although this first Pārājika arose as a case concerning a bhikkhu, it was also enacted for bhikkhunīs: "Should any bhikkhunī, with consensual intent, engage in sexual intercourse, even with a male animal, she is defeated and no longer in communion." For them, there is only no account of the "decided cases" (vinīta-vatthu), but the training rule itself exists. Therefore, it is called a "common enactment." The same method applies to "enactment for both" (ubhato-paññatti). Here, only the phrasing (name) is different. It is a common enactment because it pertains to both bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs; it is an enactment for both because it is enacted for both. There is no difference in meaning.

In the phrase "Should any person have an offense, he should disclose it," it is called "included in the introduction" (nidānogadha) because all offenses are included therein; the meaning is "entered into the introduction." "By the second recitation" means that although it is included in the introduction and belongs to the introduction, "Now these..."
139:
It reaches the state of being recited by the second recitation (uddesa) beginning with "Cattāro pārājikā dhammā". "Of the four failures (catunnāṃ vipattīnaṃ)" refers to the failure in virtue (sīla-vipatti) and so forth. In truth, the first two groups of offenses are called failure in virtue, while the remaining five groups of offenses are called failure in conduct (ācāra-vipatti). Wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) and extremist view (antaggāhika-diṭṭhi) are called failure in view (diṭṭhi-vipatti). The six training rules prescribed for the sake of livelihood are called failure in livelihood (ājīva-vipatti). Thus, among these four failures, this Pārājika is called failure in virtue.

"By one origin (ekena samuṭṭhānena)" refers to arising from a single origin consisting of two factors. Here, although the mind is a factor, the offense is committed through the body. Therefore, it is said, "It arises from the body and from the mind." "It is settled by two settlements (dvīhi samathehi sammati)" means it is appeased by two ways of settlement. When asked in person, "Have you committed an offense?", if one acknowledges, "Yes, I have committed an offense," at that very moment, quarrels, disputes, and strife are appeased. It is then possible to remove that person and perform the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā. Thus, it is settled by the two settlements: removal in the presence (sammukhā-vinaya) and acting in accordance with the acknowledgement (paṭiññātakaraṇa). No danger arises because of that legal issue of offense (āpattādhikaraṇa). The statement in the Section on Regulations (Paññatti-vagga) mentioned above, "It is not settled by any settlement," is said with reference to the meaning that it is not possible to apply those settlements to make it a non-offense.

"The regulation is the discipline (paññatti vinayo)" means the training rule prescribed as the matrix (mātikā) taught in the manner beginning with "Whatever monk (yo pana bhikkhu)". "Vibhatti" refers to the word-by-word analysis (padabhājanīya). The name "Vibhatti" is indeed a name for the Vibhaṅga. "Non-restraint (asaṃvara)" means transgression. "Restraint (saṃvara)" means non-transgression. "For whom it proceeds (yesaṃ vattati)" means for those persons who have mastered the entire Vinaya Piṭaka and its Commentaries. Those persons uphold this first Pārājika both in text (pāḷi) and in meaning (attha); for one who does not know the entire Vinaya Piṭaka cannot know the meaning of this Pārājika. "By whom was it brought? (kenābhataṃ)" is the question of who has brought this first Pārājika, both in text and meaning, down to the present day. "Brought by lineage (paramparābhataṃ)" means it was brought by a succession of disciples.

Now, to show the lineage by which it was brought, the ancient Great Elders (Mahātheras) [composed] verses in the manner beginning with "Upāli and Dāsaka"...
140: (The ancient great elders) have placed (the verses). The words that should be said regarding those verses have already been stated in the Explanation of the Introduction (Nidāna-vaṇṇanā). In this same manner, the decision should be understood in the questions and answers (pucchā-vissajjanā) of the training rules beginning with the second Pārājika.  ## The Explanation of the Section on Enactments (Paññatti-vāra) in the Mahāvibhaṅga is finished.  ## The Explanation of the Section on the Commission of Offenses (Katāpattivāra) and others  Following this Section on Enactments, there are the seven sections (vāra) whose meanings are clear: the Section on the Commission of Offenses (Katāpattivāra) beginning with "How many offenses does one who engages in sexual intercourse commit?"; the Section on Failures (Vipattivāra) beginning with "To how many of the four failures do the offenses of one who engages in sexual intercourse belong?"; the Section on Inclusion (Saṅgahavāra) beginning with "By how many of the seven classes of offenses are the offenses of one who engages in sexual intercourse included?"; the Section on Origins (Samuṭṭhānavāra) beginning with "By how many of the six origins of offenses do the offenses of one who engages in sexual intercourse arise?"; the Section on Legal Processes (Adhikaraṇavāra) beginning with "Which of the four legal processes is the offense of one who engages in sexual intercourse?"; the Section on Settlement (Samathavāra) beginning with "By how many of the seven settlements are the offenses of one who engages in sexual intercourse settled?"; and the Section on Accumulation (Samuccayavāra) which immediately follows that Section on Settlement.  After those seven sections, another Section on Enactments is stated again by way of the word 'condition' (paccaya), such as "Where was the Pārājika offense enacted on account of engaging in sexual intercourse?"; and by way of that Section on Enactments, seven other sections such as the Section on the Commission of Offenses, similar to the previous ones, are also stated. Thus, these other eight sections are also clear in meaning. In this way, these eight and the previous eight make sixteen sections shown in the Mahāvibhaṅga. After that, by the same method, sixteen sections also appear in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga. Thus, the thirty-two sections in the Twofold Vibhaṅga (Ubhatovibhaṅga) should be understood according to the method of the Pali text. In these sections, there is nothing that has not been decided previously.  ## The Explanation of the Sixteen Great Sections in both the Mahāvibhaṅga and the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga is finished.

## Explanation of the Headings of Origins

In the discourse explaining the origins (samuṭṭhāna) immediately following those 32 sections, "Anattā iti nicchayā" means they have been determined as non-self. "Sabhāgadhammānaṃ" refers to conditioned things (saṅkhata-dhamma) that are similar in nature, such as being impermanent. "Nāmamattaṃ na nāyati" means even the mere name is not apparent or known. "Dukkhahāni" means the destruction of suffering. "Khandhakā yā ca mātikā" means there are the Khandhakas and the Mātikā. Alternatively, this phrase "Khandhakā yā ca mātikā" is the original Pali text itself. "Samuṭṭhānaṃ niyato kataṃ" means an origin that is fixed. By this statement, one should understand the inclusion of the group of three training rules: the Bhūtārocana training rule, the Corivuṭṭhāpana training rule, and the Ananuññāta training rule. Indeed, only these three training rules have fixed origins that are not mixed with others.

"Sambhedaṃ nidānañcaññaṃ" refers to other mixed origins and the nidāna (setting). Here, by the word "sambheda," one should understand mixed origins. This is because, excluding those three training rules, the remaining training rules have mixed origins. By the word "nidāna," the setting, known as the place where the training rules were laid down, should be understood. "Sutte dissanti uparī" means these three—the fixed origin, the mixed origin, and the nidāna of the training rules—are apparent in the Parivāra text itself. Among those three, in the previous method of the section on laying down rules (paññatti-vāra) such as "It originates from one origin, from the body and the mind," the fixed origin and the mixed origin are apparent. As for what is called the nidāna, it is apparent above as: "Laid down in Vesālī, Rājagaha, Sāvatthī, Āḷavī, Kosambī, among the Sakkas, and among the Bhaggas." It should be understood as being apparent in the Parivāra text that follows.

The meaning of the verse "Vibhaṅge dvīsu" is: Whatever training rule is laid down in the two Vibhaṅgas and recited by monks and nuns on the Uposatha day, I shall speak of the origin of that training rule as is appropriate; listen to that origin from me.

"Sañcarittānubhāsanañca" refers to the Sañcaritta origin and the Samanubhāsana origin. "Atirekañca cīvaraṃ" refers to the Atirekacīvara origin, also known as the Kathina origin. "Lomāni padasodhammo" refers to the Eḷakaloma origin and the Padasodhamma origin. "Bhūtaṃ saṃvidhānena ca" refers to the Bhūtārocana origin and the Addhāna origin, which is traveling by arrangement. "Theyyadesanācorī ca" refers to the Theyyasattha origin, the Dhammadesanā origin (teaching Dhamma), and the Corivuṭṭhāpana origin. "Ananuññātāya terasa" refers to these 13 origins, including the one concerning a nun not permitted by her parents or husband. "Sadisā idha dissare" means that in these two Vibhaṅgas, for each of these 13 headings of origins, other similar origins are also apparent.
142:
There are also the Eḷakaloma (sheep's wool) training rule and the Padasodhamma (teaching Dhamma word by word) training rule. "Bhūtaṃ saṃvidhānena ca" refers to telling of true attainments (Bhūtārocana) and traveling by arrangement (saṃvidhitvā addhānappaṭipajjana). Traveling with thieves (Theyyasattha), teaching Dhamma to one who is not ill and has an umbrella in hand (Dhammadesanā), and ordaining a female thief (Corivuṭṭhāpana) are also included. "Ananuññātāya terasā" refers to these 13 origins concerning a woman not permitted by her parents or husband. "Sadisā idha dissare" means that in these two Vibhaṅgas, for each of these 13 headings of origins, other similar origins are also seen.

## Explanation of the Origin of the First Pārājika

Now, to show those origins, the verse beginning with "Methunaṃ sukkasaṃsaggo" is spoken. In that passage, "Methunaṃ" is the single heading of origin (samuṭṭhāna-sīsa) called the first Pārājika, and the remaining training rules are similar to that first Pārājika in terms of origin. In that passage, "Sukkasaṃsaggo" refers to the Sukkavissaṭṭhi training rule and the Kāyasaṃsagga training rule. "Aniyatā paṭhamikā" is the first Aniyata training rule. "Pubbūpaparipācitā" refers to the training rule "knowing a monk who has gone before" and the training rule on eating food arranged by a nun (bhikkhunī-paripācita-piṇḍapāta). "Raho bhikkhuniyā sahā" is the training rule on sitting in private with a nun (raho-nisajja).

"Sabhojane raho dve ca" refers to the training rule on intruding and sitting in a house where food is being eaten (anupakhajja-nisajja) and the two training rules on sitting in private (raho-nisajja). "Aṅguli udake hasanti" refers to the training rule on poking with fingers (aṅguli-patodaka) and the training rule on playing in water (udake hasadhamma). "Pahāre uggire ceva" refers to the training rule on giving a blow (pahāra-dāna) and the training rule on threatening with the palm (tala-sattika-uggiraṇa). "Tepaññāsā ca sekhiyā" refers to the 53 Sekhiya training rules mentioned at the end of the Khuddaka-vaṇṇanā, such as the one on wearing the robe all around (parimaṇḍala-nivāsana).

"Adhakkhagāmāvassutā" refers to the Adhakkhaka training rule for nuns, the training rule on traveling between villages (gāmantara-gamana), and the training rule on a lustful nun receiving food or snacks from the hand of a lustful man (avassutā avassutassa hatthato khādanīya-bhojanīya-ggahaṇa). "Talamaṭṭhañca suddhikā" refers to the training rules on striking with the palm (tala-ghātaka), smoothing with lac (jatu-maṭṭha), and receiving water for cleansing (udaka-suddhika), etc. "Vassaṃvuṭṭhā ca ovādaṃ" refers to the training rule on traveling five or six leagues after the rains retreat and the training rule on not going for exhortation (ovādāya agamana). "Nānubandhe pavattiniံ" refers to the training rule stated as: "If a nun does not follow her preceptor (pavattinī) who ordained her for two years."
143:
"Ime sikkhā" means "Imā sikkhāyo" (these training rules). Here, a change of gender has been made. "Kāyamanasikā katā" means they have been made with originations arising from body and mind.

## Commentary on the Origination of the Second Pārājika

"Adinnaṃ" is one primary origination called either Adinnādāna or the Second Pārājika. The remaining training rules are similar to that Second Pārājika in terms of origination. Among those training rules, "Viggahuttarī" refers to the Manussaviggaha training rule and the Uttarimanussadhamma training rule. "Duṭṭhullā attakāminaṃ" refers to the Duṭṭhullavācā training rule and the Attakāmapāricariya training rule. "Amūlā aññabhāgiyā" refers to the two Duṭṭhadosa training rules. "Aniyatā dutiyikā" refers to the second Aniyata training rule.

"Acchinde pariṇāmane" refers to the training rule on taking back a robe after having given it oneself, and the training rule on diverting communal gains to oneself. "Musā omasapesuṇā" refers to the Musāvāda training rule, the Omasavāda training rule, and the Bhikkhupesuñña training rule. "Duṭṭhullā pathavīkhaṇe" refers to the Duṭṭhullāpatti-ārocana training rule and the earth-digging training rule. "Bhūtaṃ aññāya ujjhāpe" refers to the Bhūtagāma training rule, the Aññavādaka training rule, and the Ujjhāpanaka training rule.

"Nikkaḍḍhanaṃ siñcanañcā" refers to the training rule on expelling from a monastery and the training rule on sprinkling water on grass and so on. "Āmisahetu bhuttāvī" refers to the training rule "Nuns are taught for the sake of material gain" and the invitation (pavāraṇā) training rule involving offering non-allowable food to a monk who has already finished his meal. "Ehi anādari bhiṃsā" refers to the training rule "Come, friend, to the village or...", the Anādariya training rule, and the training rule on frightening a monk. "Apanidhe ca jīvitaṃ" refers to the training rule on hiding bowls and so on, and the training rule on intentionally depriving a living being of life.

"Jānaṃ sappāṇakaṃ kammaṃ" refers to the training rule on using water known to contain living beings and the training rule on reopening a settled legal issue. "Ūnasaṃvāsanasānā" refers to the training rule on ordaining someone under twenty years of age, the training rule on associating with an expelled monk, and the training rule on associating with an expelled novice. "Sahadhammikaṃ vilekhā" refers to the Sahadhammikavuccamāna training rule and the training rule that comes as "They lead to anxiety." "Moho amūlakena ca" refers to the Mohanaka Pācittiya training rule and the training rule on groundless accusation of a Saṅghādisesa offense.

"Kukkuccaṃ dhammikaṃ cīvaraṃ datvā" refers to the Kukkuccaupadahana training rule, the training rule on complaining after giving consent to legal acts, and the training rule on complaining after giving a robe. "Pariṇāmeyya puggale" refers to diverting communal gains to an individual...
144:
...the training rule on diverting gains to an individual (Pariṇāmana). "Kiṃ te akālaṃ acchinde" refers to the training rule that comes as "Lady, what will this man do for you?", the distribution (Bhājana) training rule of assigning an out-of-season robe as an in-season robe, and the training rule on taking back a robe after exchanging it with a nun (Acchindana). "Duggahī nirayena ca" refers to the training rule on causing others to complain due to being poorly grasped (remembered), and the training rule on cursing with hell or with the holy life (Abhisapana).

"Gaṇaṃ vibhaṅga dubbalaṃ" refers to the training rules stated as: "He would cause an obstacle to the robe-gains of a group," "He would obstruct the legal distribution of robes," and "He would let the robe-season pass in the hope of a poor robe." "Kathinā phāsu passayan" refers to the training rules stated as: "He would obstruct the legal removal of the Kathina," "He would intentionally make a nun uncomfortable," and "Having given a nun a dwelling, being angry and displeased, he would expel her." "Akkosacaṇḍī maccharī" refers to the training rules stated as: "He would scold or revile a monk," "Being angry, she would revile a group," and "She would be stingy towards families." "Gabbhiniñca pāyantiyā" refers to the training rules stated as: "One would ordain a pregnant woman," and "One would ordain a nursing woman."

"Dvevassaṃ sikkhā saṅghena" refers to the training rules stated as: "One would ordain a probationer (sikkhamānā) who has not trained in the six rules for two years," and "One would ordain a probationer who has trained but has not been authorized by the Saṅgha." "Tayo ceva gihīgatā" refers to the training rules stated regarding a former laywoman under twelve years and a former laywoman of full twelve years: "One who has not trained in the six rules for two years," and "One who has trained for two years but has not been authorized by the Saṅgha." "Kumāribhūtā tisso" refers to the three rules stated in the manner of "A maiden under twenty years," etc. "Ūnadvādasasammatā" refers to the two training rules: "One would ordain one under twelve years," and "One would ordain one of full twelve years who has not been authorized by the Saṅgha."

"Alaṃ tāva sokāvāsaṃ" refers to the two training rules: "Enough, lady, of your ordaining," and "One would ordain an angry probationer who is a source of grief." "Chandā anuvassā ca dve" refers to the three training rules: "One would ordain a probationer by giving consent while undergoing penance (pārivāsika)," "One would ordain every year," and "One would ordain two in one year." "Samuṭṭhānā tikā katā" means they have been made with three originations (originations consisting of three factors: body, speech, and mind).

## Explanation of the Origins of Sañcaritta

By the words 'Sañcarī kuṭi vihāro', it refers to the Sañcaritta Sikkhāpada, the Saññācikāya Kuṭikaraṇa Sikkhāpada, and the Mahallakavihārakaraṇa Sikkhāpada. 'Dhovanañca paṭiggaho' refers to the training rule on having an unrelated nun wash an old robe and the training rule on receiving a robe. 'Viññattuttari abhihaṭṭhuṃ' refers to the training rule on asking an unrelated householder for a robe and the training rule on accepting more than that. 'Ubhinnaṃ dūtakena ca' refers to the two training rules that mention 'A robe-fund has been prepared' and the training rule on sending a robe-fund via a messenger.

'Kosiyā suddhadvebhāgā chabbassāni nisīdanaṃ' refers to the five training rules beginning with 'A rug mixed with silk'. 'Riñcanti rūpikā ceva' refers to the training rule on having sheep's wool washed, which is mentioned in the Vibhaṅga as 'they neglect the recitation', and the training rule on receiving gold and silver. 'Ubho nānappakārakā' refers to the two training rules on trading with gold and silver.

'Ūnabandhanavassikā' refers to the training rule on a bowl with fewer than five mends and the training rule on a rain-cloth. 'Suttaṃ vikappanena ca' refers to the training rule on asking for thread to have a robe woven and the training rule on approaching a weaver to specify the robe's requirements. 'Dvāradānasibbāni ca' refers to the training rule taught up to the fixing of a door-bolt in a door-frame, and the three training rules taught as 'giving a robe to an unrelated nun' and 'sewing a robe for her'. 'Pūvapaccayajoti ca' refers to the training rule on invitation with cakes or meal-powder, the training rule on invitation with requisites for four months, and the training rule on lighting a fire.

'Ratanaṃ sūci mañco ca tūlaṃ nisīdanakaṇḍu ca vassikā ca sugatena' refers to the seven training rules including the Ratana Sikkhāpada and the Sūcighara Sikkhāpada. 'Viññatti aññaṃ cetāpanā dve saṅghikā mahājanikā dve puggalalahukā garū' refers to the nine training rules beginning with 'Whatever nun, having asked for one thing, has another thing bought'. 'Dve vighāsā sāṭikā ca' refers to the two Vighāsa training rules taught as 'throwing or causing to throw excrement, urine, rubbish, or food scraps over a wall or fence, or throwing or causing to throw them on green plants', and the training rule on the water-cloth. The phrase 'Samaṇacīvarena ca' is taught with reference to the training rule 'One should give a recluse's robe'.

## Explanation of the Origins of Samanubhāsanā

'Bhedānuvatta, dubbaca, dūsa, duṭṭhulla, diṭṭhi' refers to the Saṅghabheda Sikkhāpada, the Bhedānuvattaka Sikkhāpada, the Dubbaca Sikkhāpada, the Kuladūsaka Sikkhāpada, the Duṭṭhullappaṭiccādana Sikkhāpada, and the Diṭṭhi-appaṭinissajjana Sikkhāpada. 'Chandaṃ ujjagghikā dve ca' refers to the training rule on going without giving consent and the two training rules on going or sitting in a house while laughing loudly. 'Dve ca saddā' refers to the two training rules stated as 'I will go/sit in a house with little sound'. 'Na byāhare' refers to the training rule stated as 'I will not speak with a mouth full of food'.

'Chamā nīcāsane ṭhānaṃ, pacchato uppathena ca' refers to the training rules on teaching Dhamma while sitting on the ground, teaching Dhamma while sitting on a low seat, teaching Dhamma to one who is sitting while one is standing, teaching Dhamma to one who is going in front while one is going behind, and teaching Dhamma to one who is going on a path while one is going off the path. 'Vajjānuvattigahaṇā' refers to the three Pārājika training rules known as concealing an offense, following (a suspended monk), and taking the hand (of a man). 'Osāre paccācikkhanā' refers to the two training rules taught as 'One should restore (a nun) without informing the performing Saṅgha and without knowing the consent of the other group' and 'I renounce the Buddha'.

'Kismiṃ saṃsaṭṭhā dve vadhī' refers to the training rules taught as 'defeated in some legal issue', 'nuns live in association', 'whatever nun says "Ladies, you should live in association"', and 'one should weep, beating oneself'. 'Visibbe dukkhitāya ca' refers to the two training rules taught as 'having unpicked or having caused to unpick a nun's robe' and 'a distressed companion'. 'Puna saṃsaṭṭhā na vūpasame' refers to the training rule on living in association again, taught as 'one should live in association with a householder or a householder's son', and the training rule where a nun, being told 'Lady, come and settle this legal issue', agrees by saying 'Very well', but later fails to settle it without any hindrance. 'Ārāmañca pavāraṇā' refers to the two training rules taught as 'entering a monastery where monks are present while knowing it and without asking permission' and 'not inviting the twofold Saṅgha regarding three matters'.

'Anvaddhaṃ sahajīviniṃ dve' refers to the training rule taught as 'every half-month a nun should expect two things from the Bhikkhu Saṅgha' and the two training rules taught as 'having ordained a companion, one should not fail to support her for two years' and 'having ordained a companion, one should not separate from her'. 'Cīvaraṃ anubandhanā' refers to the rule: 'Lady, if you give me a robe, ...'

## Antarapeyyālaṃ
## Katipucchāvāravaṇṇanā
Now, for the purpose of generating proficiency in the portions such as offenses, the teachers of the Council have spoken the Vibhaṅga by way of explanation (niddesa) and detailed explanation (paṭiniddesa), having established the Mātikā in the manner beginning with "How many are the offenses?"

Among those questions, the question "How many are the offenses?" is a question asking about the offenses that appear in both the Mātikā and the Vibhaṅga. This same method applies to the second phrase, "How many are the groups of offenses?" In this second phrase, the offenses themselves are merely called "groups (khandha)" by way of their collection. "Vinītavatthu" refers to the questions about the Dhamma that removes those offenses. The terms "vinīta," "vinaya," and "vūpasama" are one and the same in meaning. The Dhammas that remove offenses are themselves called Vinītavatthu; this is the meaning of the term here.

Now, to show those things which, when present, cause offenses to occur, and when absent, cause them not to occur, two types of questions are spoken, beginning with "How many are the acts of disrespect (agārava)?" The question "Vinītavatthu" is the question asking about the removal of those acts of disrespect. Because there are no offenses that do not reach the state of failure (vipatti), the question "How many are the failures?" is a question asking about the state of failure of the offenses. The question "How many are the origins of offenses?" is a question asking about the origins of those very offenses. The questions "roots of disputes (vivādamūla), roots of accusations (anuvādamūla)" are questions about the fundamental roots of disputes and accusations mentioned as "vivādādhikaraṇa" and "anuvādādhikaraṇa." The question "qualities of conciliation (sāraṇīyadhamma)" asks about the qualities that prevent the roots of disputes and accusations from arising. The question "grounds for schism (bhedakaravatthu)" asks about the causes of schism mentioned in the Pali such as "legal issues leading to schism." The question "legal issues (adhikaraṇa)" asks about the things that arise when grounds for schism are present. "Settlements (samatha)" refers to the question about the qualities that pacify those grounds for schism. "Five offenses" is stated by way of what appears in the Mātikā. "Seven" is stated by way of what appears in the Vibhaṅga.

It delights far away from these groups of offenses, therefore it is called "ārati" (abstinence). Or, great delight is called "ārati." It delights being free from these groups of offenses, therefore it is called "virati" (abstinence). Abstaining from each and every one is called "paṭivirati." It destroys the defilements such as greed which are the cause of enmity, therefore it is called "veramaṇī." Because of this abstinence, these groups of offenses are not committed, therefore it is called "akiriyā" (non-action). If this abstinence were absent, the committing of the group of offenses would arise; because it is the opposite of committing that group of offenses, it is called "akaraṇa" (non-doing). Because it is the opposite of falling into a group of offenses, it is called "anajjhāpatti" (non-offense). Because it shakes (destroys) the falling into a group of offenses, it is called "velā" (boundary/limit).
152:
The meaning is: It binds or prevents the path to Nibbāna; therefore, it is called a 'bridge' (setu). This term is a designation for the groups of offenses (āpattikkhandha). Because that bridge (the group of offenses) is destroyed by this prescription of the training rule, it is called 'destruction of the bridge' (setughāta). The same method applies to the remaining explanations of the Vinīta cases.

Among those who are disrespectful towards the Buddha: one who does not go to attend upon the Buddha while he is alive, or does not go to the site of a shrine (cetiya) or the Bodhi tree after his Parinibbāna, or does not pay homage to the shrine or the Bodhi tree, or wanders about the shrine courtyard with an umbrella or wearing sandals—it should be understood that such a person has no respect for the Buddha. One who, though capable, does not go to listen to the Dhamma, does not recite with intonation (sarabhañña), does not preach the Dhamma, leaves by breaking through the assembly of Dhamma listeners, or sits distracted or without regard—that person has no respect for the Dhamma. One who does not show respect to senior, middle, or junior monks, shows physical rudeness in the Uposatha hall or the Vitakkamāḷaka, etc., or does not pay homage according to seniority—that person has no respect for the Saṅgha. One who, having undertaken the three trainings, does not practice them, should be known as one who is disrespectful towards the training (sikkhā). One who, remaining in negligence and lack of mindfulness, does not develop the characteristic of heedfulness, should be known as one who is disrespectful towards heedfulness (appamāda). Likewise, one who does not practice the two kinds of hospitality—material hospitality (āmisa-paṭisanthāra) and spiritual hospitality (dhamma-paṭisanthāra)—should be known as one who is disrespectful towards hospitality. The meaning should be understood by the reverse of what was stated in the explanation of respect (gārava-niddesa).

In the explanation of the roots of dispute (vivādamūla-niddesa), the meaning of the words "disrespectful even towards the Teacher," etc., should be understood in the same way as stated for those disrespectful towards the Buddha. 'Appatissa' means one who has an unhumble manner; they live without regarding the Teacher as the superior. 'Ajjhattaṃ vā' means within one's own internal continuity or within one's own faction; it means within one's own assembly. 'Bahiddhā vā' means in another's continuity or in another's faction. 'Tatra tumhe' means in that distinction of internal and external, or in one's own or another's continuity or assembly. 'Pahānāya vāyameyyātha' means you should strive for the sake of abandoning through methods such as the development of loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā); for by the method of developing loving-kindness, etc., that root of dispute is abandoned both internally and externally. 'Anavassavāya' means for the sake of it not arising again.

'Sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī' means one who wrongly misapprehends their own view; they grasp only the wrong view they have taken up, thinking "this alone is the truth." 'Ādhānaggāhī' means one who grasps firmly.
153:
The explanation of the roots of accusation (anuvādamūla-niddesa) is similar to the roots of dispute (vivādamūla-niddesa), but the distinction is that the roots of dispute are anger (kodha), malice (upanāha), etc., of those who dispute based on the eighteen grounds for schism. However, those who dispute in such a way, having fallen into one of the failures such as failure in virtue (sīlavipatti), accuse others, saying, "Such and such a monk has fallen into such and such a failure," or "You have fallen into a Pārājika offense," or "You have fallen into a Saṅghādisesa offense." The anger, malice, etc., of those who accuse in this way are called the roots of accusation (anuvādamūla). This is the distinction here in this explanation of the roots of accusation.

In the explanation of the qualities of communal harmony (sāraṇīyadhamma-niddesa), bodily action performed with a mind of loving-kindness is called 'bodily action of loving-kindness' (metta-kāyakamma). It is performed both in presence (sammukhā) and in absence (parammukhā). Among these, helping junior monks in tasks such as making robes is called bodily action of loving-kindness in their presence. All respectful services (sāmicikamma) for elder monks, such as washing their feet or fanning them, are also called bodily action of loving-kindness in their presence. For both elders and juniors, tidying up misplaced wooden items, etc., without looking down on them, but as if they were items misplaced by oneself, is called bodily action of loving-kindness in their absence. "This quality is also one to be remembered (sāraṇīya)" means that this quality known as bodily action of loving-kindness is to be constantly remembered and is a cause for mindfulness. The meaning is that whoever performs that bodily action of loving-kindness, those for whom it is performed will have a confident mind and remember them, thinking, "Oh, what a good person!" 'Making one dear' (piyakaraṇa) means it makes that person dear to their fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī). 'Making one respected' (garukaraṇa) means it makes that person respected by their fellow practitioners. In the phrases "for the sake of being cherished," etc., it means for the sake of being cherished by fellow practitioners, for the sake of not disputing with them, for the sake of harmony (samagga), and for the sake of unity (ekībhāva).

In the phrases "verbal action of loving-kindness" (metta-vacīkamma), etc., speaking in praise such as "Elder Deva, Elder Tissa" is called verbal action of loving-kindness in their presence. When they are not in the monastery, speaking words of endearment to someone inquiring about them, such as "Where is our Elder Deva? Where is our Elder Tissa? When will he return?" is called verbal action of loving-kindness in their absence. Opening the eyes moistened with the sap of loving-kindness and looking with a clear face is called mental action of loving-kindness (metta-manokamma) in their presence. Directing the mind with the thought, "May Elder Deva and Elder Tissa be free from illness and affliction," is called mental action of loving-kindness in their absence.

'Appaṭivibhattabhogī' means enjoying gains without dividing them by material things or by persons. One who thinks, "I will give this much material gain to others, I will enjoy this much myself, but this much..."
154:
One who shares and then enjoys, saying, "I will give to this person and that person, and I will enjoy this much myself," is called a 'paṭivibhatta-bhogī' (one who shares gains). This person (the appaṭivibhatta-bhogī), however, without such sharing, gives the alms-food received starting from the seat of the elder, and enjoys only the remaining alms-food. According to the words "with those of virtue," it is also proper not to give to those without virtue. However, it is said that a monk who fulfills the 'sāraṇīyadhamma' (qualities of friendliness) should indeed give to all monks. It is also proper to select and give to those who are sick, those attending the sick, newcomers, those about to travel, and those engaged in making robes, etc. One who selects and gives in this way is not said to be making a 'puggala-vibhāga' (discrimination of persons). This is because such persons are those to whom special consideration should be given as they obtain gains with difficulty; thus, this (appaṭivibhatta-bhogī) acts in this manner.

In the words beginning with "akhaṇḍāni," if a training rule is broken at the beginning or at the end among the seven groups of offenses, that person's virtue is called "khaṇḍa" (broken virtue), like a cloth with a torn edge. If it is broken in the middle, it is called "chidda" (perforated virtue), like a cloth with a hole in the middle. If two or three are broken in succession, it is called "sabala" (spotted virtue), like a cow with a different body color such as black or red appearing on its back or belly. If it is broken at intervals, it is called "kammāsa" (mottled virtue), like a cow variegated with spots of a different color at intervals. For one whose virtues are entirely unbroken, those virtues are called akhaṇḍa, acchidda, asabala, and akammāsa. These virtues are called "bhujissa" (free) because they cause liberation from the slavery of craving. They are called "viññuppasattha" because they are praised by the wise. They are called "aparāmaṭṭha" because they are not wrongly grasped by craving and views. They are called "samādhisavaṭṭanika" because they lead to access concentration or absorption concentration. "Sīlasāmaññagato viharati" means living with a virtue that is equal to that of the monks of good virtue who reside in various regions.

"Yāyaṃ diṭṭhi" refers to Right View (sammādiṭṭhi) associated with the Path. "Ariyā" means being faultless. "Niyyāti" is called "niyyānikā" because it leads out from the round of suffering. "Takkarassa" refers to one who practices accordingly. "Dukkhakkhayāya" means for the purpose of the end of all suffering. The remaining words up to the end of the Samatha-bheda are clear in meaning.

## The Explanation of the Kati-pucchā-vāra is finished.

## Khandhaka-pucchā-vāra
## Explanation of Questions and Answers
"Upasampadaṃ pucchissanti" means I shall ask about the Upasampadā-khandhaka (the chapter on ordination). "Sanidānaṃ saniddesaṃ" means I shall ask together with the origin (nidāna) and the detailed description (niddesa). "Samukkaṭṭhapadānaṃ kati āpattiyo" means asking how many offenses there are in brief among the noble terms taught in that chapter. This is because whatever offense is prescribed by a particular term, that offense is called the offense of that term. Therefore, it is said, "Samukkaṭṭhapadānaṃ kati āpattiyo."

"Dve āpattiyo" (two offenses) means a Pācittiya offense for one who ordains a person under twenty years of age, and a Dukkaṭa offense in all other remaining terms.

"Tisso" (three offenses) means a Thullaccaya offense for those who perform the Uposatha with the intention of causing a schism, saying, "Let these people be lost, let them perish, what is the use of them?"; a Pācittiya offense for performing the Uposatha with an expelled monk (ukkhittaka); and a Dukkaṭa offense for other reasons. Thus, there are three offenses in the Uposatha-khandhaka. "Ekā" (one offense) means there is only one Dukkaṭa offense in the Vassūpanāyika-khandhaka.

"Tisso" means a Thullaccaya offense for a monk who performs Pavāraṇā with the intention of causing a schism; a Pācittiya offense if performing Pavāraṇā with an expelled monk; and a Dukkaṭa offense in the remaining terms. Thus, there are also three offenses in the Pavāraṇā-khandhaka.

"Tisso" means a Pācittiya offense for monks who lift up and kill a young calf; a Thullaccaya offense for touching the male organ with a lustful mind; and a Dukkaṭa offense in the remaining terms. Thus, there are also three offenses in the Camma-khandhaka. In the Bhesajja-khandhaka, there is a Thullaccaya offense for performing surgery or applying a tight bandage on the area around the male organ within the measure of two finger-breadths; a Pācittiya offense for eating medicinal gruel (bhojjayāgu); and a Dukkaṭa offense in the remaining terms. Thus, there are three offenses.

Kathina is merely a prescription without an offense; therefore, there is no offense in the Kathina-khandhaka. In the Cīvara-khandhaka, there is a Thullaccaya offense for wearing robes made of kusa-grass or bark; a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense for keeping an extra robe; and a Dukkaṭa offense in the remaining terms. Thus, there are three offenses.

In the Campeyyaka-khandhaka, there is only one Dukkaṭa offense. In the Kosambaka-khandhaka, Kamma-khandhaka, Parivāsika-khandhaka, and Samuccaya-khandhaka, there is also only one Dukkaṭa offense each.
156:
In the Samatha-khandhaka, if a monk who has given his consent (chanda) later complains, there is a Pācittiya offense for complaining, and a Dukkaṭa offense in the remaining terms; thus these two offenses occur. In the Khuddakavatthu-khandhaka, if one cuts off one's own male organ, there is a Thullaccaya offense; a Pācittiya offense for ruminating (eating like a cow); and a Dukkaṭa offense in the remaining terms; thus these three offenses occur. In the Senāsana-khandhaka, there is a Thullaccaya offense for disposing of heavy property (garubhaṇḍa); a Pācittiya offense for evicting someone from a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha; and a Dukkaṭa offense in the remaining terms; thus these three offenses occur.

In the matter of schism in the Saṅgha, there is a Thullaccaya offense for monks who follow a monk who causes a schism, and a Pācittiya offense for eating in a group (gaṇabhojana); thus these two offenses occur. In the Vatta-khandhaka, taught with the words "Samācāraṃ pucchissanti," there is only one Dukkaṭa offense. That Dukkaṭa offense occurs due to disrespect towards all the duties. It is the same in the Pātimokkhaṭṭhapana-khandhaka. In the Bhikkhunī-khandhaka, there is a Pācittiya offense for not performing Pavāraṇā, and a Dukkaṭa offense in the remaining terms; thus two offenses occur. In the Pañcasatika-khandhaka and Sattasatika-khandhaka, only the Dhamma was rehearsed without any offenses; there are no offenses in those Khandhakas.

## The Explanation of the Khandhaka-pucchā-vāra is finished.

## The Numerical Method
## Commentary on the Section of Ones

In the Numerical Method (Ekuttarika-naya) beginning with "Offence-making states should be known" (āpattikarā dhammā jānitabbā), the states that make an offence are the six origins of offences (āpattisamuṭṭhāna). Because a person falls into an offence by means of these six, they are called "offence-making" (āpattikara). Non-offence-making (anāpattikara) states are the seven ways of settling litigation (samatha). "Offences should be known" means that the offences taught in the respective training rules (sikkhāpada) and in the Analysis (Vibhaṅga) should be known. "Non-offence" (anāpatti) should be known by the method beginning with "There is no offence for a monk who does not consent" (anāpatti bhikkhu asādiyantassa).

"Light offence" (lahukāpatti) refers to the five classes of offences because they can be purified by a light disciplinary act (vinayakamma). "Heavy offence" (garukāpatti) refers to the Saṅghādisesa offence because it is purified by a heavy disciplinary act, and the Pārājika offence because it cannot be brought to the state of non-offence by any means. "Offence with a remainder" (sāvasesāpatti) refers to the remaining offences, excluding Pārājika. "Offence without a remainder" (anavasesāpatti) is the Pārājika offence. Two classes of offences are gross (duṭṭhulla), and the remaining are non-gross (aduṭṭhulla). The remediable dyad (sappaṭikamma-duka) is similar to the remainder dyad. The dyad of those leading to confession (desanāgāminī-duka) is included in the light dyad.

"Obstructive" (antarāyika) means that even the seven classes of offences, when committed intentionally, create an obstruction to the happy destination of heaven and an obstruction to liberation (nibbāna); thus they are called obstructive. However, an offence involving a regulation (paṇṇattivajja) committed unknowingly does not create an obstruction to heaven or liberation; thus it is called "non-obstructive" (anantarāyika). It should be noted that for one who has fallen into an obstructive offence, if he purifies himself by confessing an offence leading to confession (desanāgāminī) or by emerging from an offence leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī), or for one who stands in the state of a novice (sāmaṇera), the path to heaven and liberation is not barred.

"Blameworthy regulation" (sāvazzapaññatti) is a worldly fault (lokavajja). "Blameless regulation" (anavazzapaññatti) is a fault by regulation (paṇṇattivajja). An offence "arising from action" (kiriyato samuṭṭhitā) is an offence incurred by performing a certain act, such as a Pārājika offence. "From non-action" (akiriyato) is an offence incurred by not performing what should be done, such as the offence for not determining a robe (cīvara-anadhiṭṭhāna). "From both action and non-action" (kiriyākiriyato) is an offence incurred through both acting and not acting, such as the offence for building a hut (kuṭikāra).

"Prior offence" (pubbāpatti) is the offence first committed. "Subsequent offence" (aparāpatti) is the offence committed later by one undergoing probation (parivāsa) and so on. An "intermediate offence" (antarāpatti) occurring among prior offences is an offence occurring during the purification of the root (mūlavisuddhi). An "intermediate offence" occurring among subsequent offences is an offence occurring during the purification of value (agghavisuddhi). In the Kurundī, however, it is said: "Prior offence is that first committed; subsequent offence is that committed at the time when one is worthy of Mānatta; an intermediate offence of prior offences is that committed during probation; an intermediate offence of subsequent offences..."
158:
...is called an 'intermediate offence' (antarāpatti) when it is committed while undergoing the probation or Mānatta given for the sake of purification according to the limit of the previous offence. This explanation is also suitable in a certain sense.

An offence that is confessed after 'laying down the burden' (dhuraniķķhepa), with the thought 'I will not commit it again,' is called 'confessed and included in the count' (desitā gaṇanūpagā). An offence confessed with an impure mind and with effort (to commit it again), without laying down the burden, is called 'not included in the count' (agaṇanūpagā). This offence, though confessed, does not enter the count of confessed offences. In the eighth case (vatthu), for a bhikkhunī, it is only a Pārājika. In the nine terms beginning with 'Regulation should be known' (paññatti jānitabbā), the decision should be understood according to the method already stated in the question on the first Pārājika.

'Gross fault' (thullavajja) is a heavy offence (garukāpatti) prescribed for a coarse fault. 'Non-gross fault' (athullavajja) is a light offence (lahukāpatti). 'Connected with laypeople' (gihipaṭisaṃyutta) refers to the offence of Elder Sudhamma and the offence incurred by not making true a righteous promise; the remaining offences are not connected with laypeople. An offence incurred due to the five heinous crimes (ānantariyakamma) is 'fixed' (niyata) [in its result], while the remaining are 'unfixed' (aniyata). 'First-doer' (ādikara) refers to the first offender (ādikammika) such as Elder Sudinna. 'Not a first-doer' (anādikara) refers to those who caused supplementary regulations (anupaññatti), such as the monk who had sexual intercourse with a female monkey. One who falls into an offence only once in a while is called 'occasional offender' (adhiccāpattika). One who falls into offences constantly is called 'frequent offender' (abhiṇhāpattika).

One who accuses another of a basis (vatthu) or an offence (āpatti) is called an 'accuser' (codaka). The one thus accused is called the 'accused' (cuditaka). One who accuses with a false basis, without standing in the fifteen factors (of a righteous accuser), is called an 'unrighteous accuser' (adhamma-codaka), and the one thus accused by him is an 'unrighteously accused' (adhamma-cuditaka). The 'righteous accuser' (dhamma-codaka) and 'righteously accused' (dhamma-cuditaka) should be understood in the opposite way. One possessed of states of certain wrongness (micchattaniyata, such as heinous crimes) or states of certain rightness (sammattaniyata, such as the Noble Path) is called a 'certain person' (niyata-puggala); others are 'uncertain persons' (aniyata-puggala).

Disciples (sāvaka) are 'capable of falling into an offence' (babbhāpattika), while Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas are 'incapable of falling into an offence' (ababbhāpattika). One against whom the act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) has been performed is called 'suspended' (ukkhittaka). One against whom the other four acts, such as the act of rebuke (tajjaniyakamman), have been performed is called 'not suspended' (anukkhittaka). This non-suspended person does not disrupt the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, the communal use of the Dhamma, or the communal use of material requisites. One who is expelled by means of loss of status (liṅganāsana), punishment (daṇḍakammanāsana), or loss of communion (saṃvāsanāsana), as in 'Expel the bhikkhunī Mettiyā,' 'The corrupter should be expelled,' and 'The novice Kaṇṭaka should be expelled,' is called 'expelled' (nāsitaka). All others are 'not expelled' (anāsitaka). If there is communion (saṃvāsa) in Uposatha and so on with someone, that person is called 'one of equal communion' (samānasaṃvāsaka).
159:
A person other than one of the same communion is called one of different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka). That person of different communion is of two types: different communion by act (kammanānāsaṃvāsaka) and different communion by view (laddhinānāsaṃvāsaka). The meaning of "the suspension of the Pātimokkha should be known" is as taught in the manner beginning with: "Monks, there is one unrighteous suspension of the Pātimokkha..."

## The Explanation of the Single-fold Section is finished.

## The Explanation of the Two-fold Section

In the two-fold sections, an offense with intention is called saññāvimokkha (released by perception/intention). An offense without intention is called nosaññāvimokkha. The offense of one who has attained meditative absorptions is the offense of reporting what is real (bhūtārocana), while the offense of one who has not attained them is the offense of reporting what is not real (abhūtārocana). An offense connected with the true Dhamma refers to offenses such as teaching Dhamma word by word (padasodhamma), while an offense connected with what is not the true Dhamma refers to the offense of lewd speech (duṭṭhullavācā).

An offense connected with one's own requisites refers to offenses incurred through improper use, such as: using a nissaggiya object without forfeiting it, leaving bowls and robes in the sun for a long time, not washing soiled robes, or not baking a bowl that has collected grime. An offense connected with another's requisites refers to offenses to be incurred by such acts as spreading out communal (saṅghika) couches, stools, etc., in the open and then leaving without asking permission. An offense connected with one's own person refers to offenses taught in the manner: "for one with a soft back, one with hanging flesh, pressing the private parts with the thigh," and so on.

An offense connected with another person refers to offenses taught regarding sexual intercourse, physical contact, giving a blow, and so on. A monk who speaks the truth, saying "She is a woman with protruding flesh (sikharaṇī)," incurs a grave offense (garuka). A monk who speaks a lie, according to the training rule "In a deliberate lie, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)," incurs a light offense (lahuka). In reporting what is not real, a monk who speaks a lie regarding superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) incurs a grave offense. In reporting what is real, a monk who speaks the truth regarding superhuman states incurs a light offense.

A monk who, intending to make a Sangha act partisan (vagga), sits in a place outside the hatthapāsa (reach of hand) within the boundary (sīmā), incurs an offense if he is stationed on the ground. If he were stationed in the air even by the measure of a finger's breadth, he would not incur an offense. Therefore, it is said: "not one gone to the air." A monk who sits down pressing upon a couch or stool with legs fixed into a raised hut (vehāsakuṭi) incurs an offense as one "gone to the air." If he were to lie down after spreading that couch or stool on the ground, he would not incur an offense. Therefore, it is said: "not one gone to the ground."

A monk who is to depart (gamiya), if he goes without fulfilling the duties of a departer, incurs an offense while leaving the monastery, but not while entering another. An arriving monk (āgantuka), if he enters with an umbrella and sandals without fulfilling the duties of an arriver, incurs an offense while entering, but not while leaving the monastery.
160: A bhikkhunī commits an offense through 'taking' (ādiyamāna) if she performs a water-cleansing that is too deep (more than two finger-breadths). A monk commits an offense through 'not taking' (anādiyanta) if he uses a robe without applying the disfiguring mark (kappabindu). A monk who undertakes the practices of sectarians, such as the practice of being mute, commits an offense through 'undertaking' (samādiyanta). Monks undergoing probation (parivāsa) and the like, or those subjected to acts such as the act of censure (tajjaniyakamma), commit an offense if they do not undertake their own duties. Referring to such persons, it is said: "He commits an offense because of not undertaking it despite having an offense." A monk who sews a robe for an unrelated bhikkhunī, or who practices medicine, acts as a storekeeper, or does painting and so on, commits an offense by 'doing' (karonta). A monk who does not perform duties such as the duty to the preceptor (upajjhāya) commits an offense by 'not doing' (akaronta). A monk who gives a robe to an unrelated bhikkhunī commits an offense by 'giving' (denta). A monk who does not give robes and so on to his own co-residents (saddhivihārika) or pupils (antevāsika) commits an offense by 'not giving' (adenta). A monk who accepts a robe from an unrelated bhikkhunī commits an offense by 'accepting' (paṭiggaṇhanta). According to the statement, "Monks, exhortation (ovāda) should not be not-accepted," a monk who does not accept exhortation commits an offense by 'not accepting' (appaṭiggaṇhanta). A monk who uses a nissaggiya object without forfeiting it commits an offense through 'use' (paribhogena). A bhikkhunī who lets the five-day robe-rotation pass commits an offense through 'non-use' (aparibhogena). One commits an offense by sleeping together in the same building during the night, but not during the day. A monk who stays during the day without closing the door commits an offense during the day, but not at night. A monk who incurs offenses taught regarding the passing of one night, six nights, seven days, ten days, or a month, commits the offense at dawn (aruṇugga). A monk who eats after having finished his meal (pavārita) does not commit an offense at dawn. A monk who cuts vegetation (bhūtagāma) or the male organ commits an offense by 'cutting' (chindanta). A monk who does not cut his hair or nails (within the prescribed time) commits an offense by 'not cutting' (achindanta). A monk who conceals an offense commits an offense by 'concealing' (chādenta). A monk who does not cover himself according to the rule, "One should come covered with grass or leaves; one should not come naked; for him who comes so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," commits an offense by 'not covering.' A monk who wears robes made of kusa-grass and so on commits an offense by 'wearing' (dhārenta). A monk who does not carry the bowl according to the rule, "Monk, this bowl must be carried until it breaks," commits an offense by 'not carrying' (adhārenta). "He makes himself one of different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka)" means: while two groups of Sangha are sitting within a single boundary (sīmā), a monk sitting on one side adopts the view of the other side...
161:
He is said to make himself one of a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka) from the monks on the side where he is sitting. He becomes a quorum-filler (gaṇapūraka) for those monks in whose presence he sits, thereby spoiling the legal act (kamma). For the monks on the other side, he spoils the legal act because he has not reached the 'arm's reach' (hatthapāsa). The same method applies to one of the same communion (samānasaṃvāsaka). This is because that monk favors the views of those people; he becomes one of the same communion with them and one of a different communion with others. In the phrase 'seven offenses (sattāpattiyo), seven groups of offenses (sattāpattikkhandhā)', they are called 'offenses' because they are to be incurred, and 'groups' (khandhā) in the sense of a collection. Thus, since there are only two names, the dyad (duka) is shown by the power of the names.

In the phrase 'by means of a legal act or by taking voting tickets (salākaggāha)', recitation (uddessa) and legal act (kamma) are one kind; usage (vohāra), proclamation (anussāvana), and taking voting tickets (salākaggāha) are another kind. Usage, proclamation, and taking voting tickets are preliminary matters of the act of schism (saṅghabheda), while only the legal act and recitation are the essential measures. 'Addhānahīna' refers to one who is under twenty years of age. 'Aṅgahīna' refers to one who has a severed hand and so forth. 'Vatthuvipanna' refers to eunuchs (paṇḍaka), animals, and hermaphrodites (ubhatobyañjanaka). The remaining eight types of incapable persons (abhabbapuggala), such as those who live by stealth (theyyasaṃvāsaka), are called 'wrongdoing by action' (karaṇadukkata). It means that those with bad behavior and bad actions reach the state of being incapable in this very life due to the kamma they have committed. 'Aparipūra' refers to one who does not have a complete set of bowl and robes. 'No ca yācati' means not requesting higher ordination (upasampadā).

Regarding the shameless (alajjī) and the foolish (bāla)—even if the shameless one is a master of the Tipitaka, and even if the foolish one has sixty rains—one should not live in dependence (nissaya) on either of them. In the phrase 'of the foolish and the modest (lajjī)', dependence is given to the foolish one even by command, saying 'You, take dependence'; but to the modest one, it is given only upon request. 'Sātisāra' refers to an object involving fault, which, if transgressed, leads to an offense. 'Rejection by body' (kāyena paṭikkosanā) means rejection by bodily gestures such as hand movements. 'Acknowledging by body' (kāyena paṭijānāti) means acknowledging by bodily gestures such as hand movements. 'Upaghātikā' refers to destructions (upaghāta). 'Sikkhūpaghātikā' means destroying the training. 'Bhogūpaghātikā' means destroying the usage of property (paribhoga). Among them, not practicing the three trainings is to be known as 'sikkhūpaghātikā'. Using communal (saṅghika) or individual (puggalika) property improperly is to be known as 'bhogūpaghātikā'.

'Dve venayikā' refers to two meanings established in the Vinaya. 'Paññatta' refers to the training rules prescribed throughout the entire Vinaya Piṭaka in terms of what is allowable and what is not. 'Paññattānuloma' refers to matters to be considered according to the four Great Authorities (mahāpadesa). 'Setughāta' means the destruction of the root cause (paccaya); it means not allowing the very mind to arise with which one would do what is unallowable. 'Mattakāritā' refers to...
162:
It means doing with measure or limit, or staying within the appropriate measure. Falling into an offense by body means reaching an offense through the body-door; [falling into an offense] by speech means [reaching it] through the speech-door. Rising by body means rising from an offense through the body alone, even without a formal confession, as in the settlement by covering with grass (tiṇavatthāraka-samatha); however, one who rises after making a confession rises by speech. Internal use (abbhantara-paribhoga) refers to use by swallowing. External use (bāhira-paribhoga) refers to things like anointing the head with oil. Carrying a burden that has not yet arrived means that while not yet an Elder (Thera), one carries the burdens to be borne by Elders, such as holding the fan or inviting [someone] to teach the Dhamma; one exerts effort to complete that task. Not carrying a burden that has arrived means that although one is an Elder, one does not perform the duties of an Elder. It means neglecting everything, such as [the Buddha's allowance]: "Monks, I allow an Elder monk to speak the Dhamma himself, or to invite another; I allow the Pātimokkha to be under the charge of an Elder," and so on. Doing what should not be done with remorse while feeling remorse, and doing what should be done with remorse without feeling remorse. For these two types of persons, the taints (āsavas) increase both by day and by night. In the subsequent dyad (duka), the meaning should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated. The rest is clear as it follows the method already mentioned in various places.

## The Explanation of the Section on Dyads is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Section on Triads

In the triads, "there is an offense while the Blessed One is alive" means there is an offense that is committed while the Blessed One is still living. This method applies to all [similar phrases]. Among those offenses, the offense of causing [the Buddha's] blood to flow (lohituppāda) is committed only while he is alive. According to the statement: "Now, Ānanda, the monks address one another with the word 'friend' (āvuso); after my passing, they should not address one another thus. Ānanda, a junior monk should address an Elder monk as 'Venerable Sir' (bhante) or 'Venerable' (āyasmā)," the offense due to addressing an Elder as 'friend' is committed only after the Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna, not while he is alive. Setting aside these two offenses, the remaining offenses can be committed both while the Blessed One is alive and after his Parinibbāna.

A monk who eats food that is not leftover (anatiritta) after having finished his meal (pavāretvā) commits an offense during the [proper] time, not at the wrong time (vikāla). However, the offense of eating at the wrong time (vikāla-bhojana) is committed only at the wrong time, not during the [proper] time.
163:
The remaining offenses are committed both at the proper time and at the improper time. The offense committed by sleeping together in a single-roofed dwelling occurs at night; the offense committed by secluded meditation without closing the door occurs during the day. The remaining offenses occur both at night and during the day.

Thinking, 'I have ten years [of seniority], I have more than ten years,' a foolish and incompetent monk who supports a following commits an offense when he has ten years, but not when he has less than ten years. Thinking, 'I am wise and competent,' a newly ordained or middle-seated monk who supports a following commits an offense when he has less than ten years, but not when he has ten years. The remaining offenses are committed by both those with ten years and those with less than ten years.

Thinking, 'I have five years,' a foolish and incompetent monk who lives without dependence (nissaya) commits an offense when he has five years. Thinking, 'I am wise and competent,' a newly ordained monk who lives without dependence commits an offense when he has less than five years. The remaining offenses are committed by both those with five years and those with less than five years.

A monk who teaches the Dhamma to a layperson or a novice in groups, or a monk who preaches the Dhamma to a woman, commits such offenses with a wholesome mind. Offenses of various kinds such as Pārājika, Sukka-vissaṭṭhi, Kāyasaṃsagga, Duṭṭhullā, Attakāmapāricariya, Duṭṭhadosa, Saṅghabheda, Paharādāna, and Talasattika are committed with an unwholesome mind. Offenses such as Sahagārasayya, committed unintentionally, are committed with an indeterminate mind. All offenses that only an Arahant can commit are committed only with an indeterminate mind. Offenses of various kinds such as Methunadhamma are committed by one endowed with pleasant feeling. Offenses of various kinds such as Duṭṭhadosa are committed by one endowed with painful feeling. If an offense that is committed by one endowed with pleasant feeling is committed with an indifferent mind, it is committed by one endowed with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

'Tayo Paṭikkhepā' refers to the three prohibitions of the Blessed Buddha. Greatness of desire regarding the four requisites, discontentment, and not guarding the practice of effacing defilements—these three things the Blessed Buddha prohibited. However, the three things such as fewness of desire were permitted by the Blessed Buddha; therefore, it is said, 'Tayo Anujñātā' (Three are permitted).

Thinking, 'I have ten years,' a monk who supports a following, or thinking, 'I have five years,' a monk who does not take dependence, commits an offense if he is foolish, but not if he is wise. A monk with less than ten years who, thinking 'I am competent' because of his great learning, supports a following, or a monk with less than five years who does not take dependence, commits an offense if he is wise, but not if he is foolish. The remaining offenses are committed by both the wise and the foolish. A monk who does not enter the Vassa commits an offense during the dark fortnight, but not during the bright fortnight. A monk who does not perform Pavāraṇā on the day of Mahāpavāraṇā commits an offense during the bright fortnight, but not during the dark fortnight. The remaining offenses are committed during both the dark and bright fortnights. Entering the Vassa is allowable during the dark fortnight, but not during the bright fortnight. Performing Pavāraṇā on the day of Mahāpavāraṇā is allowable during the bright fortnight, but not during the dark fortnight. The remaining permitted activities are allowable during both the dark and bright fortnights.
164:
Entering the Vassa is allowable during the dark fortnight, but not during the bright fortnight. Performing Pavāraṇā is allowable during the bright fortnight, but not during the dark fortnight. The remaining permitted activities are allowable during both the dark and bright fortnights.

A monk who wears a rainy-season robe (vassika-sāṭika) that has been assigned (vikappana) on the first day of the waning moon following the full moon of Kattika commits an offense in the winter. In the Kurundī Commentary, however, it is said: 'If one wears it in the winter without having relinquished it (paccuddharaṇa) on the full moon day of Kattika, he commits an offense'; this statement is also well-said. For it is said: 'To be determined (adhiṭṭhāna) for four months, and to be assigned (vikappana) thereafter.' A monk who seeks a rainy-season robe when more than one month of summer remains, or a monk who makes and wears it when more than half a month remains, is said to commit an offense in the summer. A monk who, while possessing a rainy-season robe, lets the rain wet his naked body is said to commit an offense in the rainy season. A Saṅgha that performs Pārisuddhi-uposatha or Adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha commits an offense. A group (gaṇa) that performs Suttuddesa-uposatha and Adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha commits an offense. An individual who performs Suttuddesa-uposatha and Pārisuddhi-uposatha commits an offense. The same method applies to Pavāraṇā.

Saṅgha-uposatha and Saṅgha-pavāraṇā are allowable only for the Saṅgha. Gaṇa-uposatha and Gaṇa-pavāraṇā are allowable only for the group. Adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha and Adhiṭṭhāna-pavāraṇā are allowable only for the individual. One who says, 'I have committed a Pārājika offense,' etc., conceals the basis (vatthu) but not the offense (āpatti). One who says, 'I have indulged in sexual intercourse,' etc., conceals the offense but not the basis. He who mentions neither the basis nor the offense conceals both the basis and the offense.

Because it conceals, it is called 'paṭicchādi' (a covering). A bathhouse itself is a thing that conceals, thus it is called 'jantāghara-paṭicchādi.' The same method applies to other things. It is allowable for a monk inside a bathhouse with the door closed to perform preparatory tasks (parikamma). This is also allowable for a monk who has entered the water. In both places, it is not allowable to eat or consume food. Clothing (vatthapaṭicchādi) is allowable for all purposes; therefore, a monk who is covered [by clothing] is allowed to perform all activities. They emerge from the fault; they do not receive blame or reproach. The orb of the moon shines only when it is revealed, free from clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu; it does not shine when covered by any of these. Likewise, the orb of the sun shines. The Dhamma-Vinaya also shines only when it is revealed and taught in detail; it does not shine when concealed.
165:
A sick monk who, while having a need for a specific medicine, requests another medicine, commits an offense. A non-sick monk who requests medicine without having a need for it commits an offense. Regarding other offenses, both sick and non-sick monks may commit them.

Committing an offense inside the monastery but not outside: a monk who lies down by encroaching [on another's space] commits an offense inside the monastery, not outside. Committing an offense outside but not inside: a monk who, after spreading out communal beds and so on in the open, departs without putting them away, commits an offense outside, not inside. Regarding other offenses, they may be committed both inside and outside.

Committing an offense within the precinct: a visiting monk who enters the monastery with an umbrella and sandals without performing the duties of a guest commits an offense as soon as he enters the monastery precinct (upacāra-sīmā). Committing an offense outside the precinct: a monk who is about to depart and leaves without fulfilling the duties of a departing monk, such as putting away wooden items, commits an offense as soon as he crosses the monastery precinct. Regarding other offenses, they may be committed both inside and outside the precinct.

A monk who preaches the Dhamma in the midst of the Saṅgha without being invited while a more senior monk is present commits an offense. This same rule applies in the midst of a group (gaṇa) or in the presence of an individual (puggala). 'Rising' (vuṭṭhāna) by body means rising through the tiṇavatthāraka-samatha (settlement by covering with grass). For one who confesses through speech without moving the body, it is 'rising by speech'. For one who confesses by performing physical actions associated with speech, it is called 'rising by both body and speech'. In the midst of the Saṅgha, both offenses remediable by confession (desanāgāminī) and those remediable by rising (vuṭṭhānagāminī) can be cleared. However, in the midst of a group or an individual, only offenses remediable by confession can be cleared.

'Āgāḷhāya ceteyya' means intending to make it firm. It means that if the Saṅgha wishes, they may carry out an act of suspension (ukkhepaniya-kamma) against a monk who, having been subjected to an act of censure (tajjaniya-kamma) and so on, does not fulfill his duties. Regarding the phrase 'he is shameless, a fool, and unskilled (apakatatta)': a formal act should not be carried out merely because one thinks, 'This person is a fool who does not know Dhamma from non-Dhamma,' or 'This person is unskilled and does not know what is an offense and what is not.' Rather, the formal act should be carried out against one who commits an offense rooted in being a fool or being unskilled.

One who is 'failing in virtue' (sīlavipanna) in regard to higher virtue (adhisīla) is one who has committed the two classes of offenses [Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa]. One who is 'failing in conduct' (ācāravipanna) is one who has committed the five classes of offenses [Thullaccaya, Pācittiya, Pāṭidesanīya, Dukkaṭa, and Dubbhāsita]. One who is 'failing in view' (diṭṭhivipanna) is one possessed of extremist wrong views. A formal act should be carried out only against those who do not see their offense, do not remedy it, and do not relinquish their wrong views.

Physical play (kāyika dava) refers to unseemly conduct such as playing games with dice and so on. Vocal play (vācasika dava) refers to unseemly conduct such as making drum sounds with the mouth and so on. Play of both body and speech refers to dancing, singing, and so on, through both doors...
166:
## Anācāro
Misconduct (anācāra). What is called bodily misconduct (kāyika anācāra) is the transgression of a training rule (sikkhāpada) prescribed for the body-door. What is called verbal misconduct (vācasika anācāra) is the transgression of a training rule prescribed for the speech-door. What is called bodily and verbal misconduct (kāyika-vācasika anācāra) is the transgression of training rules prescribed for both doors.

"Destroying by the body" means destroying by not practicing the training rule prescribed for the body-door. For whoever does not practice that rule, he destroys it. Therefore, his failure to practice is called "bodily destruction (kāyika upaghātika)." The same method applies to the remaining two terms.

"Wrong livelihood by the body" means making a living by running errands (jaṅghapesanika) and so forth, or by the work of a physician such as lancing boils (gaṇḍaphālana) and so forth. "By speech (wrong livelihood)" means carrying messages and making announcements (sāsanuggahaṇa ārocana) and so forth. The third term is stated by way of the combination of both bodily and verbal actions.

"Enough, monk, do not quarrel" means: Monk, it is not proper; do not engage in quarreling, do not engage in strife, do not engage in dispute. "Should not be spoken to" means that not even a single word should be spoken. Even if such a person speaks, his words are not considered worth listening to. "Should not be placed in any separate position" means he should not be placed even in a single senior position, such as holding a fan and so forth.

"To one who is asking for permission" means to one who asks for leave in this way: "Venerable sir, please give me leave, I wish to speak to you." "Should not give permission" means leave should not be granted by saying, "What will you do?" "Words should not be accepted" means his words should not be accepted, his words should not be heard, and even if he wishes to take one to a certain place, one should not go there.

"The discipline of a monk endowed with three factors" means that what he knows is called his discipline. It means he should not be questioned regarding the discipline. "Opportunity to question should not be given" means that for one who asks, "Is this allowable?", leave for the question should not be given, and it should be said, "Ask someone else." In this way, he should not be questioned, nor should his question be listened to. "Discipline should not be discussed" means a disciplinary problem should not be discussed, and talk concerning what is allowable and unallowable should not be coordinated.

"Without giving up this view" means without abandoning this view, such as the claim of being a holy practitioner (brahmacārī). "Pure brahmacārī" refers to an Arahant monk whose taints are destroyed. "Falls into enjoyment" means he reaches the state of indulgence. However, because it is said "without giving up this view," if he gives up that claim of being a brahmacārī and apologizes to the Arahant, saying, "I have spoken a falsehood, please forgive me," and gives up the view that "there is no fault in sensual pleasures," he can still purify his destiny (gati).

"Unwholesome roots" are states that are both unwholesome and roots. Alternatively, they are the roots of unwholesome states. The same method applies to wholesome roots. "Misconducts (duccaritāni)" are actions that are badly practiced. Alternatively, they are perverted actions. The word "du" expresses the sense of "badly" (duṭṭhu) in the first method, and the sense of "perverted" (virūpa) in the second method. "Good conducts (sucaritāni)" are actions that are well practiced. Alternatively, they are excellent actions. Misconduct committed by the body is called bodily misconduct. The same method applies to all terms such as verbal misconduct. The remaining matters are merely indicated because the method has already been stated in various Pali texts.

## Tikavāravaṇṇanā
The explanation of the Triads is finished.
167:
Apologizing with "Please forgive me," and abandoning the wrong view that "there is no fault in sensual pleasures," he should purify his destiny. Unwholesome roots (akusalamūlāni) are those that are both unwholesome and roots, or the roots of unwholesome states. The same method applies to wholesome roots. Actions that are badly practiced or perverted are called misconduct (duccarita). Actions that are well practiced or beautiful are called good conduct (sucarita). Misconduct performed with the body as the instrument is bodily misconduct. This method is the same in all cases. The rest is clear as it follows the method already stated in various places.

## Tikavāravaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## Catukkavāravaṇṇanā
