In the tetrads, "falling into an offense by one's own speech and being rehabilitated by another's speech" means having reached a verbal offense such as padasodhamma and, having gone to the place of settlement by the tiṇavatthāraka (covering with grass) method, one is rehabilitated by the formal act (kammavācā) of another. "Falling into an offense by another's speech and being rehabilitated by one's own speech" means falling into an offense because of another's formal act regarding the non-relinquishing of a wicked view, and being rehabilitated by one's own speech when confessing in the presence of an individual. "Falling into an offense by one's own speech and being rehabilitated by one's own speech" means falling into a verbal offense such as padasodhamma by one's own speech, and being rehabilitated by one's own speech when rising from it through confession. "Falling into an offense by another's speech and being rehabilitated by another's speech" means falling into a saṅghādisesa offense requiring three warnings (yāvatatiyaka) due to another's formal act, and being rehabilitated by another's formal acts such as parivāsa (probation) and so forth.

In the subsequent tetrads, one falls into a bodily offense by the body and is rehabilitated by speech when confessing. One falls into a verbal offense by speech and is rehabilitated by the body in the tiṇavatthāraka settlement. One falls into a bodily offense by the body and is rehabilitated by the body in that same tiṇavatthāraka settlement. One falls into a verbal offense by speech and is rehabilitated by speech when confessing that same offense.

One falls into an offense while asleep, such as the offense to be counted by the number of hairs for touching a communal bed (saṅghika-mañca) without spreading one's own cover, or the offense of sleeping under the same roof (sahagāraseyya); then, upon waking and knowing he has fallen into an offense, he is rehabilitated while awake when confessing. If one falls into an offense while awake (e.g., while cleaning the monastery) and then lies down in the place of the tiṇavatthāraka settlement, he is said to have fallen into an offense while awake and been rehabilitated while asleep. The last two terms should also be understood according to the method already stated.
168:
Committing an offense without the intention to transgress is called an *acittaka* offense. Later, when confessing (*desanā*), one rises from the offense with intention. Committing an offense with the intention to transgress is called a *sacittaka* offense. A monk who is asleep in the place where the *tiṇavatthāraka* settlement is performed rises from the offense without intention. The remaining two cases should be understood according to the method already mentioned.

A person who confesses a similar offense (*sabhāga-āpatti*) incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense due to the act of confession, while confessing one of the offenses such as *pācittiya*. While confessing that, he incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense. Even while incurring that *dukkaṭa* offense, he rises from the *pācittiya* and other offenses. While rising from the *pācittiya* and other offenses, he incurs that *dukkaṭa* offense. Thus, it should be understood that this tetrad, 'He confesses while incurring an offense' (*āpattiṃ āpajjanto deseti*), is spoken with reference to a single act (*payoga*) of a single individual.

In the tetrad of action (*kamma-catukka*), one incurs an offense through a formal act (*kamma*) by not relinquishing a wicked wrong view; when confessing, one rises from the offense through a non-formal act (*akamma*). One incurs offenses such as *sukkhavissaṭṭhi* (emission of semen) through a non-formal act; one rises from the offense through a formal act such as *parivāsa* (probation). One incurs an offense of formal admonition (*samanubhāsana*) only through a formal act; one rises from it only through a formal act. One incurs the remaining offenses through a non-formal act and rises from them through a non-formal act.

In the tetrad of requisites (*parikkhāra-catukka*), the first requisite is one's own property; the second is the property of the *Saṅgha*; the third is the property of a *cetiya*; the fourth is the property of laypeople. If that property of laypeople is brought for the purpose of alms-bowls, robes, new constructions, or medicines, it is allowable to give the key and to have it kept inside the monastery.

In the tetrad of presence (*sammukhā-catukka*), one incurs an offense by not relinquishing a wicked wrong view in the presence of the *Saṅgha*; however, at the time of rising from the offense, since there is no duty to be performed with the *Saṅgha*, one rises in the absence of the *Saṅgha*. One incurs offenses such as *sukkhavissaṭṭhi* in the absence of the *Saṅgha* and rises in the presence of the *Saṅgha*. One incurs an offense of formal admonition only in the presence of the *Saṅgha* and rises only in the presence of the *Saṅgha*. One incurs the remaining offenses, such as deliberate lying (*sampajānamusāvāda*), only in the absence of the *Saṅgha* and rises only in the absence of the *Saṅgha*. The tetrad of not knowing (*ajānanta-catukka*) is similar to the tetrad of lack of intention (*acittaka-catukka*).

'Due to the appearance of the [opposite] sex' (*liṅgapātubhāvena*) means that when the sex of a sleeping monk or nun changes, an offense of sleeping in the same place (*sahagārasayya*) is incurred; this is said with reference to this point. The uncommon offenses (*asādhāraṇa-āpatti*) of both monks and nuns are cleared by the change of sex.

In the tetrad of simultaneous acquisition (*sahapaṭilābha-catukka*), when the sex of a monk changes, he relinquishes the former male sex immediately upon acquiring the new sex, because of its prior existence and its superior nature, and he becomes established in the subsequent female sex. The bodily and vocal intimations (*kāyaviññatti*, *vacīviññatti*) that occurred through male behavior and appearance cease. The designations such as 'monk' (*bhikkhu*) or 'man' (*purisa*) that occurred in this way...
169:
The designations cease. There is no offense regarding the forty-six training rules that are specific only to nuns. In the second tetrad, if the sex of a nun changes, she relinquishes the female sex, called 'subsequent' (*pacchima*), because of its later occurrence or its inferior nature, and she becomes established in the male sex, called 'former' (*purima*), in the manner already described. The intimations (*viññatti*) that are contrary to those already mentioned cease. The designations such as 'nun' (*bhikkhunī*) or 'woman' (*itthī*) that occurred in this way also cease. There is no offense regarding the one hundred and thirty training rules that are specific only to monks.

'Four self-exalted ones' (*cattāro sāmukkaṃsā*) refers to the four Great Authorities (*Mahāpadesa*). These are called '*sāmukkaṃsa*' because the Blessed One himself highlighted and set them forth even before a specific case had arisen. 'Requisites' (*paribhoga*) refers to items for consumption. Since water is not restricted by time (*akālika*), it is allowable to consume it without it being formally offered (*appaṭiggahitaka*). Items restricted to the morning (*yāvakālika*) and others are not allowable to be consumed without being formally offered. The four great foul medicines (*Mahāvikaṭa*) are allowable at the specified time because they are intended for times such as when one is bitten by a snake. 'A virtuous lay follower' (*upāsaka*) refers to one who observes the five or ten precepts.

In the tetrad of visitors and others (*āgantuka-catukka*), a monk who enters or wanders in a monastery while carrying an umbrella and wearing sandals, and with his head covered, incurs an offense only if he is a visitor (*āgantuka*), not if he is a resident (*āvāsika*). However, when not performing the duties of a resident, the resident monk incurs an offense, not the visitor. Regarding the remaining offenses occurring through the bodily and vocal doors, both incur them. Regarding uncommon offenses (*asādhāraṇa*), neither the visitor nor the resident incurs them. In the tetrad of those departing (*gamika-catukka*), a monk who leaves without fulfilling the duties of a departer incurs an offense if he is a departer (*gamika*), not if he is a resident. However, when not performing the duties of a resident, the resident monk incurs an offense, not the departer. Regarding the remaining offenses, both incur them; regarding uncommon offenses, neither incurs them.

In the tetrad of diversity of basis (*vatthunānattatā*) and others, the four *pārājika* offenses differ from each other only by basis (*vatthu*), not by the type of offense (*āpatti*). This is because all of them are simply *pārājika* offenses. The same method applies to *saṅghādisesa* and others. In the case of physical contact (*kāyasaṃsagga*) between a monk and a nun, the monk incurs a *saṅghādisesa* offense while the nun incurs a *pārājika* offense. In this way, there is diversity only by offense, not by basis. This is because physical contact itself is the basis for both. Similarly, in cases such as 'in eating garlic, a nun incurs a *pācittiya* offense while a monk incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense,' the application of the method should be understood. The four *pārājika* offenses, together with the thirteen *saṅghādisesa* offenses, [differ] both by basis and by offense...
170:
There is also the state of difference by offense. Thus, offenses such as Saᅅghādisesa differ from Aniyata and others both by object and by offense. For Bhikkhus and Bhikkhunĩs who commit the four Pārājikas together from the beginning, there is neither difference by object nor difference by offense. This same method applies when they commit them separately, and also when they commit the remaining common (sādhāraᅇa) offenses.

In the group of four starting with similarity of object (vatthusabhāga): due to bodily contact (kāyasaᅃsagga) between a Bhikkhu and a Bhikkhunĩ, there is similarity by object, but not similarity by offense. In the four Pārājikas, there is similarity by offense, but not similarity by object. This method also applies to Saᅅghādisesa and others. In the (common) four Pārājikas of a Bhikkhu and a Bhikkhunĩ, there is both similarity by object and similarity by offense. This method applies to all common offenses. In an uncommon (asādhāraᅇa) offense, there is neither similarity by object nor similarity by offense. For the matter which was the first question in the previous group of four is the second in this group; and that which was the second in the previous group is the first in this group. In the third and fourth questions, there is no distinction to be made.

In the group of four regarding the preceptor (upajjhāya): for not performing the duties to be done by a preceptor for a Saddhivihārika, the preceptor incurs an offense, but not the Saddhivihārika. For a Saddhivihārika not performing the duties to be done for a preceptor, the Saddhivihārika incurs an offense, but not the preceptor. In the remaining cases, both incur an offense; in an uncommon offense, neither incurs an offense. This same method applies to the group of four regarding the teacher (ācariya).

In the group of four regarding taking (ādiyanta): a monk who takes a pāda or more than a pāda with his own hand incurs a heavy (garuka) offense. A monk who commands another, saying "Take property worth less than a pāda," incurs a light (lahuka) offense. By this method, the remaining three terms should be understood.

In the group of four regarding those worthy of salutation (abhivādanāraha): in the dining hall of Bhikkhunĩs, starting from the ninth Bhikkhunĩ, even a preceptor Bhikkhunĩ is worthy of salutation but not worthy of rising from one's seat. Generally, for a monk who has not finished his meal, any senior monk is worthy of salutation but not worthy of rising from one's seat. Even for one who has been ordained for sixty years but is undergoing probation (parivāsa), a person ordained on that very day who approaches him is worthy of rising from one's seat but not worthy of salutation. In places where it is not prohibited, a senior monk is worthy of both salutation and rising from one's seat by a junior monk. However, a junior monk is worthy of neither salutation nor rising from one's seat by a senior monk. The first term of the group of four regarding seats (āsanāraha) is similar in meaning to the second term of the previous group, and the second term is similar to the first term.
171:
In the group of four regarding time (kāla): a monk who eats after having refused further food (pavārita) incurs an offense during the proper time (kāla), but not during the wrong time (vikāla). He incurs the offense of eating at the wrong time during the wrong time, but not during the proper time. For the remaining offenses, he incurs them both during the proper time and the wrong time. For an uncommon offense, he incurs it neither during the proper time nor the wrong time. In the group of four regarding acceptance (paᙩiggahita): material food (āmisa) accepted before the meal is allowable during the proper time, but not during the wrong time. A beverage (pānaka) is allowable during the wrong time, but not during the proper time on the next day. Seven-day-limit (sattāhakālika) and life-long-limit (yāvajĩvika) objects are allowable both during the proper time and the wrong time. The three types of objects such as temporary-limit (yāvakālika) whose time has passed, unallowable meat, objects taken by oneself (uggahitaka), and objects not formally accepted (apaᙩiggahitaka) are allowable neither during the proper time nor the wrong time.

In the group of four regarding border regions (paccantima): a monk who establishes a boundary (sĩmā) in the ocean incurs an offense in the border regions, but not in the middle regions (majjhima). A preceptor who ordains with a group of five, or one who uses multi-layered sandals, constant bathing, or skin-rugs, incurs an offense in the middle regions, but not in the border regions. A monk who says, "These four matters are not allowable here," also incurs an offense in the border regions. However, a monk who says, "These matters are allowable here," incurs an offense in the middle regions. For the remaining offenses, he incurs them in both regions. For an uncommon offense, he incurs it nowhere. In the second group of four: the four objects such as ordination with a group of five are allowable in the border regions. Showing that "This object is allowable" is also allowable only in those border regions, but not in the middle regions. Showing that "This object is not allowable" is allowable in the middle regions, but not in the border regions. The remaining allowances such as "Monks, I allow five kinds of salt" are allowable in both regions. Whatever object has been rejected as unallowable is not allowable in either region.

In the group of four regarding inside and so forth (anto-ādi): for offenses such as encroaching on a sleeping place (anupakhajja seyya), one incurs it inside the monastery, but not outside. A monk who leaves behind Saᅅgha-owned couches and so forth in the open air and departs incurs an offense outside, but not inside. For the remaining offenses, he incurs them both inside and outside. For an uncommon offense, he incurs it neither inside nor outside. In the group of four regarding inside the boundary and so forth (antosĩmā-ādi): a visiting monk (āgantuka) who does not fulfill his duties incurs an offense inside the boundary. A monk about to depart (gamiya) incurs an offense outside the boundary. For offenses such as false speech (musāvāda), he incurs them both inside the boundary and outside the boundary. For an uncommon offense, he incurs it nowhere. In the group of four regarding the village (gāma): for an offense due to the Sekhiya rules connected with the interior of a house, he incurs it in the village, but not in the forest. If a Bhikkhunĩ stays in the forest until dawn, she incurs an offense in the forest, but not in the village. For offenses such as false speech, he incurs them both in the village and in the forest. For an uncommon offense, he incurs it nowhere.
172:
The four preliminary duties (pubbakicca) refer to these four preliminary actions (pubbakaraṇa): "sweeping, lighting the lamp, setting out drinking and washing water, and preparing the seats," as stated in the ancient commentaries. However, these four should be known as the "four preliminary duties": "conveying consent and purity (chanda-pārisuddhi), announcing the season (utu-kkhāna), counting the monks (bhikkhu-gaṇanā), and conveying the instruction to the nuns (bhikkhunī-ovāda)."

The four conditions for validity (pattakalla) are: it being the Uposatha day, all monks eligible for the legal act having arrived, the absence of common offenses (sabhāgāpatti), and the absence of persons to be excluded within the forearm's length (hatthapāsa).

The four Pācittiya offenses not mixed with others (ananyapācittiya) are those stated as "based on this reason alone and no other": the training rule on encroaching on a sleeping place (anupakhajja-seyyā-kappana), the training rule beginning with "Come, friend, to the village or town...", intentionally causing remorse (kukkucca-upadahana), and eavesdropping (upassuti-tiṭṭhana).

The four formal authorizations for monks (bhikkhu-sammuṭi) are the four authorizations remaining from the thirteen types of authorizations mentioned in such rules as: "If a monk, without authorization from the monks, should be separated from his three robes even for one night...", "If he should have another new rug made without authorization from the monks...", "If he should be separated [from the robe] for more than [ten days] without authorization from the monks...", and "If he should tell a coarse offense to one who is not ordained without authorization from the monks..."

In the set of four regarding the sick (gilāna-catukka): a sick monk who, despite having a purpose for another medicine, requests a different medicine due to fickleness (lolatā), commits an offense. A non-sick monk who requests medicine without having a purpose for medicine commits an offense. In cases of lying (musāvāda) and so forth, both commit an offense. In cases that are not shared (asādhāraṇa), neither commits an offense. In all other matters, the meaning is clear.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Fours is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Fives

In the section on the Fives, "five fixed persons" refers to those who have committed the five crimes with immediate result (ānantariya-kamma). The "five offenses involving cutting" (chedanaka) should be understood as those involving a couch, a chair, a sitting cloth, a skin-eruption covering cloth, and a rainy-season cloth that exceed the prescribed measurements, as well as the Sugata-robe (which must be cut down to size).

"By five ways" means: through shamelessness, ignorance, remorse, perceiving what is unallowable as allowable, and perceiving what is allowable as unallowable. The five offenses due to lying (musāvāda) are: Pārājika, Thullaccaya, Dukkaṭa, Saṅghādisesa, and Pācittiya. "Wandering without informing" (anāmantacāra) refers to the absence of informing as in the rule: "If a monk, without informing a monk who is present, should wander among families before or after a meal." "Not determining" (anadhiṭṭhāna) refers to eating without determining the time as stated in the rule: "In a group meal, except on an occasion (samaya)..."
173:
Eating after determining the stated occasion is called determination (adhiṭṭhāna). Not doing so is called non-determination (anadhiṭṭhāna). Non-assignment (avikappanā) refers to not performing the assignment (vikappanā) mentioned in the rule on consecutive meals (parampara-bhojana). These five matters are rejected by an alms-food eater (piṇḍapātika) by the very nature of his ascetic practice (dhutaṅga).

"Suspected and strongly suspected" (ussaṅkitaparisaṅkita) means being suspected at first and then repeatedly suspected by those who see or hear [the monk]. Even if one is an Arahant with unshakable fruition, one can still be suspected; therefore, improper resorts (agocara) should be avoided. For one who is seen in such places does not escape from loss of reputation or from blame.

"Sossānika" refers to cloth dropped in a cemetery. "Pāpaṇika" refers to cloth dropped at a shop door. "Thūpacīvara" refers to cloth wrapped around an anthill as an offering. "Ābhisekika" refers to a robe discarded at a bathing place or at a king's consecration site. "Bhatapaṭiyābhata" refers to cloth that was taken to a cemetery and then brought back again. The five great thieves are explained in the training rule on superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma).

"Five offenses arise from the body" means reaching five offenses through the first origin of offenses (the body). These are the offenses stated in the intermediate repetitive section (antarappeyyāla) such as: "A monk, perceiving it as allowable, builds a hut by his own begging." "Five offenses arise from the body and speech" means reaching five offenses through the third origin of offenses (body and speech). These are the offenses stated in that same section such as: "A monk, perceiving it as allowable, builds a hut by arranging it [through others]." "Confessable" (desanāgāminiya) refers to the remaining offenses excluding Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa.

The five formal acts (kamma) are: the four acts of censure (tajjanīya), guidance (niyassa), banishment (pabbājanīya), and reconciliation (paṭisāraṇīya), and the three types of suspension (ukkhepanīya) taken as one. The five offenses in the section on "up to the third time" (yāvatatiyaka) are: the Pārājika, Thullaccaya, and Dukkaṭa incurred by a nun who follows a suspended monk and does not desist after the third admonition; the Saṅghādisesa in admonitions such as those for a follower of a schismatic; and the Pācittiya for not relinquishing a harmful view.

"Not given" (adinna) means not given by another. "Not known" (avidita) means not known because of the absence of the intention to receive. "Unallowable" (akappiya) means not made allowable by the five methods of a contemplative's allowable practice, or other unallowable meat and unallowable food. "Not made leftover" (akatātiritta) means not performing the Vinaya act for leftover food after being satisfied (pavārita).

"Gift of a festival" (samajjadāna) refers to giving theatrical shows or festivals. "Gift of a bull" (usabhadāna) refers to releasing a bull among a herd of cows. "Gift of artistic work" (cittakammadāna) refers to having artistic paintings done in a monastery after building it. This is said here with reference to suggestive artistic works (paṭibhāna-cittakamma) that arouse defilements. Although these five gifts are considered meritorious by the world, they are in fact unmeritorious and unwholesome.
174:
Only unwholesome states arise. In the phrase 'uppannaṃ paṭibhānaṃ', 'paṭibhāna' means the desire to speak. 'These five are difficult to remove' means they are not easily dispelled; however, they can be removed through appropriate means, such as suitable reflection and instruction. In the phrase 'one's own mind is clear', there are these illustrative stories:

The Elder Phussadeva, who resided in Kaṭa-andhakāra, having swept the pagoda courtyard, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and stood there, having generated joy and rapture with the Buddha as his object while looking at the pagoda courtyard, which was spread with sand as evenly as a bed of sinduvāra flowers. At that moment, Māra, manifesting as a large dark monkey like one born at the foot of a mountain, went about scattering cow dung on the courtyard. The Elder, unable to reach Arahantship, swept it again and left. On the second day, Māra did the same in the form of an old ox. On the third day, he manifested as a man with crooked feet and went about dragging his feet. The Elder thought, 'Such an ugly person does not exist in the alms-villages within a league's distance; it must be Māra.' He asked, 'Are you Māra?' Māra replied, 'Yes, Venerable Sir, I am Māra. Now I am unable to deceive you.' The Elder asked, 'Have you ever seen the Tathāgata?' He replied, 'Yes, I have.' The Elder said, 'Māra is of great power; come, manifest a form similar to the physical body of the Blessed One.' Māra said, 'Venerable Sir, it is not possible to manifest such a form exactly, but I will manifest a likeness resembling the Buddha.' He then discarded his own form and stood in a form resembling the Buddha's image. Looking at Māra, the Elder thought, 'If even this Māra, who possesses lust, hatred, and delusion, is this beautiful, how much more beautiful must the Blessed One be, who is entirely free from lust, hatred, and delusion?' Having gained joy with the Buddha as his object and developing insight, he attained Arahantship. Māra said, 'Venerable Sir, I have been deceived by you.' The Elder replied, 'Old Māra, where is the difficulty in deceiving one such as you?'

Also, at the Lokantara Monastery, a young monk named Datta, while looking after sweeping the pagoda courtyard, attained the white kasiṇa. He produced the eight attainments. Then, developing insight, he realized the three lower fruits.

In the phrase 'the minds of others are clear', there are these stories: A young monk named Tissa, having swept the Jambukola pagoda courtyard, stood holding a refuse basket in his hand. At that moment, the Elder Tissadatta, having disembarked from a boat and looking at the pagoda courtyard, knew, 'This is a place swept by one with a developed mind (one who has attained the paths and fruits).' He asked a thousand questions, and the young monk was able to answer all of them. In another monastery, an Elder swept the pagoda courtyard and completed his duty for that day. Four Elders who had come from the Yonaka country to worship the pagoda saw the courtyard and, before entering, stood at the gate. One Elder recollected eight aeons, one sixteen, one twenty (aeons)...
175:
(The young monk named Tissa, having swept the Jambukola pagoda courtyard, stood holding a refuse basket in his hand) and stood there. At that moment, the Elder named Tissadatta, having disembarked from a boat and looking at the pagoda courtyard, knew, 'This is a place swept by one with a developed mind (one who has attained the paths and fruits).' He asked a thousand questions, and the young monk answered all of the questions. In another monastery, an Elder swept the pagoda courtyard and completed his duty. Four Elders who had come from the Yonaka country to worship the pagoda saw the courtyard and, before entering, stood at the gate. One Elder recollected eight aeons, one sixteen, one twenty aeons, and one thirty aeons.

In the phrase 'deities are delighted', there is this story: It is said that in a certain monastery, a monk, after sweeping the pagoda courtyard and the Bodhi tree courtyard, went to bathe. The deities thought, 'Since the founding of this monastery, there has been no monk who has fulfilled the duty of sweeping like this.' With clear and confident minds, they stood holding flowers in their hands. When the Elder returned, he asked, 'In which village do you live?' The deities replied, 'Venerable Sir, we live right here. Since the founding of this monastery, there has been no monk who has fulfilled the duty of sweeping like this. Being pleased with your practice of the duty, we are standing here holding flowers in our hands.'

In the phrase 'it leads to being graceful', there is this story: It is said that a discussion arose concerning a minister's son and the Elder Abhaya: 'Is the minister's son graceful, or is the Elder Abhaya graceful? Let us look at both of them together in one place.' The relatives adorned the minister's son and went, saying, 'We will have him worship the Great Stupa.' The Elder's mother also had a graceful robe made and sent it, saying, 'Let my son have his hair shaved, put on this robe, and worship the Great Stupa surrounded by the community of monks.' The minister's son, surrounded by his relatives, ascended the pagoda courtyard by the eastern gate. The Elder Abhaya, surrounded by the community of monks, ascended the pagoda courtyard by the southern gate. When he met the minister's son on the courtyard, he said, 'Friend, do you dare to compete with me because of the merit of having discarded the rubbish in the place swept by an elder in the past?' It is said that in a past life, the Elder Abhaya was a senior elder who swept the pagoda courtyard in an alms-village, and the minister's son was a great lay devotee who picked up and discarded the rubbish in that swept place.

In the phrase 'the Teacher's instruction is carried out'—this duty of sweeping has been praised by the Buddhas; therefore, one who performs that sweeping is said to have carried out the Teacher's instruction. In this regard, there is this story:
176:
The Venerable Sāriputta went to the Himalayas and, without sweeping a certain mountain cave, entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) and sat there. When the Blessed One reflected, He knew that the Elder was sitting without having swept. He traveled through the air and, having displayed His footprints in the unswept area in front of the Elder, He returned. When the Elder emerged from the attainment and saw the footprints of the Blessed One, he developed a strong sense of moral shame and moral dread (hiri-ottappa). Kneeling down (having paid homage to the footprint-shrine), he thought, "Alas, the Teacher has known that I sat without sweeping. Now, I shall let myself be reproached (humbled) in the midst of the Saṅgha." He then went to the presence of the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala), paid homage, and sat down. The Blessed One asked, "Sāriputta, where did you go?" and then said, "It is not proper for you, who live and move in My vicinity, to sit without having swept." From that time on, even when the Elder stood in a place to fasten his robe-knots, he would only stand after clearing away the rubbish with his feet.

"Does not grasp the limit of one's own speech" means not grasping the limit of one's own words, such as thinking, "In this case, this much of the Pāḷi text is obtained, there is this much of a decision, and I shall speak this much of the Pāḷi text and the decision." A Vinaya master who does not grasp such things as "This is the initial speech of the accuser, this is the subsequent speech; this is the initial speech of the accused, this is the subsequent speech; this much is to be accepted, this much is not to be accepted," is called one who does not grasp the limit of another's speech. "Does not know the offense" means not knowing the distinction between the seven classes of offenses, such as Pārājika or Saṅghādisesa. "Root" (mūla) means not knowing the two roots of offenses: body and speech. "Origin" (samudaya) means not knowing the six origins (samuṭṭhāna) of offenses. It also means not knowing the basis (vatthu) of offenses like Pārājika. "Cessation" (nirodha) means not knowing the cessation of offenses, such as "This offense is settled by confession (desanā), this offense is settled by emergence (vuṭṭhāna—parivāsa, mānatta, abbhāna)." One who does not know the seven ways of settling (samatha) does not know the practice leading to the cessation of offenses.

In the pentad of legal issues (adhikaraṇa-pañcaka), "legal issue" refers to the four types of legal issues. The "roots of legal issues" refer to the thirty-three roots: 12 roots for legal issues arising from disputes (vivādādhikaraṇa), 14 for legal issues arising from accusations (anuvādādhikaraṇa), 6 for legal issues arising from offenses (āpattādhikaraṇa), and 1 for legal issues arising from duties (kiccādhikaraṇa). These will be explained clearly later. The "origin of legal issues" refers to the source (samuṭṭhāna) of legal issues. A legal issue arising from disputes arises based on the eighteen grounds for schism (bhedakara-vatthu). A legal issue arising from accusations is based on the four failures (vipatti). A legal issue arising from offenses is based on the seven classes of offenses (āpattikkhandha). A legal issue arising from duties is based on the four duties of the Saṅgha. Not knowing this classification is what is meant.
177:
The meaning is: "Does not know the cessation of legal issues" means being unable to reach the peaceful settlement of a decision by going from root to root through the true facts, the Vinaya of accusation and cross-examination, and the Teacher's instructions such as the motion (ñatti) and proclamation (kammavācā). A Vinaya master who does not know the seven ways of settling (samatha), such as "This legal issue is settled by two ways of settlement, this by four, this by three, and this by one," is called one who does not know the practice (samatha) leading to the cessation of legal issues. "Does not know the basis" (vatthu) means not knowing the basis of the seven classes of offenses, such as "This basis, like sexual misconduct, is the basis for a Pārājika; this basis, like the emission of semen, is the basis for a Saṅghādisesa." "Does not know the origin" (nidāna) means not knowing, among the seven places of origin, "This training rule was promulgated in this place, and this training rule in that place." "Does not know the regulation" (paññatti) means not knowing the original regulation (paṭhama-paññatti) for various training rules. "Supplementary regulation" (anupaññatti) means not knowing the training rules that were promulgated repeatedly. "The path of connected speech" (anusandhivacanapatha) means not knowing the facts of the case through the connection of the previous and subsequent words of the accuser and the accused (kathānusandhi) and the connection of the decision (viniścayānusandhi). "Does not know the motion" (ñatti) means not knowing the motion in all its aspects. "Does not know the performance (karaṇa) of the motion" means not knowing the function of the motion. It means not knowing that there is a formal act of motion (ñatti-kamma) in the nine instances such as reinstatement (osāraṇā), and not knowing that in formal acts with a motion as the second or fourth part, one stands having reached the state of a formal act after the motion is placed. "Neither skilled in what precedes nor in what follows" means not knowing what should be said first and what should be said later. It also means not knowing that the motion must be placed first and not later. "One who does not know the time" means preaching without being invited or requested, and not knowing the time, the field, and the opportunity for placing a motion.

"Due to foolishness and delusion" means living without knowing the benefits of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) simply out of ignorance and a state of delusion. "One of evil desires" means one who desires the gain of requisites by living in the forest. "Seclusion" (paviveka) refers to physical seclusion (kāya-paviveka), mental seclusion (citta-paviveka), and substratum seclusion (upadhi-paviveka). "Devotion to this purpose" (idamatthitā) refers to the state of having a purpose through this noble practice. It means living by relying only on that devotion to the purpose, without regard for worldly gains (lokāmisa).

"Does not know the observance" (uposatha) means not knowing the nine types of observance. "Formal act of observance" (uposatha-kamma) means not knowing the four types of formal acts of observance, such as those that are illegal and incomplete (adhammā-vaggādi). "Pātimokkha" means not knowing the two codes (mātikā). "Recitation of the Pātimokkha" (uddesa) means not knowing all nine types of Pātimokkha recitation. "Invitation" (pavāraṇā) means not knowing the nine types of invitation. The formal act of invitation is similar to the formal act of observance.
178:
In the five-fold set of uninspiring (apasādika)—'Apasādika' refers to unwholesome actions such as bodily misconduct. 'Pasādika' refers to wholesome actions such as bodily good conduct. 'Ativela' has the meaning of staying for an excessively long time in the houses of the four classes of families, exceeding the limit (such as the time for alms-food). 'Otāra' is the entering of defilements within. 'Saṅkiliṭṭha' is the defilement caused by various offenses such as grave offenses (duṭṭhullāpatti) and offenses of bodily contact (kāyasaṃsaggāpatti). In the five-fold set of purity (visuddhipañcaka), by the inclusion of pavāraṇā, the nine types of pavāraṇā should be understood. The rest of the terms are clear in all places.

## The Explanation of the Five-fold Section is finished.

## The Explanation of the Six-fold Section

In the six-fold sets—The six proper practices (sāmīci) are: 'That monk has not been rehabilitated, and those monks are blameworthy; this is the proper practice (sāmīci) therein', 'Venerable sirs, strive for your own property, let not your property be destroyed; this is the proper practice therein', 'Monk, this bowl is for you; it should be carried until it breaks; this is the proper practice therein', 'Having taken it out from there, it should be shared with the monks; this is the proper practice therein', 'It should be known, it should be asked, it should be investigated; this is the proper practice therein', 'To whomsoever it shall belong, he shall carry it; this is the proper practice therein'—thus, these six proper practices exist even in the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha. The six chedanaka (cutting) offenses are the five mentioned in the five-fold section together with the offense of the water-cloth (udakasāṭikā) for nuns. 'By six modes' (chahākārehi) means: shamelessness, ignorance, doubt (kukkucca), perceiving what is unallowable as allowable, perceiving what is allowable as unallowable, and lapse of mindfulness. Among these six, one falls into an offense due to lapse of mindfulness in cases such as exceeding one night, exceeding six nights, or exceeding seven days. The rest is as previously explained. The six benefits of a Vinaya-expert are the five mentioned in the five-fold section together with 'the Uposatha is established in that monk'.

The six maximum limits (parama) are: 'An extra robe may be kept for a maximum of ten days', 'That monk should lay aside that robe for a maximum of one month', 'That monk should consent to a robe other than that for a maximum of an inner and upper robe (santaruttara)', 'He should stand in silence for a maximum of six times for the purpose (of a robe)', 'A monk, having had a new rug made, should keep it for six years; it should be kept for a maximum of six years', 'They should be carried by one's own hand for a maximum of three yojanas', 'An extra bowl may be kept for a maximum of ten days', 'Medicines that are stored should be consumed for a maximum of seven days', 'That monk should stay apart from that robe for a maximum of six nights', 'A maximum of four kaṃsas, a maximum of two and a half kaṃsas, a maximum of two finger-breadths should be taken, a maximum of eight inches...'
179:
...bed legs not exceeding eight inches, tooth-wood not exceeding eight inches—these are the fourteen maximum limits (parama). Among these fourteen limits, the first six form one six-fold set (chakka). By removing one from that and adding one from the remaining limits, other six-fold sets should also be formed.

The three six-fold sets of 'six offenses' are taught in the Antara-peyyāla. The 'six legal acts' (kamma) are: the four acts of censure (tajjaniya), subordination (niyassa), banishment (pabbājaniya), and reconciliation (paṭisāraṇīya); one act by considering the two (acts) of not seeing and not atoning for an offense as one; and one act for not renouncing a harmful wrong view—making six in total. Regarding bathing, it refers to bathing within half a month (orenaddhamāsaṃ nahāna). The two six-fold sets such as unfinished robes (vippakatacīvara) are explained in the Kathina-khandhaka. All the rest is clear everywhere.

## The Explanation of the Six-fold Section is finished.

## The Explanation of the Seven-fold Section

In the seven-fold sets—The 'seven proper practices (sāmīci)' are to be understood as seven by adding this one to the previously mentioned six: 'That nun has not been rehabilitated, and those nuns are blameworthy; this is the proper practice (sāmīci) therein'. The 'seven unlawful acts on acknowledgment (adhammika paṭiññātakaraṇa)' are explained in the Samatha-khandhaka as follows: 'A monk has committed a Pārājika offense; being charged with the Pārājika, he acknowledges, "I have committed a Saṅghādisesa offense"; the Saṅgha deals with him for a Saṅghādisesa; this is an unlawful act on acknowledgment'. The lawful ones (dhammika) are also explained there. The seven non-offenses (anāpatti) regarding going for business within seven days are taught in the Vassūpanāyika-khandhaka. The 'seven benefits of a Vinaya-expert' are seven, including the five taught in the five-fold section along with 'the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā are established in him'. The 'seven maximum limits (parama)' are the same limits mentioned in the six-fold section, to be applied by way of the seven-fold set. The two seven-fold sets such as 'katacīvaraṃ' are explained in the Kathina-khandhaka.

'It should be seen that there is no offense for the monk', 'It should be seen that there is an offense for the monk', 'The offense for the monk should be atoned'—among these three seven-fold sets, two are unlawful (adhammika) and one is lawful (dhammika). All three are explained in the Campeyyaka-khandhaka. 'Asaddhamma' means the teachings of the wicked or bad teachings; it has the meaning of unlovely, inferior, and low. 'Saddhamma' means the teachings of the virtuous ones such as the Buddha or good teachings; it has the meaning of good and noble. All the rest is clear everywhere.

## The Explanation of the Seven-fold Section is finished.
180:
## Explanation of the Section of Eights
In the Aᅩᅩhakavāra (the section presented in groups of eight): "Eight benefits" refers to the benefits taught in the Kosambaka-khandhaka, such as: "We will not perform the Uposatha with this monk; we will perform the Uposatha excluding this monk. We will not perform Pavāraᅆā with this monk; we will not perform Saᅅgha-kamma; we will not sit in seats; we will not sit while drinking congee; we will not sit in the dining hall; we will not live under the same roof; we will not perform respectful salutation, rising to greet, saluting with joined palms, or acts of homage with this monk; we will perform them only by excluding this monk." The same method applies to the second set of eight, as that second set of eight was also taught in the Kosambaka-khandhaka in this manner.

"Eight Yāvatatiyaka offenses" refers to the four Yāvatatiyaka offenses included in the thirteen Saᅅghādisesas of the monks, and the four Yāvatatiyaka offenses of the bhikkhunĩs that are not shared with the monks from their seventeen Saᅅghādisesas, totaling eight. "Corrupting families in eight ways" means corrupting families through these eight: giving flowers, giving fruits, giving scented powder, giving clay, giving tooth-sticks, giving bamboo, providing medical treatment, or acting as a messenger on foot. In the Cĩvara-khandhaka, eight Mātikās are taught; the other eight Mātikās are taught in the Kaᅩhina-khandhaka. "By eight unrighteous things (asaddhamma)" refers to gain, loss, fame, obscurity, honor, lack of honor, evil desire, and evil friendship. The "eight worldly conditions" (lokadhamma) are: excessive attachment to gain, resentment and weariness at loss; likewise with fame and obscurity, praise and blame, attachment to pleasure, and resentment or despair at pain. "Eight-factored false speech" (musāvāda) refers to false speech endowed with eight factors, combining the seven factors mentioned in the Pali text with the factor "changing one's perception" (saā-vini-dhāya).

"Eight factors of Uposatha" means:
"One should not kill a living being, nor take what is not given,
One should not speak lies, nor be a consumer of intoxicants,
One should abstain from unchaste conduct, from sexual intercourse,
One should not eat at night, at the wrong time.
One should not wear garlands, nor use perfumes,
One should sleep on a couch or on a bed spread upon the ground;
This is called the eight-factored Uposatha,
Proclaimed by the Buddha, who has reached the end of suffering.’’
181:
In this way, the eight factors have been taught. The "eight factors of a messenger" (dũteyyaᅅga) are the eight factors taught in the Saᅅghabhedaka-khandhaka in the manner beginning with: "Here, monks, a monk is one who listens (to words) and remembers them, and one who makes others hear," and so on. The duties of ascetics (titthiyavatta) are explained in the Mahā-khandhaka (Mahāvagga, Pabbajjā-khandhaka). The eight Anatiritta and eight Atiritta are explained in the Pavāraᅆā-sikkhāpada.

"Eight persons to be respected by rising from one's seat" means that in the dining hall, one must rise from one's seat for eight senior bhikkhunĩs, and one must also give them a seat. The "laywoman" (upāsikā) is Visākhā. The "eight benefits of a Vinaya-holder" (vinayadhara) are to be understood as eight by adding these three—"The Uposatha, Pavāraᅆā, and Saᅅgha-kamma are entrusted to that person"—to the five benefits taught in the Pacaka-nipāta. The "eight supreme things" are to be understood by applying the previously mentioned supreme things to the group of eight. "One should practice well in eight things" refers to the eight things explained in the Samatha-khandhaka in the manner beginning with: "The Uposatha should not be obstructed for a monk of good standing (pakatatta), nor should the Pavāraᅆā be obstructed," and so on. The remaining groups of words have clear meanings in all places.

## The Explanation of the Section of Eights is finished.

## Explanation of the Section of Nines

In the Navaka-nipātas: "Nine grounds for resentment" (āghātavatthu) are the nine beginning with "He has done me harm." "Nine ways of removing resentment" are the nine beginning with "He has done me harm; where can I get [him not to do so]?" and thus removing resentment. "Nine things where resentment is removed" (vinĩtavatthu) are the distant avoidance, abstinence, separate avoidance, and the absolute destruction of the cause from the nine grounds for resentment. "The Saᅅgha is divided by nine causes" means: "Upāli, because of nine monks, or because of more than nine monks, there is a rift in the Saᅅgha and a schism in the Saᅅgha." The "nine supreme things" are to be understood by applying the previously mentioned supreme things to the group of nine.

"Nine things rooted in craving" (taᅆhāmũlaka) are: dependent on craving, there is seeking (pariyesanā); dependent on seeking, there is gain (lābha); dependent on gain, there is decision (vinicchaya); dependent on decision, there is slight liking and great attachment (chandarāga); dependent on chandarāga, there is the final determination of 'I' and 'mine' (ajjhosāna); dependent on ajjhosāna, there is possession (pariggaha); dependent on possession, there is stinginess (macchariya); dependent on stinginess, there is protection (ārakkhā); and because of the cause of protection, there is the taking up of sticks, the taking up of weapons, quarreling, disputing, speaking in opposition, saying 'You! You!', slandering, and lying.

"Nine types of conceit" (māna) are the nine types of conceit beginning with "I am better than the one who is better." "Nine robes" are the nine robes taught in the manner of the triple robe (ticĩvara) or the rainy-season robe, and so on. They should not be assigned (vikappana) from the time they are determined (adhiᅩᅩhāna). "Nine unrighteous gifts" are: diverting a gift intended for the Saᅅgha to another Saᅅgha, to a Cetiya, or to an individual (3 types); diverting a gift intended for a Cetiya to another Cetiya, to the Saᅅgha, or to an individual...
182:
(The nine unrighteous gifts are:) Diverting a gain intended for one Saṅgha to another Saṅgha, or to a Cetiya, or to an individual; diverting a gain intended for a Cetiya to another Cetiya, or to the Saṅgha, or to an individual; diverting a gain intended for an individual to another individual, or to the Saṅgha, or to a Cetiya—thus it is said.

The nine unrighteous acceptances and the nine unrighteous uses are the acceptance and use of those very unrighteous gifts. The three righteous gifts are: giving a gain intended for the Saṅgha to the Saṅgha itself, giving a gain intended for a Cetiya to the Cetiya itself, and giving a gain intended for an individual to the individual himself—these are the three. The acceptance and use of those very righteous gifts are also righteous acceptance and use. The nine unrighteous solicitations (saññatti) are: an individual who speaks contrary to the Dhamma, a group of monks who speak contrary to the Dhamma, and a Saṅgha that speaks contrary to the Dhamma—these three triads have been explained in the Samathakkhandhaka. Righteous solicitations have also been explained there in the same manner, starting with "an individual who speaks according to the Dhamma." Regarding unrighteous acts (adhamma-kamma), two sets of nine have been explained in the explanation of the first training rule of the Bhikkhunovādavagga by way of Pācittiya offenses. Regarding righteous acts (dhamma-kamma), two sets of nine have been explained in the same place by way of Dukkaṭa offenses. In all other remaining sets of nine, the meaning is clear.

## The Commentary on the Section of Nines is finished.

## Commentary on the Section of Tens

In the tens—the ten grounds for resentment (āghātavatthu) are the nine mentioned in the section of nines together with this one: "Resentment arises even in an improper place." The ten ways of removing resentment (āghātapaṭivinaya) should also be known as the nine mentioned there together with this one: "Resentment arises in an improper place; how can it be obtained here? Thus one removes resentment." The ten disciplined matters (vinītavatthu) are the ten consisting of abstinence from the ten grounds for resentment. Wrong view with ten bases should be understood by way of "There is no result of giving," etc. Right view should be understood by way of "There is a result of giving," etc. Extremist view (antaggāhikadiṭṭhi) should be understood by way of "The world is eternal," etc. The ten wrongnesses (micchatta) are the states starting from wrong view and ending with wrong liberation. Their opposites, starting from right view, are called the ten rightnesses (sammatta). The taking of voting tickets (salākaggāha) has been explained in the Samathakkhandhaka.

"A monk endowed with ten qualities should be appointed for a committee (ubbāhikā)" means a monk endowed with the ten qualities taught in the Samathakkhandhaka, such as "He is virtuous," etc. The ten dangers of entering a royal harem have been explained in the Rāja Sikkhāpada. The ten objects of giving (dānavatthu) are: food, drink, cloth, vehicle, garland, scent, unguent, bedding and lodging, and accessories for lamps. The ten gems (ratana) are: pearl, crystal, beryl, etc. The ten types of rag-robes (paṃsukūla) are: rag-robes from a cemetery...
183:
...cloth dropped at a market gate, cloth gnawed by mice, cloth gnawed by termites, cloth scorched by fire, cloth gnawed by cows, cloth gnawed by goats, cloth wrapped around an anthill and discarded, cloth discarded at a place of consecration, and cloth taken to a cemetery and brought back—in these rag-robes, a monk should make an effort. Regarding the ten ways of wearing robes, it is said in the Kurundī Commentary that there are ten by way of the teaching: "They wear robes that are entirely blue-black." However, in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is said there are ten by adding a bathing cloth (udakasāṭika) or a bodice (saṅkaccika) to the nine allowable robes.

Persons not to be saluted have been explained in the Senāsanakkhandhaka. The ten grounds for abuse (akkosavatthu) have been explained in the Omasavāda Sikkhāpada. The ten modes of slander have been explained in the Pesuñña Sikkhāpada. The ten types of lodgings (senāsana) are: couch, bench, bolster, pillow, coarse cloth, coverlet, mat, piece of skin, sitting cloth, grass mat, and leaf mat. Regarding the statement "They requested ten boons," Visākhā requested eight, King Suddhodana requested one, and Jīvaka requested one. The benefits of gruel and unallowable meats have been explained in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka. All other remaining matters are clear in every place.

## The Commentary on the Section of Tens is finished.

## Commentary on the Section of Elevens

In the elevens—the eleven are the eleven types of persons such as eunuchs (paṇḍaka), etc. The eleven types of sandals are the ten made of gems and one made of wood. Sandals made of grass, muñja-grass, or pabbaja-grass, etc., are included under wooden sandals. The eleven bowls are the ten made of gems together with one made of copper or wood. The eleven robes are the eleven starting with the entirely blue-black robe. The yāvatatiyaka (those involving the third announcement) are: a nun who follows a suspended monk, the eight Saṅghādisesa offenses, Ariṭṭha the monk, and Caṇḍakāḷī the nun. The eleven obstructive factors (antarāyikadhamma) are those starting with "nasi animittā," etc. The eleven robes to be determined (adhiṭṭhāna) are: the triple robe (3), the rain-bathing cloth, the sitting cloth, the coverlet, the skin-eruption covering cloth, the face-wiping cloth, the accessory cloth, the bathing cloth, and the bodice. These very robes, from the time they are determined, should not be assigned (vikappana). Buttons (gaṇṭhikā) and ties (vidhā), together with those made of thread, are eleven; all of them have been explained in the Khuddakakkhandhaka. The types of soil have been explained in the Pathavīkhaṇana Sikkhāpada. Lapses of dependence (nissaya) are eleven: five from the preceptor (upajjhāya) and six from the teacher (ācariya). Persons not to be saluted are eleven, including the naked monk; all of them have been explained in the Senāsanakkhandhaka.
184:
... have been explained in detail. The eleven paramas (excellences) should be understood by applying the elevenfold method to the fourteen paramas previously mentioned. The eleven boons are the ten boons previously mentioned together with the boon requested by Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. The eleven defects of the boundary (sīmā) will appear in the Kammavagga in the manner beginning with "they designate a boundary that is too small."

Regarding the person who abuses and threatens, there are eleven disadvantages: "Monks, for a monk who abuses, threatens, and reviles the Noble Ones and his fellow practitioners, it is impossible, there is no chance, that he will not encounter one of the eleven misfortunes. What are the eleven? He does not attain the unattained; he falls away from what he has attained; the true Dhamma is not purified for him; or he has an overestimation of himself regarding the true Dhamma; or he lives the holy life dissatisfied; or he commits a certain defiled offense; or he gives up the training and returns to the lower life (lay life); or he suffers from a severe illness; or he falls into madness or mental distraction; or he dies confused; and after the breaking up of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, or hell." In this context, "true Dhamma" (saddhamma) refers to the Word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana).

## Āsevitāya means because it has been cultivated from the beginning. Bhāvitāya means because it has been produced or increased.

Bahulīkatāya means because it has been done repeatedly. Yānikatāya means because it has been made like a well-yoked vehicle. Vatthukatāya means because it has been made so as to be a firm foundation. Anuṭṭhitāya means the sense of being repeatedly practiced or constantly established. Paricitāya means the sense of being accumulated on all sides, accumulated in all directions, cultivated, developed, and further increased. Susamāraddhāya means the sense of being well-undertaken or brought to mastery. One does not see bad dreams; one only sees good dreams that are a cause for growth. "Deities protect him" means the guardian deities provide righteous protection. "The mind is quickly concentrated" means it refers to the rapid concentration of the mind. "If he cannot penetrate the higher Dhamma" means if he has not yet realized Arahatship, which is higher than the mettā-jhāna, and dies while being a trainee (sekha) or a worldling (puthujjana), he will be reborn in the Brahma world. The remaining sentences are clear in all places.

## The explanation of the elevenfold section is finished.

## The explanation of the Ekuttarika is finished.
185:
## Answers to Questions on Uposatha and Others

In the answers to questions such as "What is the beginning of the Uposatha act?", unity is the beginning. The physical unity (kāya-sāmaggī) of the monks who have gathered after intending to "perform the Uposatha," clearing the boundary (sīmā), and bringing the consent (chanda) and purity (pārisuddhi), is the beginning. The action of reciting the Pātimokkha after performing the preliminary duties is the middle. "In that boundary, all monks, being in unity, rejoicing, and without dispute, should train themselves"—this conclusion of the Pātimokkha is the end.

The beginning of the Pavāraṇā act is also the physical unity of the monks who have gathered after intending to "perform the Pavāraṇā," clearing the boundary, and bringing the consent for Pavāraṇā. The motion (ñatti) for Pavāraṇā and the Pavāraṇā statement (invitation) are the middle, and the statement of the youngest monk in the Saṅgha, "When I see it, I shall atone for it," is the end.

In the act of censure (Tajjanīyakamma) and others, the "subject matter" (vatthu) is the reason for which the act should be performed; that reason is called the subject matter. The "person" (puggala) is the one who committed that act. "The Saṅgha has performed the act of censure against the monk named so-and-so; it is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent; thus I record this act"—this final statement of each formal act (kammavācā) is the end. The remaining words are very clear in all places.

## The explanation of the answers to questions on Uposatha and others is finished.

## The explanation of the Treatise on the Reasons (Atthavasa-pakaraṇa)

In the Atthavasa-pakaraṇa, the decision that should be stated regarding "ten reasons" (dasa atthavase) and so on has already been stated in the commentary on the first Pārājika. In "that which is the excellence of the Saṅgha is the comfort of the Saṅgha" and so on, each preceding term is the meaning of each succeeding term.

In the passage "one hundred meanings, one hundred Dhammas" and so on, one hundred terms are taught by taking each of those ten terms as a base and combining them ten times. Among those hundred terms, one hundred meanings (atthasata) should be understood by way of the latter terms, and one hundred Dhammas (dhammasata) should be understood by way of the former terms. Alternatively, the Buddha prescribed the training rules for his disciples based on ten special benefits; those benefits were previously explained in the commentary on the first Pārājika in the manner: "Therein, saṅghasuṭṭhutā means the excellent state of the Saṅgha; it is the state of accepting words like 'Excellent, Devas' as in the place where 'Excellent, Bhante' occurs. For one who accepts the words of the Tathāgata, those words..."
186:
... are for his welfare and happiness for a long time. Therefore, for the sake of making the Saṅgha accept my words as "Excellent, Bhante," I shall prescribe [the rules] by showing the disadvantage in not accepting and the benefit in accepting, without overwhelming them by force—desiring to make this meaning clear, he said "for the excellence of the Saṅgha" (saṅghasuṭṭhutāya), and so on. Because those benefits (atthavasa) appear here ten times, one hundred meanings (atthasata) should be understood, and one hundred Dhammas (dhammasata) should be understood by way of the terms that illuminate those meanings. Now, two hundred linguistic expressions (niruttisata) should be understood: one hundred linguistic expressions by way of the sounds (nirutti) that illuminate the meanings, and one hundred linguistic expressions by way of the sounds that are the Dhammas. Also, four hundred types of knowledge (ñāṇasata) should be understood: one hundred knowledges in the hundred meanings, one hundred knowledges in the hundred Dhammas, and two hundred knowledges in the two hundred linguistic expressions.

One hundred meanings, one hundred Dhammas,
Two hundred linguistic expressions,
Four hundred types of knowledge,
(Should be understood) in the treatise on the reasons (Atthavasa-pakaraṇa).

Thus, this statement was made; it was made based on the reason already mentioned.

## Thus, in the commentary on the Vinaya called the Samantapāsādikā,
## The explanation of the Mahāvagga is finished.
187:
## Commentary on the First Collection of Verses
## Commentary on the Training Rules Laid Down in the Seven Cities
'Ekāṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā' means placing the robe over one shoulder, which implies properly arranging the upper robe. 'Paggaṇhitvāna añjaliṃ' means raising the hands in salutation, glowing with the ten fingernails joined together. 'Āsīsamānarūpo vā' means having the appearance of one who aspires or longs for something. 'Kissa tvaṃ idha māgato' means for what reason and longing for what benefit have you come here? Who said this? It was the Fully Enlightened Buddha. To whom did he say this? To the Venerable Upāli. Thus, the Venerable Upāli approached the Blessed One and asked this verse beginning with 'dvīsu vinayesu'. Then the Blessed One answered that question by speaking the words beginning with 'bhaddako te ummaṅgo'. This method is the same in all places. Thus, during the Buddha's lifetime, the Elder Upāli asked all these questions and the Blessed One answered them. However, at the time of the Council, the Elder Mahākassapa asked and the Elder Upāli answered.

Among those questions and answers, 'bhaddako te ummaṅgo' means your questions are excellent. Indeed, a question is called 'ummaṅga' (emergence/tunnel) because it stands out by emerging from the darkness of ignorance. 'Taggha' is a particle used in the sense of cause or reason. It means, "Because you ask me (with a proper reason), I shall tell you." Alternatively, it can be in the sense of acceptance; for by this word 'taggha', he accepts the question and then says he will answer. The three training rules, 'samādahitvā visibbentī', 'sāmisena', and 'sasitthakaṃ', were laid down only in the Bhagga country.

## Commentary on the Four Failures
'Yaṃ taṃ pucchimhā' means that which we asked. 'Akittayī' means he spoke or answered. 'No' means to us. 'Taṃ taṃ byākataṃ' means that whatever was asked, that very thing was answered. 'Anaññathā' means answering exactly as asked, without doing otherwise.

In the phrase 'ye duṭṭhullā sā sīlavipattī', although the name 'sīlavipatti' (failure in virtue) does not actually appear in the question, this was said because of the desire to answer regarding gross (duṭṭhulla) offenses. Indeed, among the four failures, gross offenses are included in one failure (sīlavipatti), while non-gross (aduṭṭhulla) offenses are included in the other three failures. Therefore, after saying 'ye duṭṭhullā sā sīlavipattī', he said 'pārājikaṃ saṅghādiseso sīlavipattīti vuccati' (Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa are called failure in virtue) to show that failure in virtue in detail.
188:
Now, to show the non-gross offenses by means of the three failures, he spoke the words beginning with 'thullaccayaṃ'. In that context, the phrase "abuses with the intention to mock" was said to show the basis for the 'dubbhāsita' (wrong speech) offense.

'Abbhācikkhantī' (they misrepresent) means they misrepresent by saying, "I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus."

'Ayaṃ sā ājīvavipattisammataṃ' means this is known as the fourth failure called 'ājīvavipatti' (failure in livelihood), which is comprised of six training rules. By this much, the question regarding 'aduṭṭhulla' (non-gross) is answered.

Now, to answer the question 'ye ca yāvatatiyakā' (which are the rules involving the third admonition), he spoke the words beginning with 'ekādasa' (eleven).

## Commentary on Rules Involving Cutting, etc.
Since the question 'ye ca yāvatatiyakā' was answered by way of number as "the rules involving the third admonition are eleven," he then asked other intermediate questions following the sequence of numbers, such as "how many involve cutting (chedanaka)?" To answer those, he said "the rules involving cutting are six," and so on. In that context, only this part is new: "one involving breaking (bhedanaka), one involving tearing out (uddālanaka), and sixteen are known as being laid down with the word 'knowing' (jānaṃ)." The rest have already been detailed in the Mahāvagga. Among those new points, "one involving breaking" refers to the needle-case rule (sūcighara). "One involving tearing out" refers to the couch or bench stuffed with cotton (tūlonaddhamañcapīṭha) rule. 'Sodasa' means sixteen. 'Jānanti paññattā' means training rules laid down by speaking the word "knowing" (jānaṃ).

They should be understood as follows: "Knowing that Saṅgha gains have been diverted to oneself, one diverts them; knowing that a monk has arrived first, one encroaches upon him by sitting down; knowing that water contains living beings, one sprinkles it or causes it to be sprinkled on grass or clay; knowing that alms-food was prepared through the prompting of a bhikkhunī, one eats it; knowing a Pācittiya offense while being concerned with disparaging, one eats; knowing that water contains living beings, one uses it; knowing a legal issue has been settled according to the Dhamma, one reopens it; knowing a gross offense, one conceals it; knowing a person is under twenty years of age, one ordains him; knowing a caravan consists of thieves, one travels with them; knowing a monk holds such views and has not acted according to the rule, one associates with him; knowing a novice has been expelled as such, one associates with him; knowing that Saṅgha gains have been diverted to an individual, one diverts them; knowing a bhikkhunī has committed a Pārājika offense, one does not accuse her oneself; knowing a female thief is liable to execution, one ordains her without asking permission; knowing a monastery has monks present, one enters without asking permission."
189:
## Commentary on the Unshared [Rules], etc.
Now, wishing to answer the previous question, "What is shared and what is unshared?", the author says, "Two hundred and twenty," and so on. In that passage, among the training rules not shared with bhikkhunīs (i.e., those pertaining only to bhikkhus), the six Saṅghādisesas are: Vissaṭṭhi (emission of semen), Kāyasaṃsagga (physical contact), Duṭṭhullavācā (lewd words), Attakāmapāricariya (serving one's own lusts), Kuṭikāra (building a hut), and Vihārakāra (building a vihāra). Together with the two Aniyatas, these training rules are eight.

The twelve Nissaggiyas are: Dhovana (washing of robes), Paṭiggaha (receiving of robes), Koseyya (silk), Suddhakaḷaka (pure black wool), Dvebhāga (two parts), Chabbassa (six years), Nisīdana (sitting mat), the two Lomas (wool and washing of wool), Paṭhamapatta (the first bowl), Vassikasāṭika (rain-cloth), and Āraññaka (forest-dweller). These are the twelve.

The twenty-two Khuddakas (Pācittiyas) are: the entire Bhikkhunovādaka-vagga, Paramparabhojana (consecutive meals), Anatiritta (not left over), Abhihaṭa (brought), Paṇītabhojana (sumptuous food), Acelaka (naked ascetic), Ūnavīsativassa (under twenty years), Duṭṭhullachādana (concealing a serious offense), Mātugāmena saddhiṃ saṃvidhāya ekaddhānamaggapaṭipajjana (traveling along a path by appointment with a woman), Anikkantarājaka (king not departed), Santam bhikkhuṃ anာpucchā vikāle gāmappavesana (entering a village at the wrong time without informing a resident monk), Nisīdanapamāṇātikkanta (exceeding the measure of a sitting mat), and Vassikasāṭikapamāṇātikkanta (exceeding the measure of a rain-cloth). These twenty-two training rules are declared among the Khuddakas (Pācittiyas).

Among the training rules not shared with bhikkhus (i.e., those pertaining only to bhikkhunīs), the phrase "Ten are expelled from the Saṅgha" refers to the ten training rules taught in the Vibhaṅga as "expelled from the Saṅgha," which appear in the Mātikā as "Nissāraṇīya Saṅghādisesa." The twelve Nissaggiyas are also those Nissaggiyas analyzed in the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga. The Khuddakas (Pācittiyas) are also those analyzed in that Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga. Likewise, there are four Pāṭidesanīyas. Thus, in the Vibhaṅga, there are 130 training rules for bhikkhunīs that are not shared with bhikkhus. The remaining explanation in this answer regarding shared and unshared rules is clear.

Now, wishing to answer the question, "Failures and by which settlements are they settled?", the author says, "Only eight Pārājikas," and so on. In that passage, by the word "Durāsadā" (dangerous/difficult to approach), he shows the state of those Pārājikas as being accompanied by danger.
190:
He shows the state of being accompanied by danger (of these Pārājikas). Like cobras and such, these Pārājikas are difficult to approach; they are not fit to be approached; if they are committed, they lead to the destruction of the root in the Dispensation.

"Tālavatthusamūpamā" means having a simile like uprooting an entire palmyra tree and leaving only the site where the palmyra tree stood. Just as a palmyra tree that has been reduced to only its site cannot become normal again, even so, those who have fallen into Pārājika cannot become normal monks again.

Having thus shown the simile shared by all Pārājikas, wishing to show the simile taught for each individual Pārājika, he says, "Paṇḍupalāso" (a withered leaf), and so on. "Aဝirūḷhī bhavanti te" means that just as these yellowed, withered leaves and such cannot flourish again by becoming green and so on, even so, those who have fallen into Pārājika cannot flourish because they can no longer possess the original virtue (pakatisīla). By this sequence of words, in this answer to "Failures and by which settlements are they settled?", it is first shown that these eight Pārājika failures cannot be settled by any settlements (samatha). To show the failures (offenses) that can be settled, he says, "Twenty-three Saṅghādisesas," and so on. In that passage, the phrase "by three settlements" is an all-inclusive statement. Indeed, Saṅghādisesa offenses are settled by two settlements; they are not settled by Tiṇavatthāraka (covering with grass). The remaining offenses are settled by all three settlements.

"Two Uposathas, two Pavāraṇās"—this is said by way of bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs. This is said only to show the different classifications of Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, not by way of settling them through settlements. Indeed, the four—Bhikkhu-uposatha, Bhikkhunī-uposatha, Bhikkhu-pavāraṇā, and Bhikkhunī-pavāraṇā—are also analyzed classifications. "Four acts" refers to Uposatha acts such as those that are unlawful and incomplete (adhammenavagga). "Five recitations and four, not otherwise" means there are five recitations of the Pātimokkha for bhikkhus and four for bhikkhunīs; they do not occur in any other way. These are also other analyzed classifications. These classifications, "There are seven classes of offenses and four legal questions (adhikaraṇa)," are settled by settlements; therefore, he says, "by seven settlements," and so on.

Or, alternatively, based on these four classifications—"Two Uposathas, two Pavāraṇās, four acts, five recitations and four, not otherwise"—whatever offenses are committed in the manner of "they are destroyed, they are ruined," etc., since those offenses are settled only by the aforementioned types of settlements, it should be understood that those classifications are also mentioned for the purpose of showing the settlement of the offenses rooted in them. "One [settlement] for the duty" means that Kiccādhikaraṇa (legal questions of duties) is settled by one settlement.
191:
## Explanation of Offenses beginning with Pārājika

Having thus answered all the questions according to the sequence of inquiry, the following words beginning with "Pārājikaṃ" are now spoken to show merely the individual definitions of the classes of offenses (āpattikkhandha) included in the statement "There are seven classes of offenses."

In the verse beginning with "Pārājikaṃ," this is the meaning: Among the Pārājikas concerning the person, the offense, and the training rule, that which is called the Pārājika offense is spoken of. Because the person who commits that offense is defeated, has met with defeat, has fallen away from the True Dhamma, has failed, has slipped, and has been excluded, even if that person has not yet been expelled, there is no longer communion (saṃvāsa) such as the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā. For that reason, this offense is called Pārājika. The summary of the meaning here is: because one is defeated by it, this offense is called Pārājika.

In the second verse also, without emphasizing the literal wording but to show only the meaning, the words beginning with "saṅgho va deti parivāsaṃ" (the Saṅgha indeed gives the probation) are spoken. The meaning here is: for a person who has committed this offense and wishes to rise from it, the Saṅgha is required at the beginning of the rising from the offense for the purpose of giving probation (parivāsa); and in the middle, for the rest of the process, for the purpose of giving the manatta (mānatta), or for the purpose of giving the manatta together with the rehabilitation (mūlāyapaṭikassana); and at the end, for the purpose of the rehabilitation (abbhāna). Since not even a single formal act (kamma) can be performed here without the Saṅgha, and because the Saṅgha is required at the beginning as well as in the remaining middle and end, it is called "Saṅghādisesa."

In the third verse, "aniyatao na niyato" means: because it is not fixed, therefore this class of offense is called Aniyata. For what reason is it not fixed? Because the training rule is made in an indefinite way (anekāṃsikatā). How is it indefinite? It is stated there that it is to be dealt with by any one of the three cases (ṭhāna); therefore, it is called "Aniyata," and that class of offense is called Aniyata. Just as it is any one of the three cases, so too, where any one of two cases is mentioned, that offense is also Aniyata.

In the fourth verse, "accayao tena samo natthi" means: among the offenses that can be cleared by confession (desanāgāminī), there is no gross offense equal to that offense; therefore, it is called thus. Because the fault is gross (thūla), this offense is called "Thullaccaya."
192:
In the fifth verse, it is stated "having relinquished, one confesses"; because it must be confessed after relinquishing [the object], it is called "Nissaggiya."

In the sixth verse, "causes wholesome states to fall" means that for one who intentionally commits the offense, it causes the wholesome mind, known as wholesome states, to fall; therefore, because it causes the mind to fall, it is called "Pācittiya." Because that offense which causes the mind to fall is like an offense against the Noble Path and is a cause for mental confusion, it is also called "offending against the Noble Path, a ground for mental confusion."

In the verses on Pāṭidesanīya, the words beginning with "a monk being unrelated" are spoken only to show the reason for the blameworthy nature stated as "Friend, I have committed a blameworthy state." Because it must be confessed separately, that offense is called "Pāṭidesanīya."

In the verse on Dukkaṭa, "aparaddha, viraddha, and khalita" are all synonyms for "Dukkaṭa" mentioned in the phrase "yañca dukkaṭaṃ." That which is badly done or done in a deformed way is called Dukkaṭa. That Dukkaṭa is called "aparaddha" (wrongdoing) because it is not done as the Teacher taught; it is called "viraddha" (failure) because it occurs by deviating from the wholesome; it is called "khalita" (slip) because it does not reach the conduct and practice of the Noble Ones. "What a person does" is an illustration of the analogy for this Dukkaṭa. Its meaning is: just as in the world, when people do evil either openly or in secret, they make it known as a "bad deed" (dukkaṭa), so too this offense is an evil because it is loathed by the Buddha and because of its inferior nature; therefore, it should be known as "Dukkaṭa."

In the verse on Dubbhāsita, "dubbhāsita, durābhaṭṭha" means it is called "durābhaṭṭha" because it is badly spoken or wrongly uttered. A word that is badly spoken is meant by "Dubbhāsita." What else? It is also called "Dubbhāsita" because the word is defiled and because it is censured by the wise. Because of that defiled nature and because of the censure by the wise, this offense is called thus; it is called "Dubbhāsita."

In the verse on Sekhiya, by the method beginning with "this is the beginning and the conduct," it is shown that it belongs to the trainee (sekha). Therefore, because it belongs to the trainee, it is called "Sekhiya"; this is the summary of the meaning here. It should be understood that this was spoken to clarify the meaning included by the words of request, "Indeed, let us hear your words," even though it was not included in the questions beginning with "heavy or light."
193:
The same method applies to the verse beginning with "Channamativassati". In that verse, "Channamativassati" means that, first of all, if a physical house is not covered (thatched) with grass and so on, the rain leaks in (wets it). This "house" called an offense (āpatti) "leaks" if it is concealed. This is because a monk who conceals an original offense (mūlāpatti) falls into another new offense. "Viwataṃ nātivassati" means that if a physical house is well-covered and not opened (uncovered), the rain does not leak in. This "house" called an offense does not "leak" if it is opened (revealed). This is because a monk who reveals an original offense either confesses an offense that can be cleared by confession (desanāgāmī) or emerges from an offense that requires rehabilitation (vuṭṭhānagāmī), thereby being established in a state of purity. In the future, being restrained, he does not fall into another offense. Therefore, in the phrase "Channaṃ vivaretha", it means that for that reason, one should reveal a concealed offense by confessing a desanāgāmī offense or by emerging from a vuṭṭhānagāmī offense. "Evaṃ taṃ nātivassati" means that such an opened house of offense no longer leaks.

"Gati migānaṃ pavanaṃ" means that for deer being pursued by animals such as tigers in an open field, the forest thick with trees and such is their destination (refuge). Upon reaching that forest, those animals find relief. In this same way, the sky is the destination (resting place) of birds. Because it is the state that must inevitably be reached, destruction (vibhava) is the destination of conditioned things (saṅkhata dhamma). The destruction of all conditioned things is indeed their destination (gati). This is because those conditioned things are unable to remain without reaching destruction. Even after remaining for a very long time, Nibbāna is the destination of the Arahant. For the Arahant whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu) is certainly the destination (gati).
