## The explanation of the first collection of verses is finished.
194:
## Classification of Legal Processes (Adhikaraṇa)
## Explanation of the Types of Reopening (Ukkoṭa), etc.
In presenting the classification of legal processes, these ten types of reopening (ukkoṭa) are shown as the reopening of legal processes. Furthermore, to show the reopening of settlements (samatha) through the reopening of legal processes, it was said: "How many settlements does one who reopens a dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa) reopen?" and so on. In that context, one who reopens a dispute reopens two settlements: verdict in the presence (sammukhāvinaya) and decision by majority (yebhuyyasika). This means he objects to or rejects these two. One who reopens an accusation (anuvādādhikaraṇa) reopens these four settlements: sammukhāvinaya, verdict of innocence due to mindfulness (sativinaya), verdict of past insanity (amūḷhavinaya), and act of further punishment (tassapāpiyasika). One who reopens an offense (āpattādhikaraṇa) reopens these three settlements: sammukhāvinaya, acting according to acknowledgement (paṭiññātakaraṇa), and covering over as with grass (tiṇavatthāraka). One who reopens a proceeding (kiccādhikaraṇa) reopens this one settlement: sammukhāvinaya.

In the answer to the questions such as "How many types of reopening are there?", among the twelve types of reopening, three types such as "an act not done" (akata-kamma) are specifically found in the second legal process, the accusation (anuvādādhikaraṇa). Three types such as "an act not revoked" (anihata-kamma) are found in the first, the dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa). Three types such as "undecided" (aviniicchita) are found in the third, the offense (āpattādhikaraṇa). Three types such as "unsettled" (avūpasanta) are found in the fourth, the proceeding (kiccādhikaraṇa). Alternatively, all twelve types of reopening can be found in each of the legal processes.

In that context, "reopening a case arisen right there" (tatthajātaka adhikaraṇa) means that in a certain monastery, when a case arises concerning requisites such as a bowl or robe, in the manner of "This monk took my bowl, he took my robe," the resident monks (āvāsika) of that monastery assemble and, having persuaded the opposing monks by saying "Enough, venerable sirs," they settle it only by a decision not explicitly found in the Pali texts (pāḷimuttaka-vinicchaya). This is called a tatthajātaka legal process. Whatever decision it was settled by is also a type of settlement (samatha). For a monk who reopens this settlement, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

"Settled right there" (tatthajātaka vūpasanta) means if the resident monks are unable to settle that legal process, and another expert in the Discipline (vinayadhara) arrives and asks, "Venerable sirs, why..."
195:
He asks, "Is the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā being held in this monastery?" When those monks explain the matter, he settles that legal issue (adhikaraṇa) according to the text from the Khandhaka and the Parivāra. This is called a legal issue settled right in that monastery. For a monk who reopens such a settled legal issue, there is an offense of Pācittiya.

"On the road" means: Those opposing monks, saying, "We cannot abide by the decision of this Vinaya expert; he is not skilled in the Vinaya. There are elder Vinaya experts residing in such-and-such a village; let us go there and have it decided," depart. While on the road, they reflect on the cause and come to a mutual understanding, or other monks persuade them to understand. In such a case, that legal issue is also considered settled. For a monk who reopens such a legal issue settled on the road, there is also an offense of Pācittiya.

Regarding "settled on the road," it is not only settled through mutual understanding or persuasion by like-minded monks. Rather, a Vinaya expert coming from the opposite direction sees them and asks, "Friends, where are you going?" When told, "We are going to such-and-such a village for this reason," he says, "Enough, friends, what is the use of going there?" and settles that legal issue right there according to the Dhamma and Vinaya. This is called a legal issue settled on the road. For a monk who reopens such a legal issue, there is also an offense of Pācittiya.

"Arrived at that place" means: Even if told, "Enough, friends, what is the use of going there?" they do not heed the words of the Vinaya expert and continue as before, saying, "We will go to that very place and obtain a decision." Upon arrival, they report the matter to like-minded monks. The like-minded monks say, "Enough, friends, the assembly of the Saṅgha is a serious matter," and having them sit right there, they decide the matter and make them understand. This also is considered settled. For a monk who reopens such a legal issue settled upon arrival at that place, there is also an offense of Pācittiya.

Regarding "settled upon arrival at that place," it is not only settled through the persuasion of like-minded monks. Rather, the Vinaya experts settle the legal issue in the midst of the Saṅgha after it has been reported to the convened Saṅgha. This is called a legal issue settled upon arrival at that place. For a monk who reopens such a legal issue, there is also an offense of Pācittiya.

"Sati-vinaya" means: If one reopens a Sati-vinaya (verdict of mindfulness) given to an Arahant, there is an offense of Pācittiya. The same rule applies to Amūḷha-vinaya (verdict of past insanity) given to an insane monk, and to Tassapāpiyasika (verdict of specific depravity) given to a monk with many evil deeds.
196:
“Tiṇavatthārakaṃ ukkoṭeti” means that after the Saṅgha has settled a legal issue (adhikaraṇa) through the procedure of covering with grass (tiṇavatthāraka-samatha), a monk says: “An offense is truly rehabilitated only when one approaches another monk, sits in the crouching position, raises the joined palms, and confesses it. However, this procedure, where even a monk who is nodding off is rehabilitated from an offense through the tiṇavatthāraka-samatha, is too lax, and I do not approve of it.” Such a monk is said to be reopening the tiṇavatthāraka settlement, and he also incurs a Pācittiya offense.

“Reopening a legal issue by following the path of favoritism (chandāgati)” means that a person, though being a master of the Vinaya (vinayadhara), for the sake of his own preceptor and others, demonstrates “non-Dhamma as Dhamma” and so on, and reopens a previously decided legal issue by any of the twelve ways of reopening; this is called reopening a legal issue by following the path of favoritism. Among two monks who are adversaries, if one has a grudge against the other, thinking, “He has done me harm in the past,” and in order to make him lose, demonstrates “non-Dhamma as Dhamma” and so on, and reopens a previously decided legal issue by any of the twelve ways of reopening; this is called reopening a legal issue by following the path of malice (dosāgati). A dull and very deluded monk, simply because of his delusion, demonstrates “non-Dhamma as Dhamma” and so on, and reopens the case in the manner already described; this is called reopening a legal issue by following the path of delusion (mohāgati). If, among two monks who are adversaries, one is a person of inconsistent bodily actions and so on, holds deep-seated wrong views, and is supported by powerful and well-known monks in another faction, the other monk, out of fear of him, thinking, “This monk might cause danger to my life or danger to my holy life (brahmacariya),” demonstrates “non-Dhamma as Dhamma” and so on, and reopens the case in the manner already described; this is called reopening a legal issue by following the path of fear (bhayāgati).

“Tadahupasampanno” (one ordained on that very day) refers to a clever and learned novice (sāmaṇera) who, seeing monks dejected after losing in a legal decision, asks: “Why are you dejected?” Those monks tell that novice about the legal issue. The novice says: “Let it be, venerable sirs, please ordain me; I will settle that legal issue.” Those monks ordain him. On the second day, that new monk beats the drum and assembles the Saṅgha. When the monks ask, “Who assembled the Saṅgha?”, he says, “I did.” When asked, “Why did you assemble it?”, he says, “Yesterday’s legal issue was poorly decided; I will decide that legal issue.” When asked, “Where were you yesterday?”, he says, “Venerable sirs, yesterday I was not yet ordained (anupasampanna), but today I am ordained (upasampanna).” That new monk should be told: “Friend, the Blessed One has prescribed this training rule for those like you; go and confess your offense.” This same method applies to an incoming monk (āgantuka).
197:
"A person who has attained monkhood on that very day reopens [a settled case]; because of reopening, he commits a pācittiya offense." (The Blessed One has laid down this training rule.) "Go, confess the offense," (one should say). The same applies to a visiting monk (āgantuka).

"Kārako" refers to a monk who, after deciding a legal issue together with the Saṅgha, has returned to his own precinct (pariveṇa), and is told by the defeated monks: "Venerable sir, why did you decide this legal issue in this way? Should it not have been decided like this?" That monk says, "Why did you not say so from the beginning?" and reopens that legal issue. In this way, if a monk who participated in the decision reopens it, he also commits a pācittiya offense for reopening. "Chandadāyako" refers to a monk who, after giving his consent in the decision of a legal issue, sees the monks of his own side returning defeated and crestfallen, and says, "Now, I will decide it tomorrow," and causes the Saṅgha to assemble. When asked, "Why did you cause the assembly?" he says, "Yesterday's legal issue was poorly decided; I will decide that issue today." When asked, "Where were you yesterday?" he says, "I sat having given my consent (without participating)." That monk should be told: "Friend, for those like you, the Blessed One has laid down this training rule: 'A giver of consent who reopens [a case] commits a pācittiya offense for reopening.' Go, confess the offense."

## Explanation of the Origins of Legal Issues, etc.

In the phrases such as "What is the origin of a legal issue arising from disputes?" (vivādādhikaraṇaṃ kiṃnidānaṃ), "kiṃnidānaṃ" means "what is its origin (cause)?" "Kiṃsamudayaṃ" means "what is its arising?" "Kiṃjātikaṃ" means "what is its birth (source)?" "Kiṃpabhavaṃ" means "what is its source?" "Kiṃsambhāraṃ" means "what is its accumulation (requisite/cause)?" "Kiṃsamuṭṭhānaṃ" means "what is its origination?" All of these are synonyms for "cause" (kāraṇa).

In the phrases such as "vivādanidānaṃ" (originating in dispute), the dispute known as the eighteen grounds for schism (aṭṭhārasabhedakaravatthu) is the cause of this legal issue; thus it is called "vivādanidānaṃ." This is said in terms of a dispute that arises depending on a previous dispute. "Anuvādanidānaṃ" means accusation is the cause. This too is said in terms of an accusation that arises depending on a previous accusation. "Āpattinidānaṃ" means an offense is the cause. It is said in terms of an offense that arises depending on a previous offense, such as "one falls into four offenses due to a legal issue arising from offenses." "Kiccayanidānaṃ" means a formal act (kicca) is the cause; it means the four types of formal acts of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma) are the cause. This is said in terms of formal acts that arise depending on the formal acts such as the formal admonition (samanubhāsana) up to the third time for a nun who follows an expelled monk. This is the way of connecting the single term "nidāna" in the section of answers for all four types of legal issues. All terms should be connected according to this method.
198:
In the answer to the second question, "hetunidāna" etc., the state of being "hetunidāna" etc. should be understood by way of the nine wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate roots (kusalā-akusalā-abyākata-hetu). In the answer to the third question, only the wording is different. For here, the root (hetu) itself is called the condition (paccaya).

In the answer to the root-question (mūlapucchā), "twelve roots" refers to the six roots of dispute such as the pairs of anger (kodha) and malice (upanāha), the three [unwholesome roots] of greed, hatred, and delusion, and the three [wholesome roots] of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; thus there are twelve roots arising within one's own continuity. "Fourteen roots" refers to those same twelve roots together with body and speech, making fourteen. "Six roots" refers to the six originations (samuṭṭhāna) such as the body.

In the answer to the origination-question (samuṭṭhānapucchā), the eighteen grounds for schism (bhedakaravatthu) are the originations. This is because that legal issue arising from disputes arises in these eighteen grounds for schism, or it arises because of these grounds for schism which are the causes. Therefore, these are called the originations of that legal issue arising from disputes. This method applies everywhere.

In the classification such as "a legal issue arising from disputes is an offense," the phrase "by one legal issue arising from formal acts" (ekena kiccādhikaraṇena) is said to show the legal issue by which they are settled. However, these are not settled exclusively by a legal issue arising from formal acts. For there is no such thing as a legal issue arising from formal acts for a monk who is confessing an offense in the presence of an individual.

"It is not settled by any settlement (samatha)" means it cannot be settled [simply by confession] like an offense with a remainder (sāvasesāpatti). For that [offense without remainder] cannot be confessed, nor is it possible to rise from that offense and stand in the portion of purity.

The method in "it is a legal issue arising from disputes, it is a legal issue arising from accusations," etc., is quite clear.

After that, starting with "where there is a verdict of innocence (sativinaya)," six twin questions (yamakapucchā) are stated without leaving out the settlement in the presence (sammukhāvinaya). Their meaning is made clear by the answers to those questions.

In the answer to the questions such as "conjoined" (saṃsaṭṭha), "conjoined" means that because both settlements are accomplished at the very moment of the formal act (kammavācā) for the verdict of innocence, these factors—namely settlement in the presence and verdict of innocence—are conjoined, not disjoined. Just as it is impossible to separate the leaf-sheaths of a banana trunk and show them as distinct, so it is impossible to separate those settlements and show their difference. Therefore...
199:
It has been stated, "It is not possible to point out a distinction among these states by separating them one from another." This method mentioned is the way to interpret the meaning in all answers.

## Explanation of the Origins of the Seven Ways of Settling

In the answer to the question "What is its origin?", it is called "origin of the origin" (nidanānidāna) because it has the origin of that sammukhāvinaya-samatha. In this term "origin of the origin," these four types of presence—presence of the Saṅgha, presence of the Dhamma, presence of the Vinaya, and presence of the person—are the origin of sammukhāvinaya-samatha. An Arahant who has attained abundance of mindfulness and who has received an accusation is the origin of sativinaya-samatha. An insane monk is the origin of amūḷhavinaya-samatha. The presence of both the one who confesses and the one to whom the confession is made is the origin of paṭiññātakaraṇa-samatha. The inability to settle a legal process among monks who have become quarrelsome is the origin of yebhuyyasikā-samatha. A person with abundant evil is the origin of tassapāpiyasikā-samatha. The many unmonkly transgressions of monks who have become quarrelsome is the origin of tiṇavatthāraka-samatha. The sections on root causes (hetuvāra) and conditions (paccayavāra) follow the same method as previously stated.

The answer to the root question is clear. In the question on origination, although it is said, "What are the thirty-six originations of the seven ways of settling?", since sammukhāvinaya does not involve a formal act (kamma), it has no origination; therefore, only the six originations of the six ways of settling are analyzed in detail. In that analysis, by the words "action of the formal act" (kammassa kiriyā), the motion (ñatti) should be understood. "Performance" (karaṇa) means the placing of that motion at the time it should be placed. "Approaching" (upagamana) means approaching by oneself; it means performing that formal act by oneself. "Approaching by urging" (ajjhūpagamana) means approaching through exhortation; it means urging another person, such as a co-resident (saddhivihārika), saying, "Perform this formal act." "Consent" (adhivāsanā) means accepting and giving consent, saying, "This formal act is pleasing to me; let the Saṅgha perform it." "Non-rejection" (appaṭikkosanā) means not prohibiting, saying, "This formal act is not pleasing to me; do not do it in this way." Thus, the thirty-six originations should be understood by way of the six groups of six.

## Explanation of the Different Meanings of the Seven Ways of Settling, etc.

The answer to the question on different meanings is clear. In the answer to the question on legal processes (adhikaraṇa), "this dispute is not a legal process" means that this dispute between a mother and son, etc., is called a dispute (vivāda) because it is a contradictory statement, but it is not a legal process because it cannot be settled by the ways of settling (samatha). The same method applies to accusations (anuvāda), etc. In all other matters, the meaning is clear.

## The Explanation of the Classification of Legal Processes is finished.
200:
## The Second Collection of Verses

## Explanation of the Questions and Answers on Accusation, etc.

In the Second Collection of Verses (the meaning is as follows): "Accusation" (codanā) means accusing by pointing out the subject matter (vatthu) and the offense (āpatti). "Reminding" (sāraṇā) means making one remember the fault. "For what purpose is the Saṅgha?" (saṅgho kimatthāya) means for what purpose is the assembly of the Saṅgha. "For what reason is the consultation?" (matikammaṃ pana kissa kāraṇā) means for what reason is the taking of counsel (mantaggahaṇa).

"Accusation is for the purpose of reminding" means that accusation of the kind mentioned is for the purpose of making the accused person (cuditaka) remember the fault committed by him. "Reminding is for the purpose of reproof" means making one remember the fault is for the purpose of reproving that person. "The Saṅgha is for the purpose of taking up" means the Saṅgha thus assembled is for the purpose of taking up the decision, for weighing what is Dhamma and what is non-Dhamma, and for knowing what is well-decided and what is ill-decided. "Consultation is separate" (matikammaṃ pana pāṭiyekkaṃ) means the taking of counsel by the elders who are experts in the Suttas and the elders who are experts in the Vinaya is done separately for the purpose of finalizing the decision.

"Do not have resentment" (mā kho paṭighaṃ) means do not give rise to anger toward either the accused or the accuser. "If you are an investigator" (sace anuvijjako tuvaṃ) means if you are a Vinaya expert sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha to decide a legal process that has arisen.

"Contentious" (viggāhikaṃ) refers to the kind of (disputatious) speech such as "You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya," etc. "Unprofitable" (anatthasaṃhitaṃ) means do not speak such words that cause harm and cause the assembly to be disturbed and leave. In the phrase "in the Sutta or the Vinaya," etc., "Sutta" refers to the twofold analysis (ubhatovibhaṅga), i.e., the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga and Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga. "Vinaya" refers to the Khandhakas. "Conformity" (anuloma) refers to the Parivāra. "Prescribed" (paññatta) refers to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. "In accordance with" (anulomika) refers to the four great authorities (mahāpadesa).

"Observe the duty of interrogation" (anuyogavattaṃ nisāmaya) means to contemplate with wisdom the practice which is the sequence of questioning and examining. "Made by the skilled and wise one" (kusalena buddhimatā kataṃ) means the practice set forth by the Blessed One, who is skilled, wise, and has reached the perfection of knowledge. "Well-spoken" (suvuttaṃ) means well-explained (or well-prescribed). "In accordance with the training rules" (sikkhāpadānulomikaṃ) means the practice that conforms to the training rules. This is the meaning of the words. The summary of the meaning here is: "If you are an investigator (anuvijjaka), do not speak hastily; [do not speak] unprofitable words..."
201:
Do not speak words that are contrary and not connected with welfare. The Blessed One, the Refuge of the World, who is truly wise and skilled, has well-prescribed this practice of inquiry (anuyogavatta) in these Suttas and others, which is in accordance with all the training rules. Listen to that practice of inquiry; investigate and reflect upon it. Listen to the practice of inquiry without destroying your own rebirth in a happy destination (sugati) in the next life. If a Vinaya expert (vinayadhara) investigates and questions without observing this practice of inquiry with wisdom, he is said to destroy his own destination in the next life. Therefore, listen without destroying your own destination. Now, to show that practice of inquiry, he spoke the words beginning with "hitesī." In that passage, "hitesī" means seeking welfare, establishing loving-kindness (mettā) and the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (upacāramettā). "Kālena" means at the proper and suitable time, questioning only when the responsibility has been assigned to you.

"Sahasa vohāraṃ mā padhāresi" means there is speech spoken hastily by the accuser and the accused; do not carry out or accept that hastily spoken speech.

In the phrase "paṭiññānusandhitena kāraye," "anusandhita" refers to the connection between preceding and succeeding words. Therefore, one should decide by the consistency of the admission; it means one should decide by admission after noting the connection of the words. Alternatively, one should decide by admission and by consistency. For a conscientious person (lajjī), decide by admission; for a shameless person (alajjī), decide by the consistency of their conduct. Therefore, he spoke the verse beginning with "paṭiññā lajjīsu." In that verse, "vattānusandhitena kāraye" means one should decide by the consistency of conduct; whichever admission is consistent with his conduct, one should decide by that admission.

"Sañcicca" means committing an offense knowingly. "Parigūhati" means he conceals, does not confess, and does not emerge from the offense.

"Sā ahampi jānāမိ" means the answer given by you is true; I also know that problem in the same way. "Aññañca tāhaṃ" means I ask you another problem as well.

"Pubbāparaṃ na jānāti" means he does not know what was said before and what was said after. "Akovido" means unskilled in that sequence of before and after. "Anusandhivacanapathaṃ na jānāti" means he does not know the speech that connects the conversation and the speech that connects the decision.

"Sīlavipattiya codeti" means accusing with the two groups of offenses. "Ācāradiṭṭhiyā" means accusing by failure in conduct (ācāravipatti) and failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti). One who accuses by failure in conduct accuses with five groups of offenses; by failure in view...
202:
Not knowing the path of connection (anusaandhi-vacanapatha), which is the sequence of speech, means not knowing the connection of the discourse (kathā-anusaandhi) related to the words of the accused (cuditaka) and the investigator (anuvijjaka), nor the connection of the decision (vinicchaya-anusaandhi) related to the judgment of "offense" or "no offense." Accusing by failure in virtue (sīla-vipatti) means accusing with the two groups of offenses: Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa. When accusing by failure in conduct (ācāra-vipatti), one accuses with the five groups of offenses. One who accuses by failure in views (diṭṭhi-vipatti) accuses either by wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) or by extremist views (antaggāhika-diṭṭhi, i.e., eternalism or annihilationism). Accusing by livelihood (ājīva) means accusing with the six training rules (sikkhāpadas) laid down because of livelihood. In all questions and answers, the rest of the text is clear.

## The Explanation of the Second Collection of Verses is Finished.

Now, to show the duty to be performed by a Vinaya expert (vinayadhara) when such an accusation arises, the Elder Upāli spoke the words beginning with "Anuvijjakena." In that passage, the meaning of the verse beginning with "Diṭṭho diṭṭhe" is: A monk sees another monk coming out of or entering a place together with a woman. That monk who saw him accuses the other of a Pārājika. Although the other monk (the accused) admits to the seeing by the accuser, he does not admit to, nor does he fall into, a Pārājika offense based on that seeing. Thus, although the circumstance seen by the accuser—coming out or entering with this woman—agrees with the statement "I have seen it," because the accused monk does not admit to the fault based on that seeing, he is one who is suspected with an impure suspicion (asuddha-parisaṅkita) or suspected with a groundless suspicion (amūlaka-parisaṅkita). Because that accused person confesses, "I am pure from Pārājika," with him...
203:
## Section on Accusation (Codanākaṇḍa)
## Explanation of the Duties of the Investigator (Anuvijjaka-kicca-vaṇṇanā)
360-361. Now, in order to show the duties to be performed by a Vinaya expert (Vinayadhara) when such an accusation arises, the Venerable Upāli began the passage starting with "Anuvijjakeṇa." In that passage, the meaning of the verse "Diṭṭhaṃ diṭṭhena" is as follows: A monk has seen another monk either coming out of or entering a single place together with a woman. That monk who saw him accuses the other of a Pārājika offense. The other monk admits to being seen by the accuser. However, he does not incur a Pārājika offense based on that sighting, nor does he confess to it.

Thus, in this case, the matter seen by the accuser is consistent with his statement, "I have seen." However, because the other monk does not admit to the fault based on that sighting, he is one who is suspected impurely; the meaning is that he is groundlessly suspected (amūlaka-parisaṅkito). Because of that person's confession, "I am pure," the Uposatha should be performed together with him. In the remaining two verses, the method is the same. In all places, the remaining words are quite clear.

## The Explanation of the Duties of the Investigator is finished.
## Explanation of the Questions and Answers for the Accuser (Codaka-pucchā-vissajjanā-vaṇṇanā)
362-363. In the answers to the questions such as "What is the beginning of an accusation?", the phrase "Sacce ca akuppe ca" means that one must stand on truthful speech and on non-anger. Whether it is an act committed or not committed, one must speak only according to the facts. One must not give rise to anger toward the accuser, the investigator, or the Saṅgha. "Otiṇṇānotiṇṇaṃ jānitabbaṃ" means that one should know the speech that has been reached (descended) and the speech that has not been reached. In this regard, the method of knowing is as follows: one should know that "this much is the prior speech of the accuser, this much is the subsequent speech; this much is the prior speech of the accused (cuditaka), this much is the subsequent speech."

The measure of the accuser should be taken; the measure of the accused should be taken; the measure of the investigator should be taken. The investigator, without omitting even a small detail, should say, "Friend, reflect well and present it straightly." The Saṅgha should practice in this manner. In the phrase, "By which Dhamma, by which Vinaya, by which Teacher's Instruction is that legal issue (adhikaraṇa) settled?", "Dhamma" refers to the actual fact (vatthu). "Vinaya" refers to the accusation (codanā) and the reminding (sāraṇā). "Teacher's Instruction (satthu-sāsana)" refers to the completion of the motion (ñatti-sampadā) and...
204:
...and the completion of the proclamation (anussāvana-sampadā) [also settle the legal issue]. By this Dhamma, this Vinaya, and this Teacher's Instruction, the legal issue is settled. Therefore, the investigator, having accused based on the actual facts and having reminded of the offense, should settle that legal issue through the completion of the motion and the completion of the proclamation. The investigator should practice in this way. The remaining words in this section on accusation are quite clear.

The answers to the questions such as "For what purpose is the Uposatha?" are also quite clear. In the final verses, "There ca paribhāsati" means showing contempt and threateningly muttering, "What do these elders know?" "Khato upahatindriyo": he is called "khato" (uprooted/destroyed) because he destroys his own virtues by following the path of bias (chandāgati) and by such threatening speech. He is called "upahatindriyo" (one with impaired faculties) because his faculties such as faith (saddhā) are destroyed. "Nirayaṃ gacchati dummedho, na ca sikkhāya gāravo": that person who has uprooted himself and has impaired faculties is called "dummedho" (foolish) due to the absence of wisdom. Because of not practicing the three trainings (sikkhā), he has no respect for the training and, upon the dissolution of the body, goes only to hell. Therefore, it is said: "Na ca āmisaṃ nissāya... pe... yathā dhammo tathā kare." The meaning of that verse is that one should not decide depending on material gains (āmisa). One who takes material gains such as robes given by either the accused or the accuser is said to act depending on material gains. One should not do so. "Na ca nissāya puggalaṃ" means that one who follows the path of bias such as favoritism by thinking, "This person is my preceptor (upajjhāya) or my teacher (ācariya)," is said to act depending on the person. One should not do so. Rather, avoiding both dependence on material gains and dependence on persons, one should decide exactly as the Vinaya Dhamma stands.

"Upakaṇṇakaṃ jappati" means whispering in the ear, "Speak like this, do not speak like that." "Jimhaṃ pekkhati" means seeking only faults. "Vītiharati" means causing the decision to deviate or diminish. "Kummaggaṃ paṭisevati" means pointing out an offense [maliciously].

"Akālena ca codeti" means accusing at an improper time without being invited. "Pubbāparaṃ na jānāti" means not understanding the prior speech and the subsequent speech.

"Anusandhivacanapathaṃ na jānāti" means not knowing the course of speech by way of the connection of the discourse (kathānusandhi) and the connection of the decision (vinicchayānusandhi). The remaining words in the entire section on accusation have become clear.

## The Explanation of the Section on Accusation is finished.
205:
## Cūḷasaṅgāma
## Explanation of the Duties of an Investigating Monk

In the Cūḷasaṅgāma chapter, regarding the phrase 'saṅgāmāvacarena bhikkhunā', the assembly of the Saṅgha for the purpose of deciding legal issues (adhikaraṇa) is called 'saṅgāma' (battle). This is because in that assembly, monks who are enemies of oneself and enemies of the Sāsana—like the Vajjiputtaka monks of Vesālī—gather together, presenting what is not Dhamma as Dhamma and what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, thereby altering the Teacher's Sāsana. A monk who enters such an assembly to crush the views of those enemies and to demonstrate his own true doctrine, and who enters the midst of the Saṅgha to bring about a decision by overwhelming the shameless ones, is called 'saṅgāmāvacara' (one who enters the battlefield), like the Elder Yasa.

When a monk who enters such a battlefield-like assembly approaches the Saṅgha, he should do so with a humble mind (nīcacittena), having lowered the banner of pride. 'Nīcacittena' means approaching with a mind that is humbled by lowering the banner of pride. 'Rajoharaṇasamena' means approaching with a mind like a foot-wiping cloth. Just as a foot-wiping cloth feels neither lust nor anger whether it wipes dirty feet or clean feet, so too should one approach with a mind that feels neither attraction nor resentment toward pleasant or unpleasant objects.

'Yathāpatirūpe āsane' means knowing the suitable seat and sitting respectfully at one's designated place, facing the senior elders and not turning one's back to them. 'Anānākathikena' means sitting without engaging in various kinds of useless talk. 'Atiracchānakathikena' means sitting without engaging in tiracchānakathā (lowly talk) such as talk about kings, etc., which is contrary to the path and fruition, even if it is something seen, heard, or sensed.

'Sāmaṃ vā dhammo bhāsitabbo' means that in the assembly of the Saṅgha, one should either speak Dhamma oneself or urge others to do so. 'Dhamma' refers to talk concerning what is allowable or not, or talk concerning the analysis of mind and matter, samatha practice, vipassanā practice, and duties regarding standing and sitting. If a monk is capable of such talk, he should be urged: 'Friend, if a problem arises in the midst of the Saṅgha, please speak.'

'Ariyo vā tuṇhībhāvo nātimanyitabbo' means that when Noble Ones sit in silence, they do not sit like foolish worldlings; they sit while practicing a certain meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Silence through such mindfulness of a meditation subject is called 'Noble Silence' (ariya-tuṇhībhāva). That Noble Silence should not be despised by thinking, 'What is the use of practicing meditation?'; one should sit having taken up a meditation subject suitable for oneself.

'Na upajjhāyo pucchitabbo' means one should not ask, 'What is your preceptor's name?' This principle should be applied in all cases. 'Na jāti' means one should not ask about caste, such as 'Are you of the warrior caste or the priestly caste?'
206:
One should not ask about caste, such as 'Are you of the Brahmin caste?' One should not ask about lineage/scripture (āgama), such as 'Are you a reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya or the Majjhima Nikāya?' The designation of lineage (kulapadesa) should be understood only by way of the warrior caste and so on. In that person, love or hatred might arise due to one of these reasons (such as the preceptor, etc.).

One should not be a 'parisakappika' (one who arranges according to the assembly's wishes). This means one should not think and speak only what pleases the assembly. One should not make hand gestures (hatthamuddā) to signal what should or should not be said.

One should sit reflecting on the penetration of the decision, thinking, 'This Sutta (text) is found; I will say this in this decision.' One should not get up from one's seat and wander around the assembly circle. This is because if the Vinaya-expert (Vinayadhara) stands up, the whole assembly tends to stand up. The decision should not be neglected (vītihātabba). 'Na kummaggo sevitabbo' (The wrong path should not be followed) means one should not point out what is not an offense as an offense. One should not be 'sāhasika' (impetuous). This means one should not speak harsh words impulsively. One must be patient with words (vacanakkhama), having the nature of enduring harsh speech. As one who seeks welfare (hitaparisakkī), one should arouse compassion (karuṇā) and the preliminary stage (upacāra) of compassion. This is the meaning of both terms.

One should be 'anasurutta' (not having bad speech). 'Asurutta' refers to bad speech characterized by contentious talk; such talk should not be spoken. One should reflect upon oneself: 'Will I be able to decide and settle this matter?' This means one should know one's own capacity. One should also reflect on others (the assembly): 'Is this assembly conscientious (lajjī)? Can they be persuaded to understand?'

One should reflect on the accuser (codaka): 'Is the accuser one who accuses according to the Dhamma (dhammacodaka)?' One should reflect on the accused (cuditaka): 'Is the accused one who is accused according to the Dhamma (dhammacuditaka)?' The unrighteous accuser (adhammacodaka) should also be reflected upon; one should know his measure. In the remaining terms, this same method should be applied.
207:
One should proceed without omitting the words spoken by the accuser and the accused (in their entirety). One should proceed without revealing matters that have not yet come to light (acting only according to the confession). A dull or confused person should be encouraged, saying, "Are you not a son of good family?" and after inciting them to speak through interrogation, their confession should be taken. One who is fearful because they have never before entered the midst of the Saṅgha or a group should be reassured, saying, "Do not be afraid, speak confidently; we will support you," and then interrogated. A harsh person should be restrained by rebuking and threatening them. A shameless person (alajjī) should be exposed and made to confess their offense. An upright and virtuous monk should be treated only with gentle words. Only a Vinaya expert (vinayadhara) who values the Dhamma and is free from personal bias is considered impartial toward both the Dhamma and the person.

In citing the Suttas and so forth, it should be understood that the Sutta (the Pāḷi text) is for the purpose of comparing offenses and non-offenses. A simile (upamma) is for the purpose of illustrating the meaning. The meaning (attha) is for the purpose of making it known (to both sides of the Saṅgha). Cross-examination (paṭipucchā) is for the purpose of establishing the person (in their statement). Requesting leave (okāsakamma) is for the purpose of accusing based on the grounds (vatthu) or the offense (āpatti). Accusation (codanā) is for the purpose of reminding one of the fault or lack thereof. Reminding (sāraṇā) is for the purpose of making one subject to being spoken to (as a wrongdoer). Being subject to speech (savacanīya) is for the purpose of restriction, such as saying, "Do not go elsewhere from this monastery." Restriction (palibodha) is for the purpose of reaching a decision. Decision (vinicchaya) is for the purpose of weighing the fault or lack thereof to complete the matter. Completion (santīraṇa) is for the purpose of distinguishing between offense and non-offense, and between grave (garuka) and light (lahuka) offenses. The Saṅgha is for the purpose of accepting the decision and for knowing whether it was well-decided or ill-decided. (Those authorized by the Saṅgha) stand in a position of authority and leadership, and in a position that is unerring.
208:
It means that those persons who stand in the position of sovereignty, lordship, and seniority, and in an unerring position, should not be rebuked.

Now, if dull-witted persons should say, "What is the purpose of the Vinaya?", then to block their opportunity to speak, it is said: "The Vinaya is for the purpose of restraint (saṃvara)," and so forth. In that statement, "The Vinaya is for the purpose of restraint" means the entire body of Vinaya regulations is for the purpose of restraining the doors of body and speech. It means it is the strong dependence (upanissaya) for virtue, ending with the purification of livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhisīla). In all other sentences, it should be understood in this same manner.

Furthermore, herein, "non-remorse" (avippaṭisāra) means the absence of mental regret regarding whether bad or good deeds were done or not done. "Joy" (pāmojja) is weak or tender rapture (pīti). "Rapture" (pīti) is strong or mature rapture. "Tranquility" (passaddhi) is the calming of the distress of both body and mind. "Happiness" (sukha) is bodily and mental ease. Those two kinds of happiness are the strong dependence for concentration. "Concentration" (samādhi) is one-pointedness of mind (ekaggatā).

"Knowledge and vision of things as they are" (yathābhūtañāṇadassana) is tender insight, which is a designation for the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbayāṇana). One-pointedness of mind is the strong dependence for tender insight. "Disenchantment" (nibbidā) is strong insight that has reached its peak, leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī). "Dispassion" (virāga) is the Noble Path (ariyamagga). "Liberation" (vimutti) is the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). The four Noble Paths are the strong dependence for the Fruit of Arahantship. "Knowledge and vision of liberation" (vimuttiñāṇadassana) is reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa).

"Knowledge and vision of liberation is for the purpose of Nibbāna without clinging (anupādā parinibbāna)" means it is for the purpose of Nibbāna without conditions (apaccaya parinibbāna). That knowledge and vision of liberation is the cause for Nibbāna without conditions, because having reached that knowledge, one must certainly attain Nibbāna. "This talk is for this purpose" means this Vinaya talk is for the purpose of this Nibbāna without clinging. "Consultation" (mantanā) is the consultation regarding the Vinaya. "Dependence" (upanisā) means the sequence of causes starting with "Vinaya is for the purpose of restraint" is also for this purpose.

"Lending an ear" (sotāvadhāna) is listening to this sequential discourse on causes. The knowledge that arises from hearing this talk is also for this purpose. "Liberation of the mind without clinging" means the liberation of the mind known as the Fruit of Arahantship, not clinging through the four types of clinging; it means it is only for the purpose of Nibbāna without conditions.

Among the verses showing the duties of interrogation (anuyogavatta), the first verse has the meaning already stated. In the passage "One who is unskilled in the grounds (vatthu), failure (vipatti), offense (āpatti), origin (nidāna), and aspects (ākāra) does not know what comes before or after," the words "grounds" and so forth are connected with the word "does not know" (na jānāti).
209:
The word “akovido” is connected with the phrase “sa ve tādisako”. Therefore, the construction of the meaning here is: a monk who does not know the basis (vatthu) of the Pārājika and other training rules, does not know the four failures (vipatti), does not know the seven classes of offenses (āpatti), does not know the origin (nidāna) such as “this training rule was laid down in such and such a city”, does not know the sequence of words such as “this is the preceding word, this is the following word”, and does not know what has been done and what has not been done. By the phrase “samena ca”, it means not knowing what has been done and not done with the same kind of ignorance (aññāṇa) as not knowing the sequence. In this way, first, the connection with the word “na jānāti” (does not know) should be understood. In the phrase “ākāra-akovido”, “ākāra-akovido” means being unskilled in causes and non-causes (kāraṇākāraṇa). Thus, a monk who does not know the basis and so on, and is unskilled in the circumstances, is called “apaṭikkha” (one who should not be favored).

The words “kammañca adhikaraṇañca” (legal act and legal issue) are also connected with the word “na jānāti”. The construction of the meaning here is: similarly, a monk who does not know the legal act, does not know the legal issue, is unskilled in the seven ways of settling (samatha), and being affected by lust and so on, is greedy, hateful, and deluded; he follows a wrong course (agati) out of fear, follows a wrong course out of delusion, and follows a wrong course out of favoritism (chanda) and malice (dosa) because of being greedy and hateful. Being unable to make others understand, he is unskilled in persuasion (saññatti); being unable to see the cause and non-cause, he is unskilled in convincing others (nijjhatti); having obtained a following similar to himself, he has a faction; he is shameless (ahirika), possessed of dark deeds (kaṇhakamma), and lacks respect (anādara) for the Dhamma and individuals. Such a monk is called “apaṭikkha”. It means he should not be favored, should not be looked upon (with reverence), and should not be appointed to positions of authority, leadership, or lordship by consensus. The construction of the meaning for the verses showing the bright side (sukkapakkha) should be understood in the same manner as described.

## The Commentary on Cūḷasaṅgāma is finished.
210:
## Mahāsaṅgāma (The Great Conflict)
## Explanation of what should be known by one who speaks

368-374. In the Mahāsaṅgāma (Great Conflict) section, shifting from one basis (vatthu) to another means saying, “I have seen or heard the basis of the first Pārājika,” and then when questioned and examined further by the Vinaya-expert, saying, “I have not seen or heard the basis of the first Pārājika; I have only seen or heard the basis of the second Pārājika.” In this same way, shifting to other bases, shifting from one failure (vipatti) to another, and shifting from one offense (āpatti) to another should be understood. If a person says, “I have not seen or heard,” and later says, “I have seen or heard,” or if he says, “I have seen or heard,” and later says, “I have not seen or heard,” he should be known as one who admits after denying, or denies after admitting. Such a person is called “one who evades one thing with another” (aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati).

375. By the word “vaṇṇāvaṇṇā” (colors/beauty and non-beauty), the training rule on the emission of semen (sukka-vissaṭṭhi) is referred to by way of various colors such as blue/dark (nīla) and so on. By the word “vacanamanuppadāna” (giving words), the training rule on matchmaking (sañcaritta) is referred to. The three training rules beginning with bodily contact (kāyasaṃsagga) are referred to by their actual names. Thus, these five training rules should be understood as preliminary efforts (pubbapayoga) occurring prior to the Pārājika of sexual intercourse (methunadhamma).

376. “The four acts of announcement” (apalokana-kamma) refer to legal acts that are unlawful and non-quorate (adhamma-vaggādi). In the remaining terms, the method is the same. Thus, from the four sets of four, there are sixteen legal acts.

## Explanation of the reasons for not following a wrong course (agati)

370-374. “He practices for the harm of many people” means that if a Vinaya-expert decides a legal issue (adhikaraṇa) by following a wrong course such as favoritism (chanda) and so on, the Saṅgha in that monastery splits into two. The bhikkhunīs who live depending on the instruction of that Saṅgha also split into two groups. The male lay followers (upāsaka), female lay followers (upāsikā), male donors (dāyaka), and female donors (dāyikā), along with their guardian deities, likewise split into two. From there, starting from the terrestrial deities up to the Akanittha Brahma realm, the Brahmas also split into two. Therefore, it is said, “He practices for the harm of many people... for the suffering of gods and humans.”
211: "Visamanissito" means one who relies on uneven or unrighteous actions of body and so forth. "Gahananissito" means one who relies on the thicket (gahana) consisting of wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi) and extremist views (antaggāhikadiṭṭhi). "Balavanissito" means one who relies on powerful and well-known monks. "Tassa avajānanto" means knowing while disregarding the words of that junior monk (navaka). Or, because the genitive case (sāmivacana) in "tassa" stands in the sense of the accusative (upayogattha), it means disregarding that junior monk. "Yaṃ atthāya" means for which purpose. "Taṃ atthaṃ" means that purpose. In all sentences, the remaining construction is clear and obvious. ## The Commentary on the Mahāsaṅgāma is finished.
212:
## Section Explaining the Various Aspects to be Known Regarding Kathina
## Explanation of the Spreading of the Kathina Robe, etc.

In the context of Kathina, the 'eight mātikās' refer to the eight starting with pakkamananantikā mentioned in the Khandhaka. The palibodha (impediments) and ānisaṃsa (benefits) are also those that have been previously explained.

'Payogassa' (of the effort) refers to the effort such as fetching water, which is performed for the sake of the sevenfold pubbakaraṇa (preliminary duties) such as washing the robe. 'Which states are a condition by way of proximity condition (anantara-paccaya)?' means, which states are conditions by being immediate by way of the future. 'Samanantara-paccayena' means conditioning by way of contiguity (well-immediate); it asks by making the proximity condition even more immediate. 'Nissaya-paccayena' means which states are conditions by becoming as if they have reached the state of being a support or a foundation for the arising effort. 'Upanissaya-paccayena' means conditioning by way of decisive support; it asks by making the support condition even more decisive. By the words 'purejāta-paccayena', one asks about the conditionality of a state that has arisen previously. By the words 'pacchājāta-paccayena', one asks about the conditionality of a state that will arise later. By the words 'sahajāta-paccayena', one asks about the conditionality of states that arise simultaneously (without before or after). 'Pubbakaraṇassa' refers to the preliminary duties such as washing. 'Paccuddhārassa' refers to the formal relinquishing (paccuddhāra) of old robes such as the saṅghāṭi. 'Adhiṭṭhānassa' refers to the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) of the Kathina robe. 'Atthārassa' refers to the spreading (atthāra) of the Kathina. 'Mātikānañca palibodhānañca' refers to the eight mātikās and the two palibodhas. 'Vatthussa' refers to the physical object of the Kathina, such as the saṅghāṭi. The remaining method is exactly as already stated.

Having thus questioned all that is obtained and not obtained, the Teacher now gives the answer starting with the method 'pubbakaraṇaṃ payogassa', desiring to show only those states that are obtained for a particular effort, etc. The meaning of that answer is: regarding the problem stated as 'payogassa katame dhammā', etc., the answer given is—the preliminary duty (pubbakaraṇa) is a condition for the effort (payoga) by way of proximity condition (anantara-paccaya); it is also a condition by way of contiguity (samanantara), support (nissaya), and decisive support (upanissaya) conditions. This is because the sevenfold preliminary duty is performed for the sake of the preliminary duty to be accomplished through that effort; thus, it is a condition by these four conditions. However, in the case of the pre-nascence condition (purejāta-paccaya), this effort does not obtain even a single state among the mentioned states...
213:
...does not obtain; rather, the effort itself is a pre-nascence condition (purejāta-paccaya) for the preliminary duty, because the preliminary duty is accomplished only when there is effort. Therefore, it is said: 'Effort is a condition for the preliminary duty by way of pre-nascence condition.' It does, however, obtain the post-nascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya); therefore, it is said: 'The preliminary duty is a condition for the effort by way of post-nascence condition.' This is because that effort is performed for the sake of the preliminary duty that arises later. Regarding the co-nascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya), excluding the fifteen states known as mātikā, palibodha, and ānisaṃsa, no other state among effort, etc., is obtained. Only those fifteen states are accomplished together with the spreading of the Kathina, and thus they are mutual co-nascence conditions. Therefore, it is said: 'The fifteen states are a condition by way of co-nascence condition.' In this way, the answers to all terms should be understood.

## Explanation Analyzing the Origins of Preliminary Duties, etc.

The question and answer such as 'What is the origin of the preliminary duty?' etc., is quite clear.

406-7. In the two answers to the questions such as 'What is the origin of the effort?', regarding the terms 'hetu-nidāna' (root-origin) and 'paccaya-nidāna' (condition-origin), the six types of robes should be understood as both the root and the condition. They are the root and the condition for all preliminary efforts, etc. Indeed, if the six types of robes do not exist, there is no effort, nor are there preliminary duties, etc. Therefore, it is said: 'Effort has a root-origin (hetu-nidāna),' and so on.

In the Saṅgahavāra, 'vacībhedena' (by breaking into speech) means by this verbal utterance: 'I spread the Kathina with this saṅghāṭi, with this uttarāsaṅga, with this antaravāsaka.' In the question and answer on katimūla, etc., 'kiriya majjhe' (in the middle of the action) refers to the interval between the relinquishing (paccuddhāra) and the determination (adhiṭṭhāna).

'Vatthuvipanna' (defect in object) means it is an unallowable cloth (akappiya-dussa). 'Kālavipanna' (defect in time) refers to a situation where the Saṅgha gives the robe donated by donors today to the monk spreading the Kathina only on the next day. 'Karaṇavipanna' (defect in making) refers to a type of cloth that is not cut and made on that very day.
214:
## Explanation of the Distinctions to be Known Regarding the Kathina, etc.

In the answer to the question beginning with "The Kathina should be known"—"of those things only" means that when those things such as materiality (rūpa), etc., exist, it is called "Kathina"; it is simply the combination and mixing of those things. By the words "nāmaṃ nāmakammaṃ" (name, naming process), etc., it is shown that this name "Kathina" is merely a designation (paññatti) for many things, and in the ultimate sense (paramattha), there is no single entity.

"By twenty-four modes" means by the reasons previously mentioned, such as "not merely by scratching" (one should know the failure of the Kathina spreading). "By seventeen modes" means by the reasons previously mentioned, such as "the Kathina is spread with new cloth" (one should know the fulfillment of the Kathina spreading). Everything that should be said regarding the making of signs (nimittakamma), etc., has already been stated in the commentary on the Kathinakkhandhaka.

"They have simultaneous arising and simultaneous ceasing" means they arise together when they arise and cease together when they cease. "They have simultaneous arising and separate ceasing" means they arise together when they arise, but cease separately when they cease. What does this mean? All withdrawals (uddhāra) arise simultaneously with the spreading (atthāra). For when there is spreading, there is what is called withdrawal. Regarding cessation, among these (withdrawals), the first two cease simultaneously with the spreading; they reach the state of being withdrawn. This is because the cessation of the spreading and the state of being withdrawn of these (first two) occur in a single moment. The others, however, cease separately. Even when those (others) reach the state of being withdrawn, the spreading still remains. All the remaining meaning is clear in every instance.

## In the Vinaya Commentary named Samantapāsādikā,
## The Explanation of the Distinctions of Kathina is finished.
## The Explanation of the Paññatti Chapter is finished.
215:
## Upālipañcaka
## Explanation of the Anissita Chapter

In the questions of Upāli, the connection of the question beginning with "Venerable Sir, how many..." is as follows: It is said that the Elder Upāli, having gone into seclusion and reflected on all these fivefold groups (pañcaka), thought, "I will now question the Blessed One and establish the lineage of the text (tanti) for the benefit of those living in dependence (nissāya vasana), etc." He then approached the Blessed One and asked the questions in the manner beginning with "Venerable Sir, how many...". In the answers to those questions, "does not know the Uposatha" means not knowing the nine types of Uposatha. "Does not know the Uposatha-kamma" means not knowing the four types of Uposatha-kamma, distinguished as "unlawful and in an incomplete assembly" (adhammena-vagga), etc. "Does not know the Pātimokkha" means not knowing the two codes (mātikā). "Does not know the recitation of the Pātimokkha" means not knowing the nine types of Pātimokkha recitation—five for monks and four for nuns.

"Does not know Pavāraṇā" means not knowing the nine types of Pavāraṇā. "Does not know Pavāraṇā-kamma" means not knowing the four types of Pavāraṇā-kamma, distinguished as "unlawful and in an incomplete assembly" (adhammena-vagga), etc.

"Does not know offense and non-offense" means not knowing the offense and the non-offense specified in various training rules (sikkhāpada).

"One who has committed an offense and has had a legal act performed" means one who has committed an offense and, because of that very offense, has had a legal act (kamma) performed by the Saṅgha.

## Explanation of the Nappaṭippassambhana Chapter

"The legal act should not be remitted" means that because this monk does not practice the conformable duties (anulomavatta), the legal act against him should not be remitted; he should be released only as if he were still bound with a rope.

"Upāli, if the Saṅgha performs acts that should be done in harmony" means the performing of acts such as Uposatha that ought to be performed by harmonious monks. While Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, etc., are suspended, support (that would hinder harmony) should not be given. If the Saṅgha makes the monks confess their faults and achieves harmony of the Saṅgha, or performs the reconciliation by covering with grass (tiṇavatthāraka-samatha) and then performs Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, such a nature of act is called "an act to be done in harmony" (samaggakaraṇīya-kamma). "In that act" means if a monk does not approve of such an act...
216:
Even by making one's own view clear, one should approach such concord of the Saṅgha; thus, one should not hold a contrary view. In an act where they demonstrate the Teacher's Dispensation by departing from the Dhamma and Vinaya, it is not proper to make one's own view clear; one should depart after protesting [that act].

'Ussitamanthī' refers to one who speaks words abounding in greed, hatred, delusion, and conceit, whose speech is defiled and indicates what is harmful. 'Nissitajappī' refers to one who is unable to speak words of an uplifting nature by their own natural ability, but instead speaks by relying on others, such as: 'The Great King spoke thus with me, such and such a high official spoke thus, such and such a person who is my teacher or preceptor and a bearer of the Tipiṭaka spoke thus with me.' 'Na ca bhāsānusandhikusalo' refers to one who is unskilled in the connection of speech and in the connection of making decisions. 'Na yathādhamme yathāvinaye' refers to one who does not reprove by reminding [another] of an offense based on a factual basis.

'Ussādetā' refers to one who praises some individuals in such a way as: 'Our teacher is a great bearer of the Tipiṭaka, a supreme Dhamma-preacher,' and so on. In the second term, 'apasādetā' refers to one who disparages some individuals in such a way as: 'Why does that person not know the offense?' and so on. 'Adhammaṃ gaṇhāti' means taking the side that does not lead out [of saṃsāra]. 'Dhammaṃ paṭibāhati' means obstructing the side that leads out [of saṃsāra]. 'Samphañca bahuṃ bhāsati' means speaking much useless talk.

'Pasayha pavattā' refers to one who, without being requested or assigned a responsibility, speaks in a matter that does not concern them, being overwhelmed by and relying solely on conceit. 'Anokāsakammaṃ kāretvā' refers to one who speaks without having obtained permission. 'Na yathādiṭṭhiyā vyākatā' means that they do not answer by putting forward their own view, but rather, setting aside their own view, they speak as one who holds a view of Dhamma in what is non-Dhamma, which is not in accordance with the truth.

## Explanation of the Vocabulary Section (Vohāravagga-vaṇṇanā)

'Āpattiyā payogaṃ na jānāti' means not knowing: 'This offense is due to bodily action, this offense is due to vocal action.' 'Āpattiyā vūpasamaṃ na jānāti' means not knowing: 'This offense is settled by confession (desanā), this offense is settled by rehabilitation (vuṭṭhāna) [such as parivāsa or mānatta], this offense is settled neither by confession nor by rehabilitation.' Of the offense...
217:
Not being skilled in making decisions means not knowing: 'In this case, this offense occurs,' and being unable to establish the offense by extracting it according to the fault.

Not knowing the origin of a legal issue (adhikaraṇa-samuṭṭhāna) means not knowing: 'This legal issue arises based on the eighteen grounds for schism; this legal issue arises based on the four failures (vipatti); this legal issue arises based on the five or seven classes of offenses (āpattikkhandha); this legal issue arises based on the four duties of the Saṅgha (saṅghakicca).' Not knowing the preliminary effort (payoga) means not knowing: 'This legal issue has twelve root-efforts; this legal issue has fourteen root-efforts; this legal issue has six root-efforts; this legal issue has one root-effort.' The respective roots of the legal issues are themselves called 'efforts' (payoga); the meaning is not knowing all of that. Not knowing the settlement (vūpasama) means not knowing: 'This legal issue is settled by two methods of settlement (samatha); this one by three; this one by four; this legal issue is settled by one method of settlement.' Not being skilled in making decisions means not knowing how to bring a legal issue to settlement after deciding it.

Not knowing the formal act (kamma) means not knowing the seven types of formal acts, such as the act of censure (tajjanīyakamma). Not knowing the performance of the act means not knowing: 'This act should be performed in this manner.' Not knowing the basis (vatthu) of the act means not knowing: 'This is the basis for the act of censure; this is the basis for the act of subordination (niyassakamma), and so on.' Not knowing the duties (vatta) means not knowing the eighteen kinds of duties for the four lower acts among the seven acts, and the forty-three kinds of duties for the three types of acts of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma). Not knowing the settlement of the act means not knowing: 'The act should be revoked for that monk who, having practiced the duties, requests [the revocation]; the fault should be made to be confessed.'

Not knowing the basis (vatthu) means not knowing the basis of the seven classes of offenses. Not knowing the origin (nidāna) means not knowing: 'This training rule was laid down in this city; this training rule was laid down in that city.' Not knowing the regulation (paññatti) means not knowing the three types of regulations: the primary regulation (paññatti), the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti), and the regulation laid down where none existed before (anuppannapaññatti). Not knowing the 'padapaccābhaṭṭha' means not knowing the word that should be performed in the presence [of the Saṅgha]. Instead of saying 'Buddho Bhagavā,' one joins the words by reversing them as 'Bhagavā Buddho.'

Being unskilled in the Vinaya means being unskilled in the Vinaya Pāḷi and the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā).

Not knowing the motion (ñatti) means that, in brief, there are two kinds of motions: the motion specified as 'This is the motion' and the unspecified motion. Among them, the unspecified motion is called 'kammañatti.' The specified motion is called 'kammapādañatti.' It means not knowing all those motions entirely.
218:
"Not knowing the performance of the motion" means not knowing how to perform the motion for a legal act (kamma-ñatti) in nine instances, and not knowing how to perform the motion for a constituent part of a legal act (kammapāda-ñatti) in two instances. "The proclamation of the motion" means not knowing that "this motion has one proclamation, this motion has three." "Not knowing the settlement by motion" means that the four types of settlement—namely, the verdict of mindfulness (sati-vinaya), the verdict of past insanity (amūḷha-vinaya), the verdict of specific depravity (tassapāpiyasikā), and covering over as if with grass (tiṇavatthāraka)—cannot occur without a motion; not knowing these as settlements performed by motion. "Not knowing the subsiding by motion" means that a certain legal issue is settled by these four types of motion-settlement; not knowing that settlement as "this settlement was performed by motion."

"Not knowing the Sutta" means not knowing the Ubhatovibhaṅga. "Not knowing what is in accordance with the Sutta" means not knowing the four Great Authorities (mahāpadesa). "Not knowing the Vinaya" means not knowing the Khandhaka and Parivāra. "Not knowing what is in accordance with the Vinaya" means not knowing those same four Great Authorities. "Not skilled in what is possible and impossible" means not being skilled in what is a cause and what is not a cause.

"Not knowing the Dhamma" means not knowing the remaining two Piṭakas, excluding the Vinaya Piṭaka. "Not knowing what is in accordance with the Dhamma" means not knowing the four Great Authorities mentioned in the Suttanta. "Not knowing the Vinaya" means not knowing the Khandhaka and Parivāra themselves. "Not knowing what is in accordance with the Vinaya" means not knowing the four Great Authorities. In this context, the Ubhatovibhaṅga is not included; therefore, the statement in the Kurundī, "Vinaya means not knowing the entire Vinaya Piṭaka," should be accepted. "Not skilled in what comes before and after" means being unskilled in former speech and subsequent speech. The remaining words should be understood by way of the opposite of the meanings already stated, and since they have been explained previously, they are quite clear.

## End of the Commentary on the Anissita Chapter, the Appaṭippassambhana Chapter, and the Vohāra Chapter.

## Commentary on the Diṭṭhāvikamma Chapter

In the Diṭṭhāvikamma Chapter—"Diṭṭhāvikammā" means making views manifest (proclaiming beliefs); it is a designation for Vinaya acts known as the confession of offenses. "Making manifest a view regarding a non-offense" means confessing a non-offense as an offense.
219:
"By that which does not lead to confession" (adesanāgāminiyā) means making manifest a view because of a grave offense (garukāpatti) that is not remediable by simple confession; it means confessing a Saṅghādisesa offense or a Pārājika offense. "By that which has been confessed" means making manifest a view because of an offense that has already been confessed, even if it is a light offense (lahukāpatti); it means confessing again an offense that has already been confessed.

"Making manifest a view to four or five [monks]" means making it manifest just as a view is made manifest to four or five; it means four or five persons confessing an offense together. "With the mind" (manomānasena) means making manifest a view with the mind known as consciousness; it means confessing an offense only with the mind without making a verbal utterance.

"To one of a different communion" (nānāsaṃvāsakassa) means making manifest a view or confessing an offense in the presence of a monk who has a different communion either by view or by legal act. "In different boundaries" (nānāsīmāya) means making it manifest in the presence of a monk who, though of the same communion, is standing in a different boundary. Indeed, it is not proper for a monk standing in a small boundary (māḷakasīmā) to confess an offense to a monk standing in the interval between boundaries (sīmantarikā), nor for a monk standing in the interval between boundaries to confess to one standing in the boundary of non-separation (avippavāsasīmā). "To one of imperfect status" (apakatattassa) means confessing in the presence of a suspended monk (ukkhittaka) or a monk whose Uposatha or Pavāraṇā has been cancelled.

"Not fit to perform the act of giving permission" means not capable of performing it, or that it should not be performed. In this pentad (pañcaka) also, a monk of imperfect status refers to a suspended monk and a monk whose Uposatha or Pavāraṇā has been cancelled. "Intending to cause a fall" (cāvanādhippāyo) means one who desires to cause [another] to fall away from the Sasana.

"Due to dullness and extreme delusion" means being unable to understand even the meaning that has been explained due to a state of dullness and extreme delusion; merely manifesting one's own deluded state, one asks like a madman. "One of evil desires" (pāpiccho) means asking with an evil desire, thinking, "If I ask like this, people will respect me." "Out of contempt" (paribhavā) means asking with the desire to impose contempt (to disparage). This same method applies to other explanations regarding the fruit of Arahantship. In all other places, the meaning is clear. All decisions that should be stated in the Attādāna Chapter and the Dhutaṅga Chapter have already been stated above.

## End of the Commentary on the Diṭṭhāvikamma Chapter.
220:
## Commentary on the Musāvāda Chapter

In the Musāvāda Chapter—one is called 'Pārājikagāmī' because they reach a Pārājika; it means they arrive at the state of a Pārājika offense. The same logic applies to other terms. Among those lies, the lie of claiming superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) that one does not possess leads to a Pārājika. The lie of groundless accusation of a Pārājika leads to a Saṅghādisesa. A lie spoken through circumlocution, such as "Who lives in your dwelling?" (referring to oneself as another), to one who understands, leads to a Thullaccaya. If spoken to one who does not understand, it leads to a Dukkaṭa. It should be understood as a lie leading to a Pācittiya, as stated: "There is a Pācittiya for deliberate lying."

"Adassanena" means due to not seeing a Vinaya expert (vinayadhara). When scruples (kukkuccha) arise regarding what is allowable or unallowable, one should see a Vinaya expert, inquire about it, abandon the unallowable, and perform the allowable. However, a person who does not see such a Vinaya expert may perform an unallowable act, thinking it is allowable, and thus incur an offense. An offense that would be incurred in this way is avoided by seeing a Vinaya expert and is incurred only by not seeing one; hence it is said "adassanena". "Assavanena" means that even if living in the same monastery, if one does not go to attend upon the Vinaya expert to inquire, or does not hear the instructions being given to others, an offense is still incurred; hence it is said "assavanena". "Pasuttakatā" means due to the state of being asleep. An offense of sahaseyya (sleeping together) can be incurred even while asleep. One who incurs an offense by perceiving the unallowable as allowable does so with such a perception. One incurs an offense that should be incurred through forgetfulness (satisammosa), such as exceeding one night, etc. The remaining terms are clear in all places.

## The Commentary on the Musāvāda Chapter is finished.

## Commentary on the Bhikkhunovāda Chapter

In the Bhikkhunī Chapter—"alābhāya" means for the purpose of not obtaining the four requisites; it means one strives or endeavors in such a way that they do not receive the requisites. "Anatthāya" means striving while presenting harmful or malicious speech. "Avāsāya" means for the purpose of not being able to reside in their usual place; for the purpose of expelling them from the village or fields where they reside. "Sampayojeti" means connecting them to engage in the unrighteous conduct (asaddhamma) of sexual intercourse.
221:
“Venerable Sir, with how many factors should a legal act (kamma) be performed against a bhikkhunī?”—Venerable Upāli asked this question with reference to one of the seven types of legal acts.

“Should not be discussed” means that the sequence of discourse involving allowable and unallowable, the discernment of mind and matter (nāmarūpa-pariccheda), serenity (samatha), insight (vipassanā), and so on, should not be spoken. The reason is that an Arahant (khīṇāsava) monk does not deviate and speaks as a master of such discourse, whereas others do not. Therefore, in the first group of five, it was rejected by saying “not by one who is not an Asekha (Arahant),” and in the second group of five, it was stated as “by an Asekha,” and so on.

“One who has not attained the Atthapaṭisambhidā” means one who has not attained the knowledge that analytically distinguishes and understands the commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā). “One who has not attained the Dhammapaṭisambhidā” means one who has not attained the analytical insight into the Pali Dhamma. “One who has not attained the Niruttipaṭisambhidā” means one who has not attained the analytical insight into the language used for communication. “One who has not attained the Paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā” means one who has not attained the analytical insight into the knowledges known as perspicuity, such as Atthapaṭisambhidā, etc. “One who does not review the liberated mind” means one who does not review the mind liberated from defilements through the four fruits of liberation (vimutti) using the nineteen types of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa). In all places, the remaining text is clear in meaning.

## The Commentary on the Bhikkhunovāda Chapter is finished.

## Commentary on the Ubbāhika Chapter

In the Ubbāhika Chapter— “one who is not skilled in meaning” means one who is not skilled in the commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), not proficient in extracting the meaning from the commentaries. “One who is not skilled in Dhamma” means one who is not skilled in the Pali texts because of not having learned directly from the mouth of a teacher, not being confident in the Pali. “One who is not skilled in Nirutti” means one who is not skilled in the terminology of other languages. “One who is not skilled in phrasing (byañjana)” means one who is not skilled in applying rounded phonetics through soft (sithila) and hard (dhanita) sounds, etc.; it means one who lacks subtle knowledge in the distinction of syllables. “One who is not skilled in the sequence (pubbāpara)” means one who is not skilled in the preceding and following words of the commentaries, the Pali texts, the language, and the phrasing, as well as in what should be said before and what should be said after.

Words such as “one who is prone to anger” were spoken because a person overcome by anger and so on cannot know or decide what is a valid reason and what is not. One who causes confusion...
222:
"Hoti no sāretā" means he is one who confuses (mohetā), not one who causes mindfulness to arise (sāretā). How does he confuse the words of the accuser and the accused? He covers them up; it means he does not let them remember. The rest in this Ubbāhika Chapter is clear.

## The Explanation of the Ubbāhika Chapter is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Chapter on the Settlement of Legal Processes

In the Adhikaraṇavūpasama Chapter: "Puggala-garu hoti" means thinking, "This is my preceptor (upajjhāya), this is my teacher (ācariya)," and so on, and desiring his victory, one presents "what is not Dhamma as Dhamma." "Saṅgha-garu hoti" means one who decides without abandoning the Dhamma and Vinaya is called one who respects the Saṅgha. One who decides after taking robes and so on is called one who respects material things (āmisa-garu); one who decides according to the Dhamma without taking those robes and so on is called one who respects the True Dhamma (saddhamma-garu).

"By five ways, Upāli" means the Saṅgha is divided by five causes: by a [legal] act (kamma), by recitation (uddesa), by speaking (vohara-anta), by repeated informing (anussāvana), and by taking voting tickets (salākaggāha). Here, "by a legal act" (kammena) means by any one of the four legal acts such as announcement (apalokana). "By recitation" (uddesena) means by any one of the five recitations of the Pātimokkha. "Speaking" (vohara-anta) means talking; showing the eighteen grounds for schism such as "what is not Dhamma as Dhamma" through various appropriate reasons. "By repeated informing" (anussāvana) means speaking into the ear in this manner: "Venerable sirs, do you not know that I am one who went forth from a high-class family and that I am very learned? Is it appropriate for you even to think that one like me would make [others] accept what is not Dhamma and what is not Vinaya as the Teacher's Dispensation? Is the Avīci hell as cool as a forest of blue lotuses for me? Am I not afraid of the lower realms?" and so on. "By taking voting tickets" (salākaggāha) means, after informing them repeatedly in this way, supporting and strengthening their minds, making them those who do not turn back, and saying, "Take this voting ticket."

In this context, either the legal act (kamma) or the recitation (uddesa) is the standard (pamāṇa); speaking, repeated informing, and taking voting tickets are merely the preliminary components. For when one speaks by way of showing the eighteen grounds, in that [speech]...
223:
Even if one proclaims repeatedly to generate preference and has the voting tickets taken, the Saṅgha is not yet split. But when four or more monks take the voting tickets and perform a separate legal act or a separate recitation of the Pātimokkha, then the Saṅgha is said to be split. Thus, it was said in the Saṅghabhedaka-kkhandhaka Commentary: "In this way, by presenting any one of the eighteen grounds and making them understand by various reasons, 'Accept this view, prefer this view,' and having them take voting tickets and performing a separate Saṅgha act, the Saṅgha is split." In the Parivāra, however, it is said: "Upāli, by five ways the Saṅgha is split," and so forth. There is no difference in meaning between that statement in the Parivāra and the characteristic of the split of the Saṅgha mentioned here in the Saṅghabhedaka-kkhandhaka. That absence of difference in meaning has been explained now, just as it was said, "We shall clarify it in that very Parivāra Commentary."

"This is prescribed" (paññattetaṃ) means this duty of the Khandhaka is prescribed. Where is it prescribed? In the Vatta-kkhandhaka. For in that Vatta-kkhandhaka, fourteen duties of the Khandhakas are prescribed. Therefore, He said: "Upāli, I have prescribed the duty for incoming monks (āgantuka-vatta)," and so forth. "Upāli, thus there is a crack in the Saṅgha (saṅgharāji), but not yet a schism (saṅghabheda)" means that by this much cause, there is only a crack in the Saṅgha; a schism has not yet occurred. The meaning is that in due course, as this crack in the Saṅgha grows, it leads to a schism. "According to the nights" (yathārattaṃ) means according to the measure of nights, which has the meaning of "according to seniority" (yathātheraṃ). "Having made it separate" (āveṇibhāvaṃ karitvā) means having made a separate distinction. "They perform various legal acts" (kammākammāni karonti) means they perform minor and major legal acts based on successive Saṅgha acts. The rest of the words here are clear, as explained in the Adhikaraṇavūpasama Chapter.

## The Explanation of the Two Chapters on Schism-makers

In the two chapters on schism in the Saṅgha—"Having set aside his view by a legal act" (vinidhāya diṭṭhiṃ kammena) means even though he is one who holds the view regarding those non-Dhamma things that "these are non-Dhamma," he conceals that view and presents those non-Dhamma things by way of Dhamma, and then performs a separate legal act. Thus, when he performs a legal act while concealing his view, there are five factors together with that performed legal act.
