"Upāli, with these five factors..."—this statement is the application of the meaning in one group of five. In this manner, all groups of five should be understood. Here also, the three factors such as speaking (vohāra) are mentioned only as preliminary stages of the schism. By way of the legal act (kamma) and recitation (uddesa), the state of being incurable should be understood. In all other places, the meaning is clear. There is nothing here that has not been mentioned in the previous method.
224:
## Commentary on the Āvāsika Chapter
In the Āvāsika Chapter, "yathābhataṃ nikkhitto" means as if [the hell-wardens] had brought and placed [him].

"Vinayabyākaraṇa" means answering questions on the Vinaya. "Pariṇāmeti" means to fix, to show, or to speak. The remaining words here are clear.

## Commentary on the Kaṭhinatthāra Chapter
In the Kaṭhinatthāra Chapter, "otamasiko" refers to a person who has entered darkness. The forehead of one who bows to such a person might strike the leg of a bed and so forth. "Asammannāharanto" refers to a person who cannot attend to the act of bowing because they are occupied with other duties. "Sutto" refers to a person who has fallen into sleep. "Ekāvatto" refers to one who turns to one side, meaning an enemy, one who stands on the side of the foe, a disagreeable person. This person is one who should not be bowed to. If one bows to this person, he might even kick with his foot. "Aññavihito" refers to a person who is thinking of something else.

"Khādanto" refers to a person who is chewing hard food and so forth. A person who is defecating or urinating should not be bowed to because they are in an inappropriate place. "Ukkhittako" refers to a person who has been suspended by the three types of ukkhepaniyakamma; they should not be bowed to. However, the four types of persons subjected to tajjanīyakamma and so forth should be bowed to. One is also permitted to perform uposatha and pavāraṇā with them. Among those mentioned from the beginning who should not be bowed to, an offense is incurred only by a monk who bows to a naked person (nagga) or a suspended person (ukkhittaka). Bowing to others is prohibited because it is unsuitable or due to the reasons mentioned in between. After this, the ten types of persons, such as those ordained later (pacchāupasampanna), are also not to be bowed to because they are grounds for an offense. An offense is always incurred by a monk who bows to them. Thus, in these five groups of five (pañcaka), no offense is incurred for bowing to 13 types of monks, but an offense is incurred for bowing to 12 types.

"Ācariyo vandiyo" means the five types of teachers—pabbajjācariya, upasampadācariya, nissayācariya, uddesācariya, and ovādācariya—should be bowed to. In all the pañcakas, the remaining words are clear.

## The Commentary on the Kaṭhinatthāra Chapter is Finished.
## The Commentary on the Upāli Pañcaka is also Finished.
225:
## Explanation of the Origins of Offenses

In sentences such as "acittako āpajjati," for an offense involving a breach of regulation (paṇṇattivajja) such as sleeping in the same room (sahaseyya), one who commits it without perception and intention incurs the offense without consciousness (acittaka). However, when confessing the offense, they rise from it with consciousness (sacittaka). One who commits any offense with perception and intention incurs it with consciousness; one who rises from an offense through the tiṇavatthāraka procedure rises without consciousness. Regarding the same offense mentioned before, one who rises through the tiṇavatthāraka procedure incurs it without consciousness and rises without consciousness. One who confesses another sacittaka offense incurs it with consciousness and rises with consciousness. One who performs padasodhamma and so forth with the thought "I will give a gift of Dhamma" incurs an offense with a wholesome mind (kusalacitta). One who confesses with an uplifted mind thinking "I will follow the instruction of the Buddhas" rises with a wholesome mind. One who confesses while associated with dejection (domanassa) rises with an unwholesome mind (akusalacitta). One who rises through the tiṇavatthāraka procedure while asleep rises with an indeterminate mind (abyākatacitta). One who frightens others and so forth and then confesses with joy (somanassa) thinking "I will serve the Dispensation of the Buddhas" incurs an offense with an unwholesome mind but rises with a wholesome mind. One who confesses while associated with dejection rises with an unwholesome mind. In the same manner, one who rises through the tiṇavatthāraka procedure rises with an indeterminate mind. One who commits the offense of sahaseyya while falling asleep incurs the offense with an indeterminate mind. In this case of incurring with an indeterminate mind, it should be understood in the same way: "rises with a wholesome mind," and so forth.

The phrase "paṭhamaṃ pārājikaṃ katihi samuṭṭhānehi" and so forth is clear because it follows the method previously explained.

In the Pali passages such as "cattāro pārājikaṃ katihi samuṭṭhānehi," whatever origin (samuṭṭhāna) is obtained for whichever training rule (sikkhāpada) by way of the highest limit, all that has already been stated.

## The Explanation of the Origins of Offenses is Finished.
226:
## Commentary on the Second Collection of Verses
## (1) Explanation of Bodily and Other Offenses

In the answer to the verses beginning with "Kati āpattiyo kāyikā" (How many offenses are bodily?), the statement "six types of offenses arise in the body" means that through the fourth origin of offenses (body and mind) in the Antara-peyyāla, one incurs six types of offenses. These are the offenses taught in the manner beginning with: "If a monk engages in sexual intercourse, he incurs an offense of Pārājika." Because these offenses arise at the body-door (kāyadvāra), they are called "kāyika" (bodily offenses).

"Six types of verbal offenses" means that through the fifth origin of offenses (speech and mind) in that same Antara-peyyāla, one incurs six types of offenses. These are the offenses taught in the manner beginning with: "If a monk, having evil desires and being overcome by wrong ambition..."

"Three offenses for one who conceals" means: a Pārājika offense for a Bhikkhunī who conceals a [Pārājika] fault; a Pācittiya offense for a monk who conceals a Saṅghādisesa offense; and a Dukkaṭa offense for concealing one's own gross offense (duṭṭhullāpatti).

"Five offenses due to physical contact (kāyasaṃsagga)" means: a Pārājika offense for a Bhikkhunī due to physical contact; a Saṅghādisesa offense for a monk; a Thullaccaya offense for touching an object connected to the body with one's body; a Dukkaṭa offense for touching an object connected to the body with a thing to be relinquished; and a Pācittiya offense for poking with a finger. These are the five offenses caused by physical contact.

"Three offenses at dawn" means: the Nissaggiya Pācittiya offenses incurred by exceeding one night, six nights, seven days, ten days, or a month; a Saṅghādisesa offense for a Bhikkhunī staying away from her companion at night; and the offenses stated as: "He conceals it during the first watch, the second watch, and the third watch; if it remains concealed when the sun rises, it is an offense; whoever conceals it must be made to confess a Dukkaṭa offense." These are the three offenses incurred at dawn.

"Two types of Yāvatatiyaka offenses" means that although there are eleven Yāvatatiyaka offenses, by way of regulation (paññatti), there are two types: the Yāvatatiyaka of monks and the Yāvatatiyaka of Bhikkhunīs.

"One type of Aṭṭhavatthuka offense in this Dispensation" refers to the Aṭṭhavatthuka offense (offense involving eight grounds) which occurs only among Bhikkhunīs.

"Inclusion of all by a single recitation of the introduction (Nidānuddesa)" means that by this single Nidānuddesa: "Whoever has an offense, let him reveal it," all training rules (sikkhāpada) and all recitations of the Pātimokkha (Pātimokkhuddesa) are included.

"The two roots of Vinaya" are the body and speech. "Two heavy (garuka) offenses" refers to Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa. "Two types of concealing a gross offense" refers to the Pārājika offense of a Bhikkhunī who conceals a fault and the [Pācittiya offense] of a monk who conceals a Saṅghādisesa...
227:
...for one who conceals a Pārājika offense or a Saṅghādisesa offense, a Pācittiya offense is incurred; these two are called offenses for concealing a gross offense.

'Four [offenses] in the interval between villages' means: if a monk makes an agreement with a Bhikkhunī [to travel together], he incurs a Dukkaṭa offense; if he enters the precincts of another village, he incurs a Pācittiya offense; if he walks with a Bhikkhunī into a fenced village, he incurs a Thullaccaya offense at the first step and a Saṅghādisesa offense at the second step. In entering the precincts of an unfenced village, he incurs a Thullaccaya offense at the first step and a Saṅghādisesa offense at the second step. Thus, there are four offenses in the interval between villages by way of Dukkaṭa, Pācittiya, Thullaccaya, and Saṅghādisesa. 'Four [offenses] due to crossing to the other side of a river' means: if a monk makes an agreement with a Bhikkhunī, he incurs a Dukkaṭa offense; if he boards a boat, he incurs a Pācittiya offense; when crossing with a Bhikkhunī to the other side of a river, he incurs a Thullaccaya offense at the first step and a Saṅghādisesa offense at the second step. These are the four. A Thullaccaya offense for one type of meat occurs in the case of human flesh. A Dukkaṭa offense for nine types of meat occurs in the case of the remaining unallowable (akappiya) meats.

'Two [offenses] due to speaking at night' means: if a Bhikkhunī stands and speaks with a man within a forearm's length (hatthapāsa) in the darkness of night where there is no lamp, she incurs a Pācittiya offense; if she stands and speaks beyond a forearm's length, she incurs a Dukkaṭa offense. 'Two [offenses] due to speaking during the day' means: if a Bhikkhunī stands and speaks with a man within a forearm's length in a secluded place during the day, she incurs a Pācittiya offense; if she speaks beyond a forearm's length, she incurs a Dukkaṭa offense. 'Three [offenses] for the giver' means: if one gives poison to a human with the intention to kill, and that person dies because of it, one incurs a Pārājika offense. If one gives it to yakkhas or petas and they die, one incurs a Thullaccaya offense. If one gives it to an animal and it dies, one incurs a Pācittiya offense. Giving a robe to an unrelated Bhikkhunī results in a Pācittiya offense; thus there are three offenses for the giver. 'Four [offenses] in receiving' means: a Saṅghādisesa offense for grabbing the hand or grabbing the braid of hair; a Pārājika offense for receiving the male organ with the mouth; a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense for receiving a robe from an unrelated Bhikkhunī; and a Thullaccaya offense for a Bhikkhunī overcome by lust who receives food or snacks from the hand of a man overcome by lust. Thus, there are four classes of offenses (āpattikkhandha) in receiving.

## (2) Explanation of Desanāgāminī, etc.

'Five offenses requiring confession (desanāgāminī)' refers to the five light (lahuka) offenses. 'Six remediable offenses (sappaṭikamma)' refers to the remaining offenses excluding Pārājika. 'One irremediable offense (appaṭikamma) in this Dispensation' refers to the Pārājika offense alone.

'Two heavy (garuka) offenses in the Vinaya' as taught are the Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa offenses. 'Bodily and verbal offenses' means that all training rules arise in the body-door and the speech-door; in the mind-door...
228: There is not even a single training rule prescribed for the mind-door. The only kind of grain-juice (dhanyarasa) permissible in the afternoon is the medicinal loṇasovīraka (salted sour gruel). Only this juice derived from grain is permissible in the afternoon. The only authorization (sammuti) granted by a motion and fourfold proclamation (ñatticatutthakammavācā) is the authorization of an exhorter of nuns (bhikkhunovādakasammuti). Only this one bhikkhunovādakasammuti is allowed by a motion and fourfold proclamation. The two pārājika offenses involving physical contact are the methunapārājika of monks and the kāyasaṃsaggapārājika of nuns. The two grounds for communion (saṃvāsabhūmi) are: making oneself a person of equal communion by oneself, and the harmonious Saṅgha reinstating an expelled monk into the Saṅgha. In the Kurundī Commentary, however, the two grounds for communion are stated as the ground of equal communion (samānasaṃvāsakabhūmi) and the ground of different communion (nānāsaṃvāsakabhūmi). Two types of interruption of nights (ratticcheda) are prescribed for a monk undergoing probation (parivāsa) and a monk undergoing mānatta. The two dvangula (two-finger) regulations are: "one should take at most two finger-joints" and "two finger-breadths or two months". A nun incurs two offenses for striking herself. If she cries while striking, she incurs a pācittiya offense; if she does not cry, she incurs a dukkaṭa offense. The Saṅgha is split by two causes: by a formal act (kamma) and by the taking of voting tickets (salākaggāha). In this Vinaya text, according to the prescription for both, there are two initial offenses (paṭhamāpattika). Alternatively, there are eighteen: nine for monks and nine for nuns. The two functions of the motion (ñatti) are kammañatti and kammapādakañatti. In nine instances, the motion is the act (kamma), and in two instances, it stands as the basis of the act (kammapādaka). There are three offenses regarding taking life (pāṇātipāta). If one digs a pit without specific intent and a human dies, it is a pārājika; if a yakkha or peta dies, it is a thullaccaya; if an animal dies, it is a pācittiya. The three pārājika offenses by speech are: a nun who conceals a grave offense, a nun who follows an expelled monk, and a nun who commits an offense involving eight grounds (aṭṭhavatthuka). In the Kurundī Commentary, however, three are mentioned: taking what is not given by command, commanding to kill a human, and speaking of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma). The three types of suggestive speech (obhāsana) regarding sexual intercourse: praising or disparaging with reference to the excrement-way or urine-way is a saṅghādisesa; excluding those, speaking with reference to the area below the collarbone and above the kneecap is a thullaccaya; speaking with reference to the area above the collarbone and below the kneecap is a dukkaṭa. Three offenses can occur due to matchmaking (sañcaritta). If one accepts, investigates, and reports back, it is a saṅghādisesa; if one accepts and investigates but does not report back, it is a thullaccaya; if one accepts but does not investigate or report back, it is a dukkaṭa.
229: (Regarding matchmaking) ... if one reports back, a saṅghādisesa offense is incurred. If one accepts and investigates but does not report back, a thullaccaya offense is incurred. If one accepts but does not investigate or report back, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. Thus, these three groups of offenses occur due to matchmaking as the cause. Three types of persons should not be ordained (given upasampadā): those deficient in age (under 20), those deficient in limbs (angahīna), and those with a defective basis (vatthuvipanna). Their distinctions have already been mentioned. A specific detail here: those who are not fully equipped with bowl and robes, and those who are equipped but do not request (ordination), are also included among those deficient in limbs (angahīna). Those who have committed evil deeds such as matricide, etc., are to be understood as included among those with a defective basis (vatthuvipanna), which includes eunuchs (paṇḍaka), hermaphrodites (ubhatobyañjanaka), and animals. This method is stated in the Kurundī Commentary. The three ways of summarizing formal acts (kamma) are: ñattikappanā (formulating the motion), vippakatapaccattaṃ (the action in progress), and atītakaraṇaṃ (the action completed). Among these, the variety such as "should give, should do" is called ñattikappanā. The variety such as "gives, does" is called vippakatapaccattaṃ. The variety such as "has been given, has been done" is called atītakaraṇaṃ. Formal acts are summarized by these three. They are also summarized by three other factors: the basis (vatthu), the motion (ñatti), and the proclamation (anussāvana). Indeed, a formal act exists only when there is completeness of basis, motion, and proclamation; therefore, it is said "three summaries of formal acts". The three types of expelled persons (nāsitaka) are: "expel the nun Mettiyā", "an offending novice should be expelled", "a novice endowed with ten factors should be expelled", and "expel the novice Kaṇṭaka". Thus, three types of expelled persons should be understood by way of loss of the marks (linganāsanā), loss of communion (saṃvāsanāsanā), and loss by punishment (daṇḍakammanāsanā). Regarding the simultaneous proclamation of the formal act for three persons: because it was said, "Monks, I allow the proclamation for two or three persons at once," it is permissible to perform the proclamation for three persons at once with one preceptor (upajjhāya) and different chanters (kammavācā-ācariya). In taking what is not given (adinnādāna), the three offenses are: a pārājika offense for a quarter-baht or more, a thullaccaya offense for more than a māsaka, and a dukkaṭa offense for a māsaka or less than a māsaka. The four offenses due to sexual intercourse are: a pārājika offense with a corpse not yet eaten (by animals), a thullaccaya offense with a corpse mostly eaten, a dukkaṭa offense in an open mouth, and a pācittiya offense with a wooden doll (jatumāṭṭhaka). The three offenses for cutting are: a pārājika offense for cutting a lord of the forest (large tree), a pācittiya offense for cutting vegetation (bhūtagāma), and a thullaccaya offense for cutting the sexual organ. The five offenses due to discarding are: if one discards poison without intent and a human dies, it is a pārājika offense; if a yakkha or peta dies, it is a thullaccaya offense; if an animal dies, it is a pācittiya offense; if one emits semen, it is a saṅghādisesa offense; if one voids excrement or urine on green vegetation (as per the Sekhiya rules), it is a dukkaṭa offense. These are the five offenses due to discarding.
230:
"Pācittiyena dukkaṭā katā" means that in the ten training rules of the Bhikkhunovādavagga, a dukkaṭa offense is prescribed along with a pācittiya offense. "Four navakas are taught here" means that in the first training rule itself, two in adhamma-kamma and two in dhamma-kamma, thus four navakas (groups of nine) are taught. "Dvinnāṃ cīvarena ca" means that for a monk giving a robe to a nun in the presence of monks, a pācittiya offense is incurred; for a monk giving a robe to a nun in the presence of nuns, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. Thus, it means offenses are incurred due to the act of giving robes to two nuns.

"Eight pāṭidesanīyas" refers to the pāṭidesanīya offenses directly mentioned in the Pali text. "Bhuñjantāmakadhaññena pācittiyena dukkaṭā katā" means that for a nun who asks for and eats raw grain, a dukkaṭa offense is prescribed along with a pācittiya offense.

"Gacchantassa catasso" means that for a monk who travels by arrangement with a nun or a woman, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred; when entering the village precinct (gāmūpacāra), a pācittiya offense is incurred. For a nun who travels alone to another village, upon entering the village precinct, a thullaccaya offense is incurred on the first step, and a saṅghādisesa offense on the second step. Thus, these four offenses occur for one who travels. "The same for one who stands" means that four offenses also occur for one who stands. How? If a nun stands within arm's length (hatthapāsa) of a man in a dark or concealed place with the intent of friendship, a pācittiya offense is incurred. If she stands beyond arm's length, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. At dawn, if she stands while leaving the arm's length of a female companion, a thullaccaya offense is incurred. If she stands after having left, a saṅghādisesa offense is incurred. There are also four offenses for one who sits. "The same for one who lies down" means that whether that nun sits or lies down, she incurs these same four offenses.

## (၃) ပါစိတ္တိယဝဏ္ဏနာ
"Five pācittiyas" means that if five kinds of medicines are accepted and kept in various vessels or in a single vessel without being mixed, and seven days pass, that monk simultaneously incurs all five pācittiya offenses which have different bases (vatthu). It should not be said, "He incurred this one first, and this one later."

"Nine pācittiyas" means that if a monk asks for nine kinds of fine foods, takes a morsel of them together at once, puts it in his mouth, and swallows it, he simultaneously incurs all nine pācittiya offenses which have different bases.
231:
It should not be said, "He reached this offense first, and this offense later." One should confess with a single statement: "Venerable Sir, I accepted five kinds of medicines and let seven days pass, thereby reaching five offenses. I confess those offenses in your presence." If one speaks thus, the confession is completed. There is no need to speak with two or three statements. In the second explanation as well, it should be said: "Venerable Sir, I asked for and ate nine kinds of fine foods, thereby reaching nine offenses. I confess those offenses in your presence."

"One should confess by declaring the basis (vatthu)" means: "Venerable Sir, I accepted five kinds of medicines and let seven days pass. I confess those offenses in your presence according to their basis." If one confesses by declaring the basis in this way, the offenses are confessed. There is no need to mention the name of the offense. In the second explanation as well, it should be said: "Venerable Sir, I asked for and ate nine kinds of fine foods. I confess those offenses in your presence according to their basis."

"Three offenses involving admonition up to the third time" are: a pārājika offense for a nun who follows an expelled monk; a saṅghādisesa offense for the followers of schismatics such as Kokālika; and a pācittiya offense for the nun Caṇḍakāḷī who does not relinquish evil views. "Six offenses due to speech (vohāra)" means that one reaches six offenses due to speech associated with a request (viññatti). How? If, for the sake of livelihood and being of evil desire, one boastfully claims a false and non-existent superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), it is a pārājika offense. If, for the sake of livelihood, one performs matchmaking (sañcaritta), it is a saṅghādisesa offense. If, for the sake of livelihood, one says, "The one who lives in this monastery is an Arahant," it is a thullaccaya offense. If, for the sake of livelihood, a monk asks for fine foods for himself and eats them, it is a pācittiya offense. If, for the sake of livelihood, a nun asks for fine foods for herself and eats them, it is a pāṭidesanīya offense. If, for the sake of livelihood, one who is not ill asks for bean soup or rice for himself and eats it, it is a dukkaṭa offense.

"Three offenses due to eating" are: a thullaccaya offense for eating human flesh; a dukkaṭa offense for eating other unallowable meats; and a pācittiya offense for a nun eating garlic. "Five offenses due to eating" means: a nun filled with desire taking food from the hand of a man filled with desire...
232:
In that very place, a bhikkhunī who, for her own sake, asks for and receives human flesh and garlic, and then mixes them with other excellent foods and remaining unallowable meats and consumes them, incurs these five offenses due to the food: Saṅghādisesa, Thullaccaya, Pācittiya, Pāṭidesanīya, and Dukkaṭa.

Regarding the 'five grounds' (pañca ṭhānāni): if a bhikkhunī follows an expelled monk and, despite being exhorted up to three times, does not desist, she incurs a Dukkaṭa for the formal announcement (ñatti), a Thullaccaya for each of the two formal acts (kammavācā), and a Pārājika offense at the conclusion of the formal acts. In matters such as striving for a schism in the Saṅgha, a Saṅghādisesa is incurred; in not relinquishing a harmful wrong view, a Pācittiya is incurred. Thus, all offenses requiring exhortation up to the third time fall into these five grounds. Offenses occur to the five classes of co-religionists (sahadhammikas). Among these five, offenses strictly apply only to the two classes: Bhikkhus and Bhikkhunīs. For Sikkhamānās, Sāmaṇerīs, and Sāmaṇeras, because it is unallowable, it is not called an 'offense' (āpatti). For this reason, they should not be made to confess an offense, but rather a disciplinary punishment (daṇḍakamma) should be imposed on them. 'Legal matters (adhikaraṇa) also pertain only to these five' is the meaning. Indeed, the formal settlement and discourse regarding the bowls, robes, etc., of these five classes is called 'adhikaraṇa'; for laypeople, it is called a lawsuit (aḍḍakamma).

Settlement (vinicchaya) occurs only for the five classes of co-religionists. This means the legal matter of these five is settled and stilled (vūpasanta). 'Non-offense (anāpatti) also pertains only to these five' is the meaning. 'Beautiful through three grounds' means being beautiful because of the three factors such as the Saṅgha. Indeed, a person who has committed a transgression and then rehabilitates a remediable offense in the midst of the Saṅgha, a group, or in the presence of an individual, becomes a monk of original status (pākatika) with freshly purified virtue. Therefore, it is said that one is beautiful through three grounds.

'Two bodily offenses at night' means: if a bhikkhunī, in the darkness of night, stands, sits, or lies down within the reach (hatthapāsa) of a man, she incurs a Pācittiya; if she stands, etc., beyond the reach, she incurs a Dukkaṭa. Thus, she incurs two offenses originating from the body-door at night. 'Two bodily offenses by day' means: in the same manner, she incurs two offenses in a secluded place during the day. 'One offense for one who stares' means: 'Bhikkhus, one should not stare with lust at the female anatomy...'
233:
'...should be scrutinized. If anyone should stare, there is an offense of Dukkaṭa.' This is the one offense for one who stares. 'One offense due to alms-food' refers to the Dukkaṭa offense mentioned in this Pali passage: 'Bhikkhus, one should not look at the face of a woman who gives alms.' At the very least, a monk who looks up at the face of a Sāmaṇerā who is giving rice gruel (yāgu) or curry also incurs a Dukkaṭa. However, in the Kurundī Commentary, it is stated: 'One offense due to alms-food is the Pācittiya offense incurred by a monk who eats alms-food that was prepared by a bhikkhunī.'

A person who clearly sees the eight benefits (aṭṭha āniśaṃsa) taught in the Kosambaka Khandhaka (should confess their offense through faith in others). The 'three types of suspended (ukkhittaka) persons' are: one suspended for not seeing an offense, one for not atoning for an offense, and one for not relinquishing a harmful wrong view. The proper conduct of these suspended monks in the forty-three duties is called 'tecattālīsa sammāvattanā' (forty-three right conducts).

Lying (musāvāda) falls into five grounds: Pārājika, Saṅghādisesa, Thullaccaya, Pācittiya, and Dukkaṭa. The statement 'fourteen is the maximum' was explained below using the method of 'ten days at most,' etc. The twelve Pāṭidesanīya offenses consist of four for monks and eight for bhikkhunīs. What is the 'confession of faults (accayadesanā) of four persons'? It refers to: the confession of the archers sent by Devadatta (to kill the Buddha), the confession of the female attendant of Elder Anuruddha, the confession of Vaḍḍha the Licchavī, and the confession of the monks who arrived after being subjected to the act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) by Elder Vāsabhagāmiya. This is known as the confession of faults of four persons.

Lying that is endowed with eight factors, starting from 'he has the intention beforehand: I will speak a lie' and ending with 'misrepresenting the perception,' is called 'eightfold lying.' The factors of the Uposatha have also been taught in the manner of 'one should not kill living beings,' etc. The eight factors of a messenger (dūteyyaṅga) are those taught in the Saṅghabhedaka Khandhaka in the manner: 'Here, bhikkhus, a monk is both a listener and one who makes others hear,' etc. The eight practices of sectarians (titthiyavatta) have been taught in the Mahākhandhaka.

'Ordination by eight proclamations' (aṭṭhavācikā upasampadā) is said with reference to the ordination of bhikkhunīs. 'Eight persons should be honored by rising and offering a seat' means that in the refectory, other bhikkhunīs should rise from their seats and offer them to the eight (senior) bhikkhunīs.
234:
A place should be given. A monk who is an exhorter of nuns (bhikkhunovādaka) should be authorized as a monk endowed with eight qualities.

In the verse beginning with 'Ekassa chejjaṃ'—among nine persons, whichever monk, having taken a voting ticket (salākā), breaks the Saṅgha, for that monk alone there is severance [from the Dispensation]; he incurs a Pārājika offense like Devadatta. The four monks who follow the schismatic, such as Kokālika and others, incur a Thullaccaya offense. For the four monks who speak according to the Dhamma (dhammavādī), there is no offense. These offenses and non-offenses for all [monks] have only the single basis of schism in the Saṅgha (saṅghabheda).

In the verse beginning with 'Nava āghātavatthūni'—the Saṅgha is split by nine monks. 'Ñattiyā karaṇā navā' means that there are nine formal acts to be performed by a motion (ñatti). The rest is clear.

## (4) Explanation of Persons Not to Be Saluted, etc.

'Dasa puggalā nābhivādetabbā' refers to the ten persons mentioned in the Senāsanakkhandhaka. It means that one should not pay respect to them, nor perform the gesture of salutation (añjali), nor show them the duties of the Khandhakas such as offering drinking water or holding a fan, nor should the hands be raised in salutation. A monk who acts thus toward these ten persons incurs a Dukkaṭa offense. 'Dasa cīvaradhāraṇā' means that the keeping of an extra robe for up to ten days is permitted.

'Pañcannaṃ vassaṃvuṭṭhānaṃ, dātabbaṃ idha cīvaraṃ' means that [robes] should be given only in the presence of the five classes of co-religionists (sahadhammika) who have completed the rains retreat. 'Sattannaṃ sante' means that in the presence of these seven persons—the four consisting of one who has gone to another region, one who is insane, one who is mentally deranged, and one afflicted by pain, plus the three who have been suspended (ukkhittaka)—if there is a suitable recipient, [robes] may be given even in their absence. 'Soḷasannaṃ na dātabbaṃ' means that [robes] should not be given to the remaining sixteen types of persons mentioned in the Cīvarakkhandhaka, such as eunuchs (paṇḍaka) and others.

'Katisataṃ rattisataṃ, āpattiyo chādayitvānā' means: how many hundreds of offenses have been concealed for a hundred nights? 'Dasasataṃ rattisataṃ, āpattiyo chādayitvānā' means: have a thousand offenses been concealed for a hundred nights? The summary meaning here is: if a monk incurs a hundred Saṅghādisesa offenses every day and conceals them for ten days, he has concealed a thousand offenses for a hundred nights. That monk [should undergo penance for] all those offenses...
235:
'Dasāhapaticchanna' means that a monk who has practiced parivāsa for ten nights after requesting it shall be released from the offense. 'Twelve defects of legal acts have been taught' means that just as the act of announcement (apalokana-kamma) has three types—unlawful and by an incomplete group (adhammena-vagga), unlawful and by a complete group (adhammena-samagga), and lawful and by an incomplete group (dhammena-vagga)—so too the legal act with a motion (ñatti-kamma), the legal act with a motion as the second (ñattidutiya-kamma), and the legal act with a motion as the fourth (ñatticatuttha-kamma) each have three types. Thus, by making three types for each act, twelve defects of legal acts have been taught.

'Four accomplishments of legal acts' means that just as the act of announcement is lawful and by a complete group (dhammena-samagga), so too the remaining acts such as the legal act with a motion are lawful and by a complete group. Thus, four accomplishments of legal acts have been taught. 'Six types of legal acts' means that six types have been taught: an act that is unlawful and by an incomplete group, an act that is unlawful and by a complete group, an act that is seemingly lawful but by an incomplete group, an act that is seemingly lawful but by a complete group, an act that is lawful and by an incomplete group, and an act that is lawful and by a complete group. 'Among these, only one is performed according to the Dhamma' means that among these six types of acts, only the act that is lawful and by a complete group (dhammena-samagga-kamma) is designated as an act performed according to the Dhamma. In the answer to the second verse as well, only this dhammena-samagga-kamma is designated as the act performed according to the Dhamma.

'Yaṃ desitaṃ' means those groups of offenses which have been pointed out, spoken, and made manifest. In the words beginning with 'Anantajinena', Nibbāna is called 'Ananta' (Infinite) because it is devoid of end or limit. The Blessed One is called 'Anantajina' (Infinite Victor) because he conquered, attained, and fully reached that Nibbāna by crushing the mass of defilements (kilesa), just as a king conquers a kingdom by crushing a host of enemies. That same Blessed One is called 'Tādī' (The Steadfast) because he is without fluctuation in the face of pleasant and unpleasant objects. He is called 'Vivekadassī' (Seer of Seclusion) because he has seen the five kinds of seclusion known as: seclusion by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-viveka), seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhana-viveka), seclusion by eradication (samuccheda-viveka), seclusion by tranquilization (paṭipassaddhi-viveka), and seclusion by escape (nissaraṇa-viveka). Those groups of offenses were pointed out by that Infinite Victor, the Steadfast One, the Seer of Seclusion.

In this context, the connection of words is as follows: among the seven groups of offenses pointed out by the Teacher, not even a single offense can be settled without the means of settlement (samatha). Rather, the six samathas and the four legal issues (adhikaraṇa)—all these matters are settled and reach resolution through the settlement in the presence (sammukhāvinaya). However, here, only the sammukhāvinaya alone settles and reaches the state of samatha without the other samathas. Indeed, there is no such thing as its non-accomplishment without another samatha. Therefore, it is said: 'In this Dispensation, only one samatha settles independently of other samathas.' This meaning has been stated in the ancient commentaries. We, however, taking only the meaning of negation (paṭisedha) for the particle 'vinā', interpret: 'Among these groups of offenses, one offense, being without the samathas...'
236:
Regarding the word "Samathehi," we favor this meaning: among these seven groups of offenses, the single group of Pārājika offenses is settled without the settlement procedures (samatha). It has also been stated: "That Pārājika offense which is without remainder—that offense is not settled by any legal issue (adhikaraṇa), at any place, or by any settlement procedure (samatha)."

Regarding the phrase "one hundred and fifty minus six" (144): "Upāli, in this Dispensation, a monk represents non-Dhamma as Dhamma; regarding that non-Dhamma, he has the view of non-Dhamma, and regarding the schism, he has the view of non-Dhamma; regarding that non-Dhamma, he has the view of non-Dhamma, and regarding the schism, he has the view of Dhamma; regarding that non-Dhamma, he has the view of non-Dhamma, and regarding the schism, he is doubtful; regarding that non-Dhamma, he has the view of Dhamma, and regarding the schism, he has the view of non-Dhamma; regarding that non-Dhamma, he has the view of Dhamma, and regarding the schism, he is doubtful; regarding that non-Dhamma, he is doubtful, and regarding the schism, he has the view of non-Dhamma; regarding that non-Dhamma, he is doubtful, and regarding the schism, he has the view of Dhamma; regarding that non-Dhamma, he is doubtful, and regarding the schism, he is doubtful." In this way, by virtue of the eighteen grounds for schism taught in the Saṅghabhedaka-kkhandhaka, the 144 types of persons who go to the woeful states (apāya) should be understood.

Regarding the "eighteen who do not go to the woeful states": "Upāli, in this Dispensation, a monk represents non-Dhamma as Dhamma; regarding that non-Dhamma, he has the view of Dhamma, and regarding the schism, he has the view of Dhamma; without concealing his view, without concealing his approval, without concealing his preference, and without concealing his intention, he makes it known repeatedly and causes them to take the voting tickets (salāka), saying, 'This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher's instruction; take this, approve of this.' Upāli, such a person, though a schismatic, is not one who goes to the woeful states, not one who goes to hell, not one who remains there for an aeon, and is not incurable." Thus, by treating each ground individually, there are eighteen persons as taught at the end of the Saṅghabhedaka-kkhandhaka. In the explanation of the 144 persons, the eighteen sets of eight (aṭṭhaka) mentioned are also present.

## (5) Soḷasakkammādivaṇṇanā

The answers to all the verses beginning with "Kati kammāni" are clear in themselves.

## The Explanation of the Second Collection of Verses is Finished.
237:
## Sedamocanagāthā
## (1) Avippavāsapañhāvaṇṇanā

In the Sedamocanagāthā, "Asaṃvāso" (non-communion) refers to the absence of communal living through acts such as Uposatha and Pavāraṇā. If it is asked whether some form of partaking (sambhoga) is possible despite this non-communion, unallowable partaking is not possible. However, the mother (who is a bhikkhunī) alone is permitted to perform duties such as bathing and feeding the child. "Avippavāsena anāpatti" (no offense by not being apart) refers to the absence of an offense for sleeping together under the same roof. The answer to the riddle "This problem has been thought of by the wise" should be understood through the bhikkhunī who is the mother of the child. This is because it was said in reference to her own young son.

The "Avissajjitagāthā" (unresolved verse) was spoken in reference to heavy articles (garubhaṇḍa). Its meaning has already been stated in the decision (vinicchaya) on heavy articles.

"I do not speak of the ten persons" refers to the ten persons mentioned in the Senāsanakkhandhaka. "The eleven to be avoided" refers to the eleven persons to be avoided as taught in the Mahākkhandhaka; these are also not what is meant. This problem was spoken in reference to a naked (nagga) monk.

Regarding the problem "How is one uncommon in training?", it was spoken in reference to a monk who was formerly a barber. This is because he is not permitted to keep barber's tools, whereas others are permitted. Therefore, he is uncommon (asādhāraṇa) in terms of the training.

"What do the Buddhas call that person?"—this problem was spoken in reference to a created Buddha (nimmitabuddha).

"Avoiding the area below the navel" means setting aside the area below the navel. This problem was spoken in reference to a headless trunk (kabandha) peta, who has eyes and a mouth on his chest.

"A monk builds a hut by his own choice"—this problem refers to a small hut roofed with grass. The second problem refers to a hut made entirely of clay.

"He may reach the heavy Pārājika (offense of excision)"—this problem was spoken in reference to a bhikkhunī who conceals the (Pārājika) fault of another bhikkhunī. The second problem refers to unfit persons (abhabba-puggala) such as eunuchs (paṇḍaka). Those eleven persons have already reached Pārājika (defeat/loss of status) even while they were in the state of laypeople.
238:
'Vācā' refers to not speaking with words. It means not uttering even a sound, intending for others to hear, thinking, 'These people will hear my words.' This question is stated regarding the falsehood (musāvāda) mentioned as: 'If one does not disclose an existing offense, it is a deliberate lie.' For that monk sitting silently with an improper pledge (as if he has no offense when he does), there is no offense at the mind-door (manodvāra). However, because he does not disclose an offense that should be disclosed, it should be understood that this offense arises at the word-door (vacīdvāra) due to the omission of what ought to be done.

The question 'Four Saṅghādisesas' is stated regarding a bhikkhunī who has reached the other side of a river belonging to another village at dawn. Having left her own village in the last watch of the night, as soon as she reaches the other side of the river at dawn as described, she simultaneously incurs four Saṅghādisesa offenses characterized by: staying away from her robes (rattivippavāsa), entering another village (gāmantara), crossing a river (nadīpāra), and being separated from the group (gaṇamhā-ohīyana).

The question 'Can offenses be various?' is stated regarding two bhikkhunīs who are ordained on one side (ekato-upasampannā). Among them, for a monk who receives a robe from the hand of a bhikkhunī ordained only on the monks' side, there is a Pācittiya offense. For a monk who receives from the hand of a bhikkhunī ordained only on the bhikkhunīs' side, there is a Dukkaṭa offense.

'Four people consulting' refers to a teacher and three students who stole goods worth six māsakas. For the teacher, three māsakas were by his own hand and three were by command; therefore, he incurs a Thullaccaya offense. For the other students, one māsaka each was by their own hand and five were by command; therefore, they incur Pārājika offenses. This is a summary here. The detailed explanation was given in the commentary on the Pārājika for taking what is not given (adinnādāna) under the section on theft by arrangement (saṃvidāvahāra).

## (2) Pārājikādipañhāvaṇṇanā

The question 'There is no hole in that house' is stated regarding small huts covered with cloth (dussakuṭi) and so forth, and the Santata-peyyāla.

The verse 'Oil, honey, molasses' is stated regarding a person who has undergone a change of sex (liṅgaparivatta).

The verse 'By Nissaggiya' is stated regarding the diversion (pariṇāmana) of offerings. A monk who diverts two robes from gains already dedicated to the Saṅgha, saying, 'One for me, one for another...'
239:
'...Give one to me, give one to him,' diverting them with a single verbal effort (vacīpayoga), incurs both a Nissaggiya Pācittiya and a Suddha Pācittiya simultaneously.

The question 'Kammañca taṃ kuppeyya vaggapaccayā' is stated regarding the village boundary (gāmasīmā) in cities such as Bārāṇasī, which are twelve leagues in extent.

The verse 'Padavītihāramattena' is stated regarding matchmaking (sañcaritta). Its meaning was also stated in the explanation of the Sañcaritta training rule.

The question 'Sabbāni tāni nissaggiyāni' is stated regarding having an unrelated bhikkhunī wash robes. If a bhikkhunī, holding the edge of all three robes where they are soiled by crow droppings or mud, washes them with water, those robes become Nissaggiya even while they are on the monk's body.

'Saraṇagamanampi na tassa atthi' means that there is also no ordination by taking refuge (saraṇagamana-upasampadā). This question is stated regarding the ordination of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.

'Haneyya anariyaṃ mando' means he might kill that woman who is not his mother, or that man who is not his father, or a non-noble person. This question is stated regarding a father who has become a woman and a mother who has become a man due to a change of sex.

The question 'Na tenānantaraṃ phuseti' is stated regarding animal parents, such as the animal parents of the hermit Migasiṅga and Sīhakumāra.

The verse 'Acodayitvā' is stated regarding ordination by messenger (dūtenupasampadā). The verse 'Codayitvā' is stated regarding the ordination of eunuchs (paṇḍaka) and others. In the Kurundī, it is said: 'The first verse refers to eight formal acts in the absence of the person (asammukhā-kamma), and the second verse refers to a formal act against one who is without offense.'

'For one who cuts, there is an offense' means: for one who cuts a great tree (vanappati), there is a Pārājika; for one who cuts grass, vines, etc., there is a Pācittiya; for one who cuts the genitals, there is a Thullaccaya. 'For one who cuts, there is no offense' refers to one who cuts his own hair and nails. 'For one who conceals, there is an offense' refers to one who conceals his own offense or the offense of another. 'For one who covers, there is no offense' refers to one who covers or roofs a house, etc.
240:
In the verse beginning with “Saccaṃ bhaṇanto,” a monk who speaks the truth, saying, “You are a woman with a protrusion (sikharaṇī), you are a hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka),” commits a heavy offense (Saṅghādisesa). However, in the case of deliberate lying (sampajāna-musāvāda), a light offense (lahuka) is committed due to the falsehood. In the case of falsely claiming superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), the monk who lies commits a heavy offense (Pārājika). In the case of claiming actual superhuman states, the monk who speaks the truth commits a light offense (Pācittiya).

## (3) Explanation of the Questions on Pācittiya and Others

The verse beginning with “Adhiṭṭhitaṃ” is spoken with reference to a monk who uses a robe that is to be forfeited (nissaggiya) without having relinquished it.

The verse beginning with “Atthaṅgate sūriye” is spoken with reference to a ruminating (romanthaka) monk.

The meaning of the verse beginning with “Na rattacitto” is as follows: A monk with a lustful mind commits the Pārājika offense of sexual intercourse. A monk with a mind intent on theft commits the Pārājika offense of taking what is not given. A monk who intends to kill another person commits the Pārājika offense of killing a human being. However, a monk who causes a schism in the Saṅgha has neither a lustful mind nor a mind intent on theft, nor does he intend to kill another. Nevertheless, when such a monk who causes a schism gives a voting ticket (salāka), it is an act of uprooting from the Sasana (Pārājika). For the monk who follows the schismatic and accepts the voting ticket, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is committed.

The question “Gaccheyya aḍḍhayojanaṃ” is spoken with reference to the foot of a single tree belonging to one family, which is like a well-established banyan tree.

The verse “Kāyikāni” is spoken with reference to a monk who takes hold of the hair or fingers of many women at once.

The verse “Vācasikāni” is spoken with reference to a monk who speaks harsh words in the manner of “You are all women with protrusions (sikharaṇī),” and so on.

“Tissitthiyo methunaṃ taṃ na seveti” refers to three types of females (human, non-human, and animal). Among these females, whatever is called sexual intercourse, he does not engage in it. “Tayo purise” means he does not approach and engage in sexual intercourse with three types of males. “Tayo anariyapaṇḍake” means he does not approach and engage in sexual intercourse with these six types of persons: the three types of ignoble persons known as hermaphrodites (ubhatobyañjanaka) and the three types of eunuchs (paṇḍaka). “Na cācare methunaṃ byañjanasmiṃ” means he does not practice sexual intercourse even by way of a derivative Pārājika (anuloma-pārājika). “Chejjaṃ siyā methunadhamma-paccayā” means that a Pārājika offense may occur because of the practice of sexual intercourse. This question is spoken with reference to an Aṭṭhavatthukā Bhikkhunī.
241:
This question is spoken with reference to an Aṭṭhavatthukā Bhikkhunī. Indeed, when that Aṭṭhavatthukā Bhikkhunī strives to engage in physical contact (kāyasaṃsagga), which is a preliminary to sexual intercourse, she is uprooted from the Sasana (Pārājika) because of the sexual nature of the act.

The verse “Mātaraṃ cīvaraṃ” is spoken with reference to creating a reminder for the sake of a rain-cloth (vassikasāṭika) outside the period for receiving rain-cloths. The decision on this verse has already been stated in the explanation of the Vassikasāṭika Sikkhāpada.

The verse “Kuddho ārādhako hoti” is spoken with reference to the conduct of ascetics (titthiya). Indeed, when a titthiya (who wishes to ordain) is fulfilling his duties, if he becomes angry when the virtues of the titthiyas are spoken of, he is one who pleases (the monks). If he becomes angry when the virtues of the Triple Gem are spoken of, he is blameworthy. The details of this are stated in that very Titthiyavatta. The second verse is also spoken with reference to that same Titthiyavatta.

The verse beginning with “Saṅghādisesaṃ” is spoken with reference to a nun who, being lustful, receives alms-food from the hand of a lustful man and swallows it after mixing it with human flesh, raw garlic, choice food (paṇītabhojana), and other types of unallowable (akappiya) meat besides human flesh.

The verse “Eko upasampanno eko anupasampanno” is spoken with reference to a novice (sāmaṇera) situated in the sky. Indeed, if one of two novices sits suspended even a hair’s breadth from the ground by psychic power, he is called unordained (anupasampanna). The Saṅgha, while staying in the sky, should not perform a legal act (vinayakamma) for a person on the ground; if they do, the act is invalid.

The verse “Akappakataṃ” is spoken with reference to a monk whose robe has been snatched away. The decision on this verse has been stated in detail in that very Acchinnacīvara Sikkhāpada.

“Na deti na paṭiggaṇhāti” means the instigating nun does not give, and the instigated nun does not receive from her hand. “Paṭiggaho tena na vijjati” means that for that very reason, there is no receiving by the instigated nun from the hand of the instigator. “Āpajjati garukaṃ” means that even so, the nun who instigates the receiving of alms-food from the hand of a lustful man commits a Saṅghādisesa offense. “Tañca paribhogapaccayā” means that she reaches that offense because of the consumption by the instigated nun...
242:
...reaches (the offense). Indeed, at the conclusion of the meal by the instigated nun, a Saṅghādisesa offense occurs for the instigating nun. The second verse is spoken with reference to the instigation by that same nun in the receiving of water and tooth-wood (dantapona).

“Neither a nun nor reaching an offense” means that among the seventeen Saṅghādisesas prescribed for nuns, if a nun reaches any one of the offenses and conceals it out of disrespect, she does not reach an offense because of the concealment; she does not reach another new offense. She only receives the fortnightly penance (pakkhamānatta) for the concealed or unconcealed offense. This person, however, is not a nun, and although she reaches a heavy offense with a remainder and conceals it, she does not reach an offense. “This problem has been considered by the wise” means this problem is said to be spoken with reference to a suspended (ukkhittaka) monk. There is no performance of legal acts (vinayakamma) with that suspended monk; therefore, although he reaches a Saṅghādisesa offense and conceals it, he does not reach an offense (of concealment).

## The Explanation of the Sedamocanagāthā is Finished.
243:
## Pañcavagga
## Commentary on the Kammavagga

In the Kammavagga, the distinctions in the performance of the four types of formal acts (kamma) have already been mentioned in the Samathakkhandhaka. Even though they have been mentioned, the decision regarding these formal acts becomes clear only when explained from the beginning; therefore, I shall speak from the very beginning regarding what should be said about these four formal acts. 'Cattāri' (four) is a statement defining the number of formal acts. 'Kammāni' (formal acts) indicates the defined formal acts.

An Apalokana-kamma (act of announcement) is a formal act to be performed by clearing the Saṅgha within the boundary (sīmā), bringing the consent (chanda) of those entitled to give it, and making an announcement three times with the approval of the harmonious Saṅgha. A Ñatti-kamma (act with a motion) is a formal act to be performed with a single motion (ñatti) with the approval of the harmonious Saṅgha, following the same method mentioned. A Ñattidutiya-kamma (act with a motion as the second) is a formal act to be performed with one motion and one proclamation (anussāvanā), thus making the proclamation the second [part] after the motion, with the approval of the harmonious Saṅgha following the same method. A Ñatticatuttha-kamma (act with a motion as the fourth) is a formal act to be performed with one motion and three proclamations, thus making the proclamations the fourth [part] after the motion, with the approval of the harmonious Saṅgha following the same method.

Among those four types of formal acts, an Apalokana-kamma should be performed only by announcement; it should not be performed by way of a Ñatti-kamma, etc. A Ñatti-kamma also should be performed only by establishing a single motion; it should not be performed by way of an Apalokana-kamma, etc. In the case of a Ñattidutiya-kamma, however, there are acts that may be performed by announcement and acts that may not.

Among those acts, these six types—namely, Sīmāsammuti (authorization of a boundary), Sīmāsamūhanana (removal of a boundary), Kaṭhinadāna (offering of the Kaṭhina robe), Kaṭhinuddhāra (removal of the Kaṭhina), Kuṭivatthudesanā (designation of a site for a hut), and Vihāravatthudesanā (designation of a site for a monastery)—are serious (garuka) acts and therefore are not fit to be performed by mere announcement; they must be performed only by proclaiming a Ñattidutiya-kammavācā. The remaining thirteen authorizations (sammuti) and authorizations such as Senāsanaggāhaka (assigner of lodgings), Matakacīvaradāna (offering of robes of a deceased monk), etc., are light (lahuka) acts and therefore are fit to be performed even by announcement; however, they should certainly not be performed by way of a Ñatti-kamma or a Ñatticatuttha-kamma. Some teachers say that if performed by way of a Ñatticatuttha-kamma, it becomes firmer, and therefore it should be [so] performed. Even though they say so, if it were thus, there would be a confusion of formal acts (kammasaṅkara); therefore, it has already been rejected, stating that it should not be performed. If there is a deficiency in syllables, or a deficiency in words, or a word poorly recited...
244:
...(deficiency in letters or phrases) may occur; for the sake of correcting such deficiencies, it is proper to recite it repeatedly. Such repeated recitation serves to make an unshakeable act (akuppakamma) firm; in the case of a shakeable act (kuppakamma), it stands as a valid act (due to the re-recitation).

A Ñatticatutthakamma must be performed only by announcing the motion (ñatti) and three proclamations (kammavācā); it must not be performed by way of announcement (apalokanakamma) and so forth. "They fail in five ways" means they fail due to five reasons.

In the passage, "One performs in absence an act that should be performed in presence; it is an unlawful act (adhammakamma) that has failed in its basis (vatthuvipanna)," there are acts to be performed in presence (sammukhākaraṇīya) and acts to be performed in absence (asammukhākaraṇīya). Among them, what is called an act to be performed in absence (asammukhākaraṇīya) is of eight kinds: ordination by messenger (dūtenupasampadā), turning over the alms-bowl (pattanikkujjana), turning the alms-bowl back up (pattukkujjana), the authorization for an insane monk (ummattakasammuti), the authorization for trainee families (sekhasammuti), the Brahma-punishment (brahmadaṇḍa) for the monk Channa, the act of publicizing (pakāsanīyakamma) regarding Devadatta, and the act of not saluting (avandanīyakamma) to be performed by the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha against a monk who shows disrespect. All these should be understood according to the method stated in the respective Pali and Commentaries. These eight types of acts, even if performed in absence, are considered well-performed and are unshakeable (akuppa).

All other remaining acts must be performed only in presence. They must be performed only by bringing them to the fourfold Sammukhāvinaya (Discipline in the Presence): the presence of the Saṅgha, the presence of the Dhamma, the presence of the Vinaya, and the presence of the person (puggala). Only when performed in this way are they considered well-performed. If not performed in this way, because they are performed without the basis (vatthu) known as Sammukhāvinaya, they are called acts that have failed in their basis (vatthuvipanna). Therefore, it is said, "One performs in absence an act that should be performed in presence; it is an unlawful act that has failed in its basis."

In acts such as Paṭipucchākaraṇīya (acts to be performed after questioning), the performance of questioning (paṭipucchā) and so forth is the very basis (vatthu). It should be understood that because they are performed without that basis, those acts also fail in their basis (vatthuvipanna). This is merely the literal meaning here. "One performs as Apaṭipucchā an act that is Paṭipucchākaraṇီya" means one performs without questioning, without accusing, and without reminding of the offense, an act that should be performed only after questioning, accusing, and reminding. "One performs as Appaṭiññāya an act that is Paṭiññāyakaraṇီya" means one performs by force against one who prevaricates, without an acknowledgment, an act that should be performed according to the acknowledgment given after being brought to acknowledge. One worthy of Sativinaya (Discipline for the Mindful) is an Arahant like the Elder Dabba Mallaputta. One worthy of Amūḷhavinaya (Discipline for the Non-confused) is an insane person like the monk Gagga. One worthy of Tassapāpiyasikakamma (Act for one who is more sinful) is a person with many offenses like the monk Upavāḷa. This method is the same in all cases.
245:
Performing the Uposatha on a non-Uposatha day means performing the Uposatha on a day that is not an Uposatha day. An Uposatha day refers to the day of harmony (sāmaggī) for a divided Saṅgha during the eleven months excluding the month of Kattika, as well as the previously mentioned 14th and 15th days. Performing the Uposatha on any day other than these three types of Uposatha days is called 'performing the Uposatha on a non-Uposatha day'. This is because in a monastery where there is a dispute over minor matters such as bowls and robes, the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā is suspended; once that legal issue (adhikaraṇa) is settled and they say, 'We have become harmonious,' they do not get the chance to perform the Sāmaggī-uposatha before the regular Uposatha day. Those who do so are said to have performed the Uposatha on a non-Uposatha day.

Performing Pavāraṇā on a non-Pavāraṇā day means performing Pavāraṇā on a day that is not a Pavāraṇā day. A Pavāraṇā day refers to the day of harmony for a divided Saṅgha within the month of Kattika (from the 1st waning day of Assayuja to the full moon of Kattika), a day that has been postponed (due to some reason), and the two full moon days (the full moon of Assayuja and the full moon of Kattika). Performing Pavāraṇā on any day other than these four types of Pavāraṇā days is called 'performing Pavāraṇā on a non-Pavāraṇā day'. Here too, because a minor dispute has been settled, they do not get the chance to perform the Sāmaggī-pavāraṇā; those who do so are said to have performed Pavāraṇā on a non-Pavāraṇā day. Furthermore, ordaining someone who is under twenty years of age, or someone who has previously committed a Pārājika offense, or any of the eleven types of unsuitable persons, results in an unrighteous act (adhamma-kamma) due to a failure in the object (vatthu). In this way, formal acts fail because of the object.

Regarding failure due to the motion (ñatti), 'not specifying the object' means not mentioning the name of the person for whom the formal act, such as ordination (upasampadā), is being performed. When one should say, 'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This Dhammarakkhita is the candidate for ordination from the Venerable Buddharakkhita,' if one says, 'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. [He] is the candidate for ordination from the Venerable Buddharakkhita' (omitting the candidate's name), this is 'not specifying the object'.

'Not specifying the Saṅgha' means not using the name of the Saṅgha. When one should say, 'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This person is Dhammarakkhita,' if one says, 'Venerable sirs, listen to me. This person is Dhammarakkhita' (omitting the word 'Saṅgha'), this is 'not specifying the Saṅgha'.

'Not specifying the person' means not mentioning the name of the candidate's preceptor (upajjhāya). When one should say, 'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This Dhammarakkhita is the candidate for ordination from the Venerable Buddharakkhita,' if one should say...
246:
...if one says, 'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This Dhammarakkhita is the candidate for ordination' (omitting the preceptor's name), this is 'not specifying the person (preceptor)'.

'Not specifying the motion (ñatti)' means not specifying (not reciting) the motion in any way. In a formal act with one motion and one announcement (ñatti-dutiya-kamma), one omits the motion and performs the announcement (anussāvana) twice. In a formal act with one motion and three announcements (ñatti-catuttha-kamma), one also omits the motion and performs the announcement four times. Doing so is called 'not specifying the motion'.

'Placing the motion last' means first performing the announcement with the kammavācā and then saying, 'This is the motion (esā ñatti),' followed by 'The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent; thus I bear this in mind.' In this way, the motion is placed last. Due to these five ways mentioned, formal acts fail from the side of the motion.

Regarding failure due to the announcement (anussāvana), the object and so forth should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The way of not specifying the object etc. is as follows: in the first announcement, 'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me,' or in the second and third announcements, 'A second time I speak this matter, a third time I speak this matter, venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me,' when one should say, 'This Dhammarakkhita is the candidate for ordination from the Venerable Buddharakkhita,' if one says, 'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me, [he is the candidate] of the Venerable Buddharakkhita' (omitting the candidate's name), this is 'not specifying the object'. When one should say, 'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This person is Dhammarakkhita,' if one says, 'Venerable sirs, listen to me. This person is Dhammarakkhita' (omitting the word 'Saṅgha'), this is 'not specifying the Saṅgha'. When one should say, 'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This Dhammarakkhita is the candidate for ordination from the Venerable Buddharakkhita,' if one says, 'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This Dhammarakkhita is the candidate for ordination' (omitting the preceptor's name), this is 'not specifying the person'.

'Deficient announcement (sāvanaṃ hāpeti)' means not performing the announcement with the kammavācā at all, but instead reciting only the motion twice in a ñatti-dutiya-kamma, or reciting only the motion four times in a ñatti-catuttha-kamma. In this way, one makes the announcement deficient. Furthermore, in a ñatti-dutiya-kamma, after reciting one motion, if one omits a letter or mispronounces a word while reciting the one announcement, this person also makes the announcement deficient. In a ñatti-catuttha-kamma, after reciting one motion, if one performs the announcement with the kammavācā only once or twice, or [omits] a letter or a word...
247:
Alternatively, it should be understood that one who omits (letters or words) or one who pronounces them poorly causes the anussāvana (proclamation) to fail.

Regarding the phrase 'pronounces poorly', this is the decision: one who speaks a different letter when another should be spoken is said to 'pronounce poorly' (duruttaṃ karoti). Therefore, a monk performing a kammavācā should carefully observe these (ten types of articulation):

'Soft (sithila), hard (dhanita), long (dīgha), short (rassa),
heavy (garu), light (lahu), and nasal (niggahita),
connected (sambandha), distinct (vavatthita), and released (vimutta);
the classification of the mental impulse that produces articulation (vyañjanabuddhi) is tenfold.'

Among these ten, 'soft' (sithila) refers to the first and third letters in the five groups (vaggas). 'Hard' (dhanita) refers to the second and fourth letters in those same groups. 'Long' (dīgha) refers to sounds like 'ā' which are spoken with a long duration. 'Short' (rassa) refers to sounds like 'a' which are spoken with half that duration. 'Heavy' (garuka) is the long sound itself. Or, as in the case of Venerable Buddharakkhita Thera's 'yassa nakkhamatī', it refers to a letter followed by a conjunct consonant. 'Light' (lahuka) is the short sound itself. Or, as in the case of Venerable Buddharakkhita Thera's 'yassa na khamatī', it refers to a letter not followed by a conjunct consonant. 'Nasal' (niggahita) refers to what is spoken with a nasal sound by pressing the vocal organs without releasing them and with the mouth not fully open. 'Connected' (sambandha) refers to speaking by connecting with the following word, such as 'tuṇhissā' or 'tuṇhassā'. 'Distinct' (vavatthita) refers to speaking by separating from the following word, such as 'tuṇhī assā' or 'tuṇha assā'. 'Released' (vimutta) refers to speaking without a nasal sound, by releasing the vocal organs and with the mouth open.

Among those ten types, when 'suṇātu me' should be spoken, changing the 't' to 'th' and saying 'suṇāthu me' is called making a soft sound hard. Similarly, when 'pattakallaṃ, esā ñattī' should be spoken, saying 'patthakallaṃ, esā ñatthī' and so on is the same. When 'bhante saṅgho' should be spoken, changing 'bh' and 'gh' to 'b' and 'g' and saying 'bante saṅgo' is called making a hard sound soft. When 'suṇātu me' should be spoken with an open mouth, but saying 'suṇāṃtu me' or when 'esā ñattī' should be spoken but saying 'esāṃ ñattī' with a nasal sound and the mouth not open is called making a released sound nasal. When 'pattakallaṃ' should be spoken with a nasal sound and the mouth not open, but saying 'pattakallā' with an open mouth and without a nasal sound is called making a nasal sound released.
248:
Thus, in a place where a soft sound (sithila) should be made, making it hard (dhanita); where a hard sound should be made, making it soft; where a released sound (vimutta) should be made, making it nasal (niggahita); and where a nasal sound should be made, making it released—these four types of articulation within a kammavācā spoil the act (kamma). For one who speaks thus speaks a different letter where another should be spoken; he is said to 'pronounce poorly'. However, regarding the remaining six types of articulation such as long (dīgha) and short (rassa), one should perform the kammavācā by speaking the long sound where it is long and the short sound where it is short, exactly as they are established, without destroying the traditional lineage of recitation. If, however, one does not do this and speaks a short sound where a long one should be, or a long sound where a short one should be; likewise, if one speaks a light sound where a heavy one should be, or a heavy sound where a light one should be; or if one speaks a distinct sound where a connected one should be, or a connected sound where a distinct one should be—even if spoken thus, the kammavācā is not invalidated. These six types of articulation do not spoil the act.

The Theras who are experts in the Suttas (Suttantika) say: "The letter 'd' becomes 't', 't' becomes 'd', 'c' becomes 'j', 'j' becomes 'c', 'y' becomes 'k', and 'k' becomes 'y'. Therefore, when 'd' etc. should be spoken, speaking 't' etc. is not contradictory." This statement is not acceptable when it comes to kammavācā. Therefore, a master of the Vinaya (Vinayadhara) must not change 'd' to 't'... ...nor 'k' to 'y'. One should perform the kammavācā by purifying the grammar according to the Pali text and avoiding the aforementioned faults in the ten types of articulation. Otherwise, it is called causing the proclamation (sāvana) to fail.

"Proclaiming at the wrong time" means performing the anussāvana act first without establishing the ñatti (motion) beforehand at a time or occasion that is not suitable for reciting the kammavācā, and only establishing the ñatti afterwards. Thus, through these five ways, acts fail because of the proclamation (anussāvana).

Regarding the failure of the boundary (sīmavipatti), a boundary that cannot accommodate twenty-one monks is called an "extremely small boundary" (atikhuddakasīmā). In the Kurundī commentary, it is said: "A boundary in which twenty-one monks are unable to sit." Therefore, such a boundary, even if consecrated, is not considered consecrated; it is just like village land, and an act performed in that boundary fails. This principle applies to the remaining boundaries as well. Among these, an "extremely large boundary" (atimahatīsīmā) refers to a boundary consecrated exceeding three yojanas even by a hair's breadth. "Broken signs" (khaṇḍanimittā) refers to a boundary with disconnected markers. It is proper to establish it only after announcing the sign in the east, then successively in the south, west, and north, and then announcing again the sign previously announced in the east. If done thus, it is a boundary with unbroken signs (akhaṇḍanimittā).
249:
If the marks (nimitta) are announced in order (starting from the east) and the announcement stops at the north, it is a boundary with broken marks (khaṇḍanimittā). A boundary is also called khaṇḍanimittā if it is designated by making a single mark between two marks, such as a tree with only bark and heartwood (not suitable as a mark), a stump, a mound of earth, or a mound of sand. A boundary designated by using a shadow, such as the shadow of a mountain, as a mark is called a boundary with shadow marks (chāyānimittā). A boundary designated without announcing any marks in any way is called a boundary without marks (animittā).

Designating a boundary while standing outside the boundary means designating it while standing outside the marks after they have been announced. Designating a boundary in a river, ocean, or natural lake means that although a boundary is designated in such places as a river, it is considered not designated because of the Pali text: "Monks, the entire river is not a bound boundary (abaddhasīmā), the entire ocean is not a bound boundary, the entire natural lake is not a bound boundary." Mixing a boundary with another boundary means mixing one's own boundary with the boundary of others. Overlapping means overlapping one's own boundary with the boundary of others. The full details of how mixing and overlapping occur have already been stated in the Uposathakkhandhaka. Thus, these eleven types of boundaries are not bound boundaries (baddhasīmā); they are merely like village territories (gāmakhetta), and a legal act (kamma) performed while sitting in those boundaries fails. Therefore, (the Elder Upāli) said: "By these eleven ways, legal acts fail because of the boundary."

487-488. Regarding the failure of a legal act due to the assembly (parisā), there is nothing that is not clear. The characteristics of being entitled to the act (kammapattalakkhaṇa) and being entitled to give consent (chandārahalakkhaṇa) mentioned in that context have already been stated later in the manner beginning with: "Four monks who are of normal standing (pakatatta) are entitled to the act (kammapatta)." In that statement, "being of normal standing and entitled to the act" means that in a legal act to be performed by a group of four, four monks who are of normal standing, not suspended (ukkhittaka), not expelled from the Sangha, and of pure virtue, are entitled to the act (kammapatta), worthy of the act, suitable, and the masters of the act. Without those four, that act cannot be performed, and neither their consent (chanda) nor their purity (pārisuddhi) comes (to the Sangha). As for the remaining monks, even if they number a thousand, if they are of common communion (samānasaṃvāsaka), they are all entitled to give consent (chandāraha). Whether they come after giving their consent and purity or not, the legal act stands. A person for whom the Sangha performs a legal act such as probation (parivāsa) is neither entitled to the act (kammapatta) nor entitled to give consent (chandāraha). However, because the Sangha performs the act based on that person as the subject (vatthu), he is called "worthy of the act" (kammaraha). The same principle applies to other legal acts.
250:
Furthermore, the method beginning with "four legal acts" (cattāri kammāni) was stated (by the Elder Upāli) to show that individuals such as eunuchs (paṇḍaka) are not suitable subjects (avatthu). The rest of the procedure in this section is clear.

## Apalokanakammakathā

495-496. Now, to show the distinctions among those legal acts, (the Elder Upāli) spoke the words beginning with: "In how many grounds does the act of announcement (apalokanakamma) apply?" In the text: "The act of announcement applies to five grounds—reinstatement (osāraṇa), expulsion (nissāraṇa), shaving of the head (bhaṇḍukamma), brahma-punishment (brahmadaṇḍa), and the characteristic of the act (kammalakkhaṇa) is the fifth," the words "osāraṇa nissāraṇa" are stated in this order for the sake of euphonic phrasing. In reality, expulsion (nissāraṇa) occurs first, and reinstatement (osāraṇa) occurs later.

Among those acts, the destruction by punishment (daṇḍakammanāsanā) performed upon the novice Kaṇṭaka should be known as "expulsion" (nissāraṇa). Therefore, at present, if a novice speaks words of blame against the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Sangha, or points out what is not allowable as allowable, or has wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) endowed with extremist views (antaggāhikadiṭṭhi), that novice should be restrained up to three times and made to renounce that view. If he does not renounce it, the Sangha should be assembled and told, "Renounce it." If he still does not renounce it after being told, a competent monk should perform the act of announcement (apalokanakamma) and expel him from the Sangha. The act should be performed thus:

"Venerable Sirs, I inform the Sangha. This novice named so-and-so is a holder of wrong views who speaks ill of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. So that he may not obtain the right to sleep in the same place for two or three nights with the monks, which other novices obtain, does the Sangha approve of his expulsion?" Thus he should ask. A second and a third time he should ask in the same way. Then (he is expelled with the words): "Hey, you ignorant one, go away, perish!"

If that novice later asks for forgiveness, saying, "Venerable Sirs, I did this because of foolishness, ignorance, and misfortune. I beg forgiveness from the Sangha," he should be made to ask for forgiveness up to three times and then reinstated into the Sangha by the act of announcement (apalokanakamma) itself. He should be reinstated thus: A competent monk in the midst of the Sangha, with the permission of the Sangha, should announce:

"Venerable Sirs, I inform the Sangha. This novice named so-and-so was a holder of wrong views who spoke ill of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. The right to sleep in the same place for two or three nights with the monks, which other novices obtain..."
251:
That novice, who was expelled so as not to share lodgings, now delights in good conduct, lives with humility, has entered the state of a modest person (lajjī), and remains established in shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa). Having performed the prescribed punishment, he confesses his fault. (The monk should ask:) 'Does the Saṅgha approve of granting this novice the harmony of physical association as before?'

This should be announced three times. In this way, the act of announcement (apalokana-kamma) applies to both reinstatement (osāraṇā) and expulsion (nissāraṇā). The act of shaving the head (bhaṇḍu-kamma) has already been mentioned in the commentary on the Mahākhandhaka. The Brahma-punishment (Brahmadaṇḍa) has already been mentioned in the Pañcasatika-khandhaka. However, this Brahma-punishment was not only prescribed for Venerable Channa; if any other monk is harsh-spoken and lives attacking, reviling, and disparaging the monks with ill-spoken words, the Brahma-punishment should also be imposed on him. And it should be imposed in this way: a competent monk, with the permission of the Saṅgha, should inform the Saṅgha in its midst:

'Venerable Sirs, the monk named so-and-so is harsh-spoken; he lives attacking the monks with ill-spoken words. Let that monk say whatever he wishes. The monks should neither speak to, nor admonish, nor instruct this monk named so-and-so. Venerable Sirs, I ask the Saṅgha: Does the Saṅgha approve of the imposition of the Brahma-punishment on the monk named so-and-so?' For a second time I ask, for a third time I ask: 'Venerable Sirs, does the Saṅgha approve of the imposition of the Brahma-punishment on the monk named so-and-so?'

When that monk later conducts himself well and asks for forgiveness, the Brahma-punishment should be revoked. And it should be revoked in this way: a competent monk should inform the Saṅgha in its midst:

'Venerable Sirs, the Saṅgha of monks imposed the Brahma-punishment on the monk named so-and-so. That monk, delighting in good conduct, living with humility, has entered the state of a modest person and remains established in shame and fear of wrongdoing. Having reflected, he remains in future restraint. Venerable Sirs, I ask the Saṅgha: Does the Saṅgha approve of the revocation of the Brahma-punishment for that monk?'

Having announced this three times, the Brahma-punishment should be revoked by the act of announcement (apalokana-kamma) itself.

The fifth, known as 'kamma-lakkhaṇa' (characterized by the act), refers to the matter which the Blessed One taught in the Bhikkhunī-khandhaka: 'At that time, the group-of-six monks, intending "If only they would be infatuated with us," poured muddy water on the bhikkhunīs, and exposing their bodies to the bhikkhunīs...'
252:
(The monks) exposed their thighs to the bhikkhunīs, exposed their genitals to the bhikkhunīs, mocked the bhikkhunīs, and associated with the bhikkhunīs, intending 'If only they would be infatuated with us.' Regarding these matters, the Blessed One prescribed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for those monks and said: 'Bhikkhus, that monk should be made one who is not to be saluted (avandiya) by the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha.'
