Then the bhikkhunīs thought: 'What kind of punishment should be performed?' They reported this matter to the Blessed One, who said: 'Bhikkhus, that monk should be made one who is not to be saluted (avandiya) by the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha.' Thus, the act of non-salutation (avandiya-kamma) was authorized. This act of non-salutation is the fifth case of 'kamma-lakkhaṇa' (characterized by the act) of this apalokana-kamma. For its characteristic is the act (kamma) itself, not reinstatement (osāraṇā) and so forth; therefore, it is called 'kamma-lakkhaṇa.' The performance of that act was taught in that very place (the Bhikkhunī-khandhaka). However, I shall also speak of it here to show it in detail along with its revocation. By the agreement of the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha assembled at the nunnery, a competent bhikkhunī should announce:

'Ladies, this venerable one named so-and-so displays unseemly behavior to the bhikkhunīs. I ask the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha: Does it approve of making this venerable one one who is not to be saluted?' For a second time... for a third time I ask the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha.

Having announced this three times, the act of non-salutation should be performed by the act of announcement (apalokana-kamma). From then on, that monk should not be saluted by the bhikkhunīs. If that monk, while not being saluted, arouses shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa) and conducts himself well, he should ask the bhikkhunīs for forgiveness. When asking for forgiveness, he should not go to the nunnery but, in the monastery itself, approach the Saṅgha, a group, or a single monk, and having sat in a squatting position and raised his joined palms (añjali), he should ask for forgiveness, saying: 'Venerable Sirs, having reflected, I remain in future restraint; I will not display unseemly behavior again. May the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha forgive me.' That Saṅgha or group should send a monk, or if he asked a single monk, that monk himself should go and say to the bhikkhunīs: 'This monk, having reflected, remains in future restraint. This monk, having confessed his fault, has asked the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha for forgiveness. May the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha make this monk one who is to be saluted (vandiya).' He should then be made one who is to be saluted. And it should be done in this way: by the agreement of the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha assembled at the nunnery, a competent bhikkhunī should announce:

'Ladies, the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha previously made this venerable one named so-and-so one who is not to be saluted, saying that he displays unseemly behavior to the bhikkhunīs. That venerable one, having entered the state of modesty, having reflected, remains in future restraint, and having confessed his fault...'
253:
“I have informed the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha to forgive; does the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha approve of performing the act of paying homage to this venerable one?”—this must be said three times. Only through such an apalokana-kamma (act of announcement) should the act of paying homage be performed.

In this matter, this is the decision on the characteristics of the act (kamma-lakkhaṇa) which is outside the Pāḷi text. Although this kamma-lakkhaṇa was prescribed based on the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, it is also applicable to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. Whatever apalokana-kamma the Bhikkhu Saṅgha performs at the place for distributing voting tickets, the place for congee, the place for meals, or the place for Uposatha, that too is a kamma-lakkhaṇa.

For those whose robes have been stolen (by robbers), whose robes are worn out, or whose robes are lost, the Saṅgha should be assembled, and a competent monk, having informed them up to three times and performed the apalokana-kamma, should give the robes. A monk who distributes small items (appamattaka-vissajjaka) can give needles and such, as described in the Senāsanakkhandhaka, to a monk making robes even without performing apalokana-kamma. In giving such needles, etc., that monk alone has authority. If he wishes to give items exceeding that, he must do so after performing apalokana-kamma. For in giving items beyond that, only the Saṅgha is the owner (master).

Medicine for the sick can also be given by oneself as described in that Senāsanakkhandhaka. For a monk who desires medicine beyond that, it must be given after performing apalokana-kamma. For a greatly ill monk (mahāgilāna) who is weak, or whose physical movements are impaired, or whose alms-round path is cut off, if one wishes to give a nāḷi (measure) of rice daily, or half a nāḷi, or five or ten nāḷis of rice in a single day from the produce of a large monastery, it must be given only after performing apalokana-kamma.

It is proper to give through apalokana-kamma the payment of a troublesome debt for a virtuous and beloved monk from the monastery's produce; or non-removable monastery bedding and furniture for a learned monk who carries the burden of the Saṅgha; or food provisions for those such as kappiya-kārakas (lay attendants) who are performing the duties of the Saṅgha.

It is proper to have the communal (saṅghika) monastery repaired using monastery produce donated for the sake of the four requisites. However, to prevent the criticism that “this monk is managing as if he were the owner,” he should have it repaired only after asking permission from the Saṅgha at the place for distributing voting tickets, etc., or at an intermediate assembly. Even from produce specifically donated for the sake of robes and alms-food, the monastery should be repaired after performing apalokana-kamma. Although it is proper even without apalokana-kamma, to cut off the criticism that “this monk is very bold in having the monastery repaired from produce donated for robes and alms-food,” it should be repaired only after performing apalokana-kamma.
254:
At a shrine (cetiya), one who builds a new umbrella (chatta), a railing (vedikā), a Bodhi-tree house (bodhighara), or a throne-house (āsanaghara) that has not yet been built, or one who repairs what is worn out, or one who performs plasterwork, should do so by encouraging people. If there is no one to do it, it should be done from the property deposited for the shrine. If there is no deposited property, it should be done from the produce of that monastery or with communal (saṅghika) property after performing apalokana-kamma. With communal property, it is proper to perform the work for the shrine after asking permission. However, with the property of the shrine, it is not proper to perform communal (saṅghika) work even if permission is asked. But it is proper to take it temporarily and then restore it to its original state.

Monks performing plasterwork, etc., at a shrine, if they do not receive even enough food for sustenance from the alms-round or from the Saṅgha, it is proper for them to take just enough for sustenance from the shrine's property and consume it while performing their duties. It is not proper to provide a meal for the Saṅgha with fish, meat, etc., using the excuse “we are performing the duties.” Regarding fruit-bearing trees planted in the monastery which have been taken possession of by the Saṅgha and receive care, and whose fruits are distributed and consumed after striking the bell, apalokana-kamma need not be performed for those trees. If they are trees not yet taken possession of, apalokana-kamma should be performed. That apalokana-kamma may be performed at the places for distributing voting tickets, drinking congee, or eating meals, and at intermediate assemblies. It is especially proper at the Uposatha hall. Because at the Uposatha hall, the consent (chanda) and purity (pārisuddhi) of monks who have not arrived are brought, therefore that apalokana-kamma is well-purified.

And it should be done in this way: a competent monk, with the approval of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, should announce:

“Venerable Sirs, within the precinct (upacāra-sīmā) of this monastery, there are roots, bark, leaves, shoots, flowers, fruits, and edibles, etc., belonging to the Saṅgha. Does the Saṅgha approve that all these may be consumed by all monks who come and go as they please? Thus I ask the Saṅgha.” This should be asked three times.

An apalokana-kamma performed by four or five monks is indeed well-performed. In a monastery where two or three people reside, the apalokana-kamma performed by those monks sitting together is just like one performed by the Saṅgha. In a monastery where there is only one monk, the agreement (katikavatta) made by that monk while sitting after performing the preliminary duties (pubbakaraṇa-pubbakicca) on the Uposatha day is also just like one made by the Saṅgha.
255:
## 
It is permissible for a monk making a formal agreement (katika) to do so according to the fruiting season, or by defining a period such as four months, six months, or a year, or even without defining a specific period. If a period is defined, the agreement must be renewed after consuming the fruits according to that definition. If no period is defined, it remains valid for as long as the trees exist. If other trees are planted from the seeds of those trees, the same agreement applies to them as well.

However, if they are planted in another monastery, the Saṅgha of that monastery where they are planted is the owner. For trees planted later in the original monastery using seeds brought from elsewhere, a new agreement must be made. Once the agreement is made, they stand as personal property; it is permissible to consume the fruits and so on as one pleases. If, in that monastery, various areas are fenced off to create private enclosures (pariveṇa) and are cared for, they stand as the personal property of those monks. Others do not have the right to consume them; however, those monks should consume them after giving a tenth portion to the Saṅgha. The same rule applies to a monk who protects a tree in the middle of the monastery by surrounding it with branches.

When a venerable monk who is worthy of respect arrives at an old monastery, people bring various fruits, saying, "The Elder has arrived." If a learned monk who has mastered the entire Pariyatti (scriptures) previously resided there, one should consume the fruit without hesitation, thinking, "Surely, a long-standing agreement must have been made here." Fruits in a monastery are also permissible for those who observe the dhutaṅga of alms-round; it does not violate their ascetic practice. Novices (sāmaṇeras) give many fruits to their own teachers and preceptors; other monks, not receiving any, may complain, but this is merely a matter of complaint.

If there is a famine and about sixty people depend on a single jackfruit tree for survival, at such a time, the fruit should be distributed and eaten for the sake of supporting everyone; this is the proper practice (sāmīci). As long as the agreement is not rescinded, the consumption by those monks is indeed well-consumed. When is an agreement rescinded? It is when the harmonious Saṅgha assembles and announces, "From today onwards, let them distribute and eat." In a monastery with only one monk, the previous agreement is rescinded even if announced by that single monk. If, after the agreement is rescinded, the novices neither pluck fruits from the trees nor pick them up from the ground to give to the monks, but instead wander about kicking the fallen fruits with their feet, they should be encouraged by being given a share ranging from a tenth portion up to half of the fruit. Surely, out of greed for such increase, they will bring and give them.
256:
## 
(The novices) will bring and give the fruits. When food becomes abundant again and lay-attendants (kappiyakārakas) come to protect the trees by fencing them with branches and so on, the novices should not be given an extra share; the fruits should only be consumed after distribution.

Hearing that "there are various fruits in the monastery," people from nearby villages come for the sake of the sick or pregnant women and beg, "Give us a coconut, give us a mango, give us a breadfruit." If they ask thus, should it be given or not? It should be given. For if it is not given, they become displeased. The monk who gives should assemble the Saṅgha and give only after performing the act of notification (apalokana-kamma) by announcing it three times. Alternatively, a formal agreement (katika) should be established. It should be done in this way: a competent monk, with the consent of the Saṅgha, should announce:

"People from nearby villages come and beg for fruits for the sick and others. Does it please the Saṅgha not to prohibit those taking two coconuts, two palmyra fruits, two jackfruits, five mangoes, or five bananas, and not to prohibit those taking fruit from such and such trees?" This should be stated three times.

From then on, one should not say "Take them" to those who beg in the name of the sick and others, but should only explain the rule: "It has been arranged not to prohibit those taking coconuts and so on within this limit, or those taking fruit from such and such trees." One should not follow them and say, "This mango tree has sweet fruit; take from here." At the time of fruit distribution, a monk appointed (by the Saṅgha) should give a half-share to those who arrive; if he is not appointed, he should give after asking permission from the Saṅgha.

If a traveler whose provisions are exhausted, a caravan leader, or some other person of authority comes and begs, it should be given only after asking permission. If someone takes and eats by force, they should not be prevented. For if he is angry, he might cut down the trees or cause other harm. To one who comes to a private enclosure and begs in the name of the sick, one should say, "We have planted these for shade and such; if there is fruit, you know (what to do)." If the trees are heavily laden with fruit and they eat according to the fruiting turn while the trees are fenced with thorns, it should be given by one who is without expectation. One who takes by force should not be prevented; the reason here is the same as stated previously.
257:
If the Saṅgha possesses a fruit orchard and there is no one to look after it, if someone looks after it as a matter of duty, that orchard belongs only to the Saṅgha. Alternatively, if the Saṅgha assigns the responsibility to a capable monk, saying, "Good man, please look after this orchard," and that monk looks after it as a matter of duty, it likewise belongs only to the Saṅgha. However, for a monk who desires development (phātikamma), it is given for development with a share of one-third or one-half. If he does not wish to look after it for that much, saying, "This task is very heavy," then it should be said, "Make everything as if it were your own property, and look after it while giving only a tenth part as the base share to the Saṅgha." However, because it is heavy property (garubhaṇḍa), it must not be given away by way of absolute transfer (mūlaccHejja). If that monk, while enjoying the fruits and giving the base share, builds a new monastery or maintains an existing one and hands over the orchard to his disciples, those disciples must also give the base share. When the monks themselves are able to look after it, the permission to look after it must not be given to those disciples. They should not be prohibited when the fruits have already appeared after they have looked after it; they should only be prohibited when they are just beginning to make an effort to look after it. It should be said, "You have already consumed many fruits; do not look after it anymore, the Bhikkhu Saṅgha itself will look after it."

If there is no one looking after it by way of duty, nor by way of development (phātikamma), and the Saṅgha is unable to look after it, and someone looks after it without asking, increases the profit, and desires it, it is given by making a development through the act of announcement (apalokanakamma). Thus, all of this is the characteristic of the act (kamma). The act of announcement (apalokanakamma) applies to these five instances.

In the variety of the bases for the act of motion (ñattikamma): "Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This person named [Name] is the candidate for ordination of the venerable [Name]. I have instructed him. If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, let the candidate named [Name] come." Having made this motion, saying "Come," such admission of a candidate for ordination into the Saṅgha is called Osāraṇā (Admission).

"Venerable Sirs, listen to me. This monk named [Name] is a Dhamma-preacher. Neither the Sutta nor the Sutta-vibhaṅga comes to him. Without considering the meaning, he obstructs the meaning with the shadow of the words. If it is suitable to the venerable ones, let us cause this monk named [Name] to leave, and the rest of us shall settle this legal issue." Thus, in the Ubbāhikā decision, the removal of a Dhamma-preacher monk from the Saṅgha is called Nissāraṇā (Removal).

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. Today is the fifteenth-day Uposatha. If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha." Thus, the motion set forth by way of the act of Uposatha is called Uposatha.
258:
"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. Today is the fifteenth-day Pavāraṇā. If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Pavāraṇā." Thus, the motion set forth by way of the act of Pavāraṇā is called the Pavāraṇā motion.

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This person named [Name] is the candidate for ordination of the venerable [Name]. If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, I shall instruct this person named [Name]." "If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, let this person named [Name] instruct this person named [Name]." "If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, I shall question this person named [Name] regarding the obstructive factors." "If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, let this person named [Name] question this person named [Name] regarding the obstructive factors." "If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, I shall question this person named [Name] regarding the Vinaya." "If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, let this person named [Name] question this person named [Name] regarding the Vinaya." "If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, I, being questioned regarding the Vinaya by this person named [Name], shall answer." "If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, let this person named [Name], being questioned regarding the Vinaya by this person named [Name], answer." Thus, the motion set forth to authorize oneself or another is called the Sammuti (Authorization) motion.

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This robe is a Nissaggiya (forfeiture) robe of the monk named [Name], which has been forfeited to the Saṅgha. If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this robe to the monk named [Name]." "If it is suitable to the venerable ones, let the venerable ones give this robe to the monk named [Name]." Thus, the giving of forfeited robes, bowls, and so on is called the Dāna (Giving) motion.

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named [Name] remembers his offense, reveals it, makes it manifest, and confesses it. If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, I shall accept the offense of the monk named [Name]." "If it is suitable to the venerable ones, I shall accept the offense of the monk named [Name]." The monk accepting the offense must ask, "Do you see it?" The other must answer, "Yes, I see it." The former should say, "Restrain yourself in the future." Thus, the acceptance of an offense is called the Paṭiggaha (Acceptance) motion.

"Venerable ones who are residents, listen to me. If it is suitable to the venerable ones, let us now perform the Uposatha, let us recite the Pātimokkha, and let us perform the Pavāraṇā at the coming time." Monks, if those monks who are makers of quarrels, makers of strife, makers of disputes, makers of idle talk, and makers of legal issues in the Saṅgha should reside together at that time, the resident monk who is experienced and capable must inform the resident monks: "Venerable ones who are residents, listen to me..."
259:
When it is suitable for the venerable ones, saying, 'Let us now perform the Uposatha, let us recite the Pātimokkha, let us postpone the Pavāraṇā until the coming waxing moon phase'—such a postponement of the Pavāraṇā is called 'Paccukkaḍḍhanā'.

All monks must assemble together. Having assembled, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha: 'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. While we have been living in strife, quarreling, and disputing, we have committed many things unbecoming of monks, both in speech and in physical transgression. If we were to deal with one another regarding these offenses, it might lead to harshness, malice, and schism in the Saṅgha. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha settle this legal issue by means of the Tiṇavatthāraka-samatha (settlement by covering with grass), except for grave offenses (thullavajja) and those connected with the laity.' The 'Sabbasaṅgāhika-ñatti' (all-inclusive motion), which is the first of all motions performed by this Tiṇavatthāraka-samatha, is known as the 'Kamma-lakkhaṇa' (characteristic of the act).

Similarly, following that Sabbasaṅgāhika-ñatti, two motions are made, one for each side. Thus, the Ñatti-kamma (formal motion) reaches these nine instances, including the aforementioned types such as Osāraṇā (reinstatement), Nissāraṇā (expulsion), and so on, up to the ninth Kamma-lakkhaṇa.

Regarding the different instances of the Ñatti-dutiya-kamma (a motion with one resolution): Nissāraṇā (expulsion) as taught in the Khandhaka by way of Pattanikkujjana (turning over the bowl) regarding Vaḍḍha the Licchavi, and Osāraṇā (reinstatement) as taught by way of Pattukkujjana (turning the bowl upright) for the same person, should be understood.

Sammuti (authorization) should be understood by way of these authorizations: Sīmā-sammuti (authorization of a boundary), Ti-cīvarena-avippavāsa-sammuti (authorization to be not separated from the three robes), Santhata-sammuti (authorization for a rug), and the authorizations for: Bhattuddesaka (meal-allocator), Senāsanaggāhāpaka (lodging-assigner), Bhaṇḍāgārika (storekeeper), Cīvarapaṭiggāhaka (robe-receiver), Cīvarabhājaka (robe-distributor), Yāgubhājaka (congee-distributor), Phalabhājaka (fruit-distributor), Khajjabhājaka (food-distributor), Appamattakavissajjaka (disposer of minor items), Sāṭiyaggāhāpaka (undergarment-assigner), Pattaggāhāpaka (bowl-assigner), Ārāmika-pesaka (attendant-sender), and Sāmaṇera-pesaka (novice-sender). Dāna (giving) should be understood by way of Kathina-cīvara-dāna (giving of the Kathina robe) and Mataka-cīvara-dāna (giving of robes on behalf of the deceased).

Uddhāra (withdrawal) should be understood by way of Kathinuḍḍhāra (withdrawal of the Kathina). Desanā (designation) should be understood by way of designating the site for a hut (kuṭivatthu) or a monastery (vihāravatthu). Regarding the Tiṇavatthāraka-samatha, excluding the three motions—namely the Sabbasaṅgāhika-ñatti and the one motion for each side—the Kamma-lakkhaṇa should be understood by way of the two Ñatti-dutiya-kammavācā (motions with one resolution), one for each side. Thus, the Ñatti-dutiya-kamma reaches these seven instances.
260:
Regarding the different instances of the Ñatti-catuttha-kamma (a motion with three resolutions): Nissāraṇā (expulsion) should be understood by way of the seven disciplinary acts beginning with Tajjanīya-kamma (act of censure), and Osāraṇā (reinstatement) by way of the revocation (paṭippassambhana) of those same acts. Sammuti (authorization) should be understood by way of the Bhikkhunovādaka-sammuti (authorization of an exhorter of nuns). Dāna (giving) should be understood by way of granting Parivāsa (probation) and Mānatta (penance). Niggaha (restraint) should be understood by way of the Mūlāyapaṭikassana-kamma (act of sending back to the beginning). Samanubhāsanā (formal admonition) should be understood by way of these eleven formal admonitions: 'The eight followers of the suspended one, the monk Ariṭṭha, and the nun Caṇḍakāḷī—these are the ones subject to three admonitions.' Kamma-lakkhaṇa (characteristic of the act) should be understood by way of Upasampadā-kamma (act of ordination) and Abbhāna-kamma (act of rehabilitation). Thus, the Ñatti-catuttha-kamma reaches these seven instances.

Having thus shown the acts (kamma), the failure of acts (kamma-vipatti), and the various instances of acts free from failure, the author now says 'Catu-vagga-karaṇe kamme' etc., to show the definition of the Saṅgha that performs those acts. The meaning of those words should be understood in the same manner as explained in the section on the failure of acts due to the assembly (parisa).

## The Commentary on the Kamma-vagga is finished.

## Commentary on the Atthavasa-vagga and others

Now, to show the benefits of the laying down of the training rules (sikkhāpada) which are the basis for those acts, the author begins with 'Dve atthavase paṭicca' etc. In that passage, 'diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ verānaṃ saṃvarāya' means for the sake of restraining (closing off) the five types of enmity/danger pertaining to the present life, such as killing (pāṇātipāta) and so on. 'Samparāyikānaṃ verānaṃ paṭighātāya' means for the sake of removing, completely cutting off, and preventing the arising of enmities pertaining to the future life, which are known as the suffering of the result (vipāka-dukkha). 'Diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ vajjānaṃ saṃvarāya' means for the sake of restraining those same five enmities. 'Samparāyikānaṃ vajjānaṃ' refers to those same sufferings of the result. Indeed, in this context, the sufferings of the result are called 'vajja' (faults/offenses) because they are things to be avoided. 'Diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ bhayānaṃ' refers to blame, accusation, the performance of acts such as Tajjanīya-kamma, the suspension of the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, and the act of proclaiming ill-repute. These are called dangers pertaining to the present life; [the training rules are] for the sake of restraining these. Dangers pertaining to the future life are simply the sufferings of the result; [the training rules are] for the sake of removing them. 'Diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ akusalānaṃ' means...
261:
(The training rules are prescribed) for the sake of restraint from the five enmities and the ten varieties of unwholesome courses of action (akusalakamma-patha). They are called 'future unwholesome deeds' because of the sense that one cannot endure the resultant sufferings; (the rules are prescribed) for the sake of dispelling those unwholesome deeds. 'For the sake of compassion for the laity' means for the sake of showing compassion by protecting the faith of the householders. 'For the sake of cutting off the factions of those with evil desires' means the Gaṇabhojana Sikkhāpada (training rule on group meals) was prescribed for the sake of breaking up the formation of groups by persons with evil desires. The rest of the text is clear in meaning. Everything that should be said here has already been stated in the commentary on the first Pārājika.

## The explanation of the training rules by way of benefit is finished.

In the passages beginning with 'Pātimokkha,' the recitation of the Pātimokkha (Pātimokkhuddesa) is of five kinds for monks and four kinds for bhikkhunīs. In the passages beginning with 'granting of probation (parivāsa),' 'the act of reinstatement (osāraṇīya) is prescribed' means that for a monk who is observing the 18 duties or the 43 duties, the act of reinstatement (into the Saṅgha) is prescribed. It means the legal act by which one is reinstated is prescribed. 'The act of removal (nissāraṇīya) is prescribed' means the legal act by which quarrelsome persons and others are removed (from the Saṅgha) is prescribed.

In the passages beginning with 'Apaññatta' (not prescribed), 'prescribing what was not yet prescribed' refers to the prescribing of a training rule that had not been prescribed by anyone in the intervening period, excluding the seven groups of offenses and the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa. The Vinītakathā, such as the Makkaṭi-vatthu (Monkey Story), is called 'subsequent prescription' (anupaññatti) after the training rule has already been prescribed. The rest of the text is clear in meaning.

## The explanation of the Ānisaṃsa Chapter is finished.

Now, in order to show the ninefold summary (saṅgaha) of all training rules by way of each individual aspect, the passage beginning with 'Nava Saṅgahā' is stated. Therein, 'Vatthu-saṅgaha' means summary by basis (vatthu). In this manner, the meaning of the remaining terms should be understood. The connection of the meaning here is as follows: Since there is not even a single training rule prescribed for a matter that is not a basis (avatthu), all training rules are summarized by basis; thus, Vatthu-saṅgaha should be understood first.
262:
Because two groups of offenses are included in failure in virtue (sīla-vipatti), five groups of offenses are included in failure in conduct (ācāra-vipatti), and six training rules are included in failure in livelihood (ājīva-vipatti), therefore all training rules are summarized by failure (vipatti); thus, Vipatti-saṅgaha should be understood.

Because there is not even a single training rule that is free from the seven classes of offenses, therefore all training rules are summarized by offense (āpatti); thus, Āpatti-saṅgaha should be understood.

Because all training rules were prescribed in the seven cities (such as Vesālī, etc.), they are summarized by origin/location (nidāna); thus, Nidāna-saṅgaha should be understood.

Because there is not even a single training rule prescribed without a person who transgresses, therefore all training rules are summarized by person (puggala); thus, Puggala-saṅgaha should be understood.

All training rules are summarized by the five groups of offenses and the seven groups of offenses. All training rules do not arise without the six origins (samuṭṭhāna), therefore they are summarized by origin. All training rules are summarized by the legal issue of offenses (āpattādhikaraṇa) among the four types of legal issues (adhikaraṇa). All training rules reach settlement through the seven ways of settling (samatha), therefore they are summarized by settlement. Thus, in this Summary Chapter (Saṅgaha-vagga), the summaries by way of group (khandha), origin (samuṭṭhāna), legal issue (adhikaraṇa), and settlement (samatha) should also be understood. The rest of the arrangement follows the method already stated.

## In the Vinaya Commentary named Samantapāsādikā,
## The explanation of the Nava-saṅgahita Chapter is finished.
## The explanation of the obscure terms of the Parivāra is also finished.
263:
## Concluding Remarks
By this much of the sequence of words (to conclude):
The Lord, the Refuge of the world of beings, the Victorious One who conquered the five Māras, while disciplining the host of beings worthy of discipline, taught the Vinaya Piṭaka, which is the teaching analyzed into the Two Vibhaṅgas, the Khandhakas, and the Parivāra. The commentary on that Vinaya Piṭaka, named Samantapāsādikā, has been completed with a textual extent of slightly more than twenty-seven thousand ganthas.

In the quality of this Samantapāsādikā commentary being 'completely pleasing' (samantapāsādika), there are these reasons:
Because it has come down from the lineage of teachers; because it illustrates the various origins and stories; because it avoids the doctrines of others; because it purifies its own doctrine; because it cleanses the syllables and letters; because it shows the meaning of terms; because it shows the order of the Pali arrangement; because it decides the training rules; and because it shows the various methods of the Vibhaṅga.

Because there is nothing that is not pleasing to the wise who look into this commentary, and because it was explained by (the Venerable Buddhaghosa) who is skilled in disciplining those worthy of discipline through the Vinaya teaching taught by the Lord of the World, who has compassion for the world, the wise call this commentary 'Samantapāsādikā.'

Having studied and learned from the presence of the Elder who is famous by the name Buddhamitta, who is renowned, skilled in the Vinaya, and wise, these three Sinhalese commentaries: the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, the Mahāpaccari, and the Kurundī.

There is the great monastery, the Mahāvihāra, situated on a portion of the ground in the Mahāmeghavana garden, adorned with the (Southern Branch of the) Great Bodhi tree of the Teacher. To the south of that Mahāvihāra, there is the noble precinct named Padhānaghara, frequented by the community of monks who possess pure conduct and virtue.

(The lay devotee known as Mahānigamasāmī), born of a noble family, who always serves the Saṅgha, and who has clear faith in the Triple Gem without confusion (is the one who requested this work).
264:
## Conclusion of the Work

(The lay devotee) renowned as 'Mahānigamasāmi', (who was born of a noble family, who constantly serves the Saṅgha, and has faith in the Triple Gem), caused to be built in that (precinct named Padhānaghara) a delightful palace surrounded by a beautiful wall.

In that palace, which is endowed with cool shady trees and excellent ponds, (I) residing there—

Have undertaken this Vinaya Commentary (Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā), complete with decisions on meanings and purposes, dedicated to the Elder named Buddhasiri, who is of pure virtue and conduct.

Of King Siripāla, the abode of glory and of great retinue, who protects the whole of Laṅkādīpa without any danger—

This (Vinaya Commentary), which was commenced in the 20th auspicious Jaya year (of his reign), has reached completion upon reaching the 21st year.

Just as this (Vinaya Commentary) reached its conclusion in only one year without any obstacles, even though the world was troubled with dangers,

So may all the efforts of all people in the world, which are associated with the Dhamma, reach completion quickly and without any danger.

By me, who has composed this (Vinaya Commentary) for the sake of the long endurance of the Dispensation, having great reverence for the True Dhamma, whatever merit has been accumulated—

By the power of all that merit, may all living beings be able to partake of the taste of the True Dhamma of the Buddha, the King of Dhamma.

May the True Dhamma endure for a long time. May the rain fall in due season. May the clouds (deva) satisfy all beings for a long time. May the King protect the earth righteously.

Adorned with extremely pure faith, wisdom, and energy; endowed with a collection of virtues such as virtue (sīla), conduct (ācāra), uprightness, and gentleness; capable of penetrating with wisdom the depths of his own and other doctrines; possessed of sharp wisdom; having unimpeded power of knowledge in the Buddha’s Dispensation regarding the various aspects of the Tipitaka scriptures together with the commentaries; being a great grammarian; possessed of the beauty of sweet and noble speech arising from the perfection of the vocal organs; a speaker of appropriate and liberated speech; the best of speakers; a great poet; surrounded by the retinue of the various analytical insights (paṭisambhidā); adorned with qualities such as the six higher powers (abhiññā)...
265:
...being an ornament to the lineage of the Elders residing in the Mahāvihāra, who are lamps of the Theravāda lineage and whose wisdom is well-established in the superhuman states (jhāna, magga, phala); possessed of vast and pure wisdom; the Elder who bears the name "Buddhaghosa" given by the venerable teachers—by him, this Vinaya Commentary named Samantapāsādikā was composed—

As long as the very name "Buddha" of the Great Sage (Mahesi), the Chief of the World, who is of pure mind and possessed of the quality of equanimity (tādi), exists in the world,

May this (work) remain in the world, showing the method of the purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi) to the sons of noble families who seek liberation from the world.

## The Vinaya Commentary named
## Samantapāsādikā is finished.
